## **Marketing authorisation** 

An application for MA (centralised process) was made to the European Medicines Agency on 29 August 2014. The Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) recommended a positive opinion for the MA for evolocumab in the treatment of primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia on 22 May 2015. The European Commission approved the MA for evolocumab in all European Union Member States on July 21 2015. The anticipated date of availability in the UK is August 2015. Evolocumab is not currently approved outside of the EU; regulatory reviews are ongoing.

## **Approved indication in primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia:** 

- Evolocumab is indicated in adults with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) or mixed dyslipidaemia, as an adjunct to diet: 

- in combination with a statin or statin with other lipid-lowering therapies in patients unable to reach LDL-C goals with the maximum tolerated dose of a statin 

- alone or in combination with other lipid-lowering therapies in patients who are statinintolerant, or for whom a statin is contraindicated 

The effect of evolocumab on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality has not yet been determined. 

Before finalising this indication and during the CHMP review of the evolocumab MA application, only one ‘major objection’ was raised, which regarded the proposed target population. The CHMP expressed concern around the clinical significance of the evolocumab lipid-lowering effects, which it deemed to be uncertain in the absence of a proven CV benefit, and what it deemed to be insufficient data to establish long-term safety (including safety in patients achieving very low LDL-C levels). It suggested, therefore, that the target population should be restricted to patients at high risk of a CV event (Day 120 list of questions). Further to Amgen’s response to the list of questions and an oral explanation at Day 180, the CHMP agreed (with a of vote 26 to 6) that a MA could be granted provided that the indication was revised to reinforce the second-line use by adding language related to use after maximally-tolerated statins. 

It is noted that there are no special conditions attached to the MA. Please refer to Appendix I for a copy of the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) for evolocumab. 

## **Health technology assessments** 

Evolocumab will be subject to health technology assessment (HTA) by the Scottish Medicines Consortium (SMC) in accordance with their remit to assess newly licensed medicines. We anticipate submitting a New Product Assessment Form for evolocumab in September to October 2015, and anticipate publication of SMC advice in early 2016 in accordance with their timelines and submission scheduling process.

## _**2.4 Changes in service provision and management**_ 

Evolocumab is anticipated to be used in patients who remain at high CV risk despite treatment with conventional lipid-lowering therapy (i.e. statin and/or other lipid-lowering therapies in addition to diet and lifestyle advice). High CV risk patients include patients with or without existing CVD and in whom LDL-C levels remain unacceptably high, and those with confirmed or suspected familial hypercholesterolaemia (identified through clinical assessment or through cascade screening). The high-risk nature of these patients means that they are easily identifiable (e.g. without existing CVD but at high residual risk due to other concomitant conditions such as diabetes) and warrant referral to specialist secondary care lipid clinics or risk review clinics, where their lipid profiles can be rigorously optimised. It is in these secondary care clinics where combinations of lipid-lowering therapies are optimised, drug intolerance (to e.g. statins) can be addressed, and additional investigations or advance treatments can be considered (e.g. family cascade screening in FH, lipoprotein apheresis). Therefore, it is in such secondary care clinics that we anticipate evolocumab (a novel lipid-lowering therapy) will be initiated, followed up, and managed until the point at which it is deemed clinically appropriate to discharge to primary care for ongoing monitoring thereafter. It is anticipated that evolocumab will be commissioned by clinical commissioning groups because the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia (except HoFH) is not currently within the scope of specialised commissioning through NHS England. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 97 -->

No additional tests or investigations for selection of patients appropriate for evolocumab, or any additional monitoring, will be required over and above those which are part of routine clinical practice. Requirements for general ongoing monitoring (secondary and primary care settings) associated with the management of hypercholesterolaemia with lipid-lowering therapies (efficacy and adverse events) are described in Section 5.5. Further, with respect to method of administration, evolocumab is intended for patient self-administration after proper training, as outlined in the SmPC (Appendix I). Evolocumab will be available as a prefilled pen or syringe to facilitate self-administration. Costs associated with patient training to allow self-administration are detailed in Section 5.5. If required, administration of evolocumab can also be performed by an individual who has been trained to administer the product (e.g. a healthcare professional or carer). 

No additional infrastructure will be required to support the use of evolocumab. Patient training for self-administration through a healthcare professional (e.g. nurse) will be required at the outset. Further, as specified in the SmPC (Appendix I), no additional concomitant therapies are required to be administered with evolocumab. 

## _**2.5 Innovation**_ 

Evolocumab is an innovative, first-in-class therapy with a novel, targeted mechanism of action and convenient two-weekly or monthly subcutaneous self-administration, without the need for dose adjustment. Four robust phase 3 RCTs demonstrated that evolocumab provided consistent and intensive reductions in LDL-C of up to approximately 72% compared with placebo and up to approximately 46% compared with ezetimibe, in addition to any background lipid-lowering therapies patients were receiving e.g. statins. These reductions were consistent regardless of patient population and patient characteristics (including risk or presence of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia); dosing regimen; and presence and type of background lipid-lowering therapy. Supplementary evidence from ongoing, long-term extension studies showed that this reduction was maintained for more than 2 years. Analyses of the safety and tolerability data from individual studies and an integrated data set of over 6,000 patients (representing 7,235 patient-years of exposure) show that evolocumab has a favourable safety and tolerability profile. The type and incidence of adverse events observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations < 0.6 mmol/L and < 1.0 mmol/L were generally similar to those observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations ≥ 1.0 mmol/L. Antievolocumab antibodies were infrequent, non-neutralising, and not associated with clinically relevant adverse events. Further, exploratory safety data from the long-term extension studies suggest that evolocumab is associated with a reduction in CV events of approximately 50%, which is consistent with that predicted (per CTTC) given the magnitude of its LDL-C lowering. 

The robust and long-term effects of evolocumab on LDL-C and other lipids, combined with its favourable safety and tolerability profile, demonstrate that evolocumab represents a major clinical advancement and revolutionary step-change in the management of primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia. Evolocumab will, for the first time, enable clinicians to provide high-risk patients who would otherwise remain vulnerable to CV events (because of inadequate LDL-C reduction with

## **3 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway** 

- CVD is the largest cause of death in the UK; in 2013 a third of all deaths (approximately 192,000 annually or 500 per day) were estimated to be attributable to CVD, including approximately 99,000 due to CHD and 34,000 due to ischaemic stroke. The Department of Health CVD Outcomes Strategy has recognised that England underperforms when compared with similar countries in terms of CV mortality. Preventing premature mortality due to CVD therefore remains a national priority and is a key indicator in the Department of Health NHS Outcomes and Public Health Outcomes Frameworks. 

- Non-fatal major CV events can also lead to serious long-term consequences such as functional disability, impaired HRQoL, and increased risk of subsequent CV events. 

- CVD also represents a significant economic burden; in 2009, CVD was responsible for 6% (approximately £7 billion of total healthcare expenditure in the UK. Between 2014 and 2020, the (estimated) direct cost of CVD is expected to rise from approximately £10 billion per year to approximately £12 billion per year, underlying the importance of making available new cost-effective therapeutic options to reduce the incidence and long-term costs of CVD. 

- The risk of a CV event is a composite of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Elevated LDL-C plays a critical role in atherosclerotic plaque formation, and is the principal modifiable risk factor for CVD. FH, a hereditary condition, leads to life-long markedly elevated LDL-C levels. Additional risk factors for CV events include increased age, male gender, smoking, existing CVD, diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease. 

- The evidence supporting LDL-C as a therapeutic target and surrogate for CV outcomes is robust and multi-faceted (epidemiological studies, studies of genetic variants, and interventional studies with LDL-C-lowering therapies). A meta-analysis of 26 interventional studies (169,138 individuals with a median follow-up 4.9 years) conducted by the CTTC showed that for every 1 mmol/L reduction in LDL-C the annual risk of major CV events was reduced by 22%, with a continued benefit observed even with low LDL-C levels (< 2.0 mmol/L). 

- Interventions to achieve LDL-C control in patients with elevated LDL-C and in those with high CV risk are prescribed to reduce the risk of CV events, and have been shown to significantly reduce the risk of CV events irrespective of the type of intervention. 

- Following lifestyle changes, statins are considered the cornerstone of therapy to reduce LDL-C levels; however, the maximum dose of high-intensity statin licensed in the UK achieves a maximal LDL-C reduction of up to 55%. For patients with elevated LDL-C levels despite treatment with statins, ezetimibe and other lipid-lowering therapies may be additionally prescribed, but their potency is limited, with LDL-C reductions in the order of 10% to 20%. 

- Existing treatment options adequately reduce LDL-C levels in most patients; however, there remains a cohort of high-risk patients (e.g. patients with non-familial hypercholesterolaemia at high residual risk due to presence of additional risk factors, and patients with HeFH) for whom existing treatment options are inadequate and who remain particularly vulnerable to CV events. These patients have a substantial unmet medical need. 

- Although evolocumab would be beneficial for many patients whose LDL-C remains 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 100 -->

inadequately controlled by maximally-tolerated doses of statins or who are statin intolerant/contraindicated (per its anticipated MA), the priority for use of evolocumab is in those patients who are at the highest residual risk and are most vulnerable to CV events, where evolocumab represents both a clinically- and cost-effective treatment option for the NHS. These include: 

- Patients without existing CVD but at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (based on QRISK2 score) 

- Patients with existing CVD at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (e.g. diabetes mellitus or CKD) 

- Patients with HeFH 

## **Overview of the disease/condition** 

Hyperlipidaemia is the heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by an excess of lipids (i.e. cholesterol, phospholipids, triglycerides) in the bloodstream. Primary hyperlipidaemia is usually due to genetic causes (monogenetic or polygenetic) and environmental factors, such as diet and lifestyle, whilst primary non-familial hyperlipidaemia is hyperlipidaemia that is not due to a specific genetic disorder (although there are polygenetic influences). Mixed dyslipidaemia is generally defined as elevated LDL-C and high triglycerides and/or low HDL-C. Finally hypercholesterolaemia, a type of hyperlipidaemia, specifically refers to the presence of high levels of cholesterol, including LDL-C, in the blood. 

The risk of a CV event is a composite of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Elevated LDL-C, the primary component of total cholesterol, plays a critical role in atherosclerotic plaque formation, and is the principal modifiable risk factor for CV events.[2] CVD is a general term that includes CHD, vascular diseases of the brain, and diseases of blood vessels. Atherosclerotic CV events include myocardial infarction (MI) and unstable angina (collectively referred to as CHD), IS and transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs), and peripheral arterial disease.[3-6] FH, a hereditary condition, may lead to life-long markedly elevated LDL-C levels.[11,12] In addition to elevated LDL-C, other important risk factors for CV events include existing CVD, diabetes mellitus, and CKD.[2] 

**Elevated LDL-C** : Elevated LDL-C is a principle driver of CV risk.[7-10] Large-scale, epidemiological studies have demonstrated a direct relationship between LDL-C levels and the rate of new-onset CHD and CHD events, including mortality.[7,8,10,11] Data from the Munster Heart Study (PROCAM) in Germany, which prospectively followed 4,849 men aged 40 to 65 years for at least 8 years, showed that higher LDL-C was the most important modifiable risk factor for severe coronary events, including MI and cardiac mortality.[8] 

**Familial hypercholesterolaemia:** FH is a hereditary condition caused by various genetic mutations that lead to life-long markedly elevated LDL-C levels resulting in a 20-fold increased lifetime risk for premature CVD.[12,13] In FH, elevated LDL-C leads to atherosclerotic plaque formation in the coronary arteries and proximal aorta at an early age and, over time, this prolonged exposure to elevated LDL-C renders affected individuals extremely vulnerable to the consequences of severe atherosclerotic disease, such as MI and stroke.[14-16] It is estimated that one in every three patients with FH has CHD.[17] Compared with non-FH hyperlipidaemic patients off lipid-lowering therapy, individuals with FH had 13-fold and 10- 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 101 -->

fold higher risks of CHD in relation to being off and on lipid-lowering therapy, respectively (adjusted odds ratios [ORs] off lipid-lowering therapy 13.2, 95% confidence interval [CI] 10.0, 17.4; OR on lipid-lowering therapy 10.3, 95% CI 7.8, 13.8).[17] 

Diagnosis of FH is typically made based on lipid levels and patient age, as well as family history. Early diagnosis and treatment can improve life expectancy in patients with FH.[18] Unfortunately, many patients with FH are never diagnosed with the condition, and many are diagnosed only after their first CHD event. There are two variants of FH: patients who have inherited the gene for FH from one parent are classified as having HeFH and patients who have inherited the gene from both parents are classified as having HoFH. HoFH is an extremely rare condition affecting approximately 1 in 1 million individuals and is not part of the current appraisal, and so will not be discussed in any further detail.[12,19,20] LDL-C levels in patients with HeFH are typically 2- to 3-fold higher than normal (approximately 5 to 10 mmol/L).[21,22] In the UK, HeFH has an estimated prevalence of 1 in 500 people.[20,23] Based on a population of 56 million in England and Wales as measured in the most recent UK census (2011), this translates to approximately 112,000 affected individuals with HeFH.[24] 

**Existing CVD:** Data from the multinational REduction of Atherothrombosis for Continued Health (REACH) registry show that patients with a history of an ischaemic event at baseline were at higher risk for ischaemic events (including a composite endpoint of CV-related mortality, MI, and stroke) during the study compared with patients without a history of ischaemic events (HR 1.71; 95% CI 1.57, 1.85; p < 0.001).[25] Event rates were highest in those who experienced an ischaemic event within 1 year of study enrolment. Thus, one of the strongest predictors of future ischaemic risk is a recent history of ischaemic events.[25] Another analysis based on data from the REACH registry showed that significant risk predictors of recurrent CV events and CV mortality in patients with existing CVD include the number of vascular beds affected, occurrence of a CV event in the previous year, HF, and atrial fibrillation.[26] Depending on gender and clinical outcome, survivors of an MI have a chance of illness and death that is 1.5 to 15 times higher than the general population. Among men and women 65 years of age or older who survive a first MI, 22% will experience a recurrent MI or fatal CHD event and 5% to 8% will experience a stroke within 5 years of the initial MI.[4] 

**Diabetes mellitus:** Diabetes mellitus is an independent risk factor for CVD and is associated with a higher risk of CVD, particularly in women.[2] CVD is the major cause of both morbidity and mortality in patients with diabetes.[2] Data from the National Diabetes Audit show that in 2012 to 2013 in England and Wales, patients with diabetes had a 139% additional risk of unstable angina, 94% additional risk of MI, and 63% additional risk of stroke over a 1-year follow-up period compared with people without diabetes.[27] These data also show that in 2013, people with diabetes in England and Wales were 34% more likely to die than people without diabetes.[27] Furthermore, in patients with existing CVD, diabetes mellitus significant increased the risk of further CV events and CV mortality.[26] 

**CKD:** Decreasing glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is independently associated with CVD, and CKD is widely acknowledged as a CHD-risk equivalent.[2] It is estimated in NICE guidelines that approximately 7,000 excess strokes and 12,000 excess MIs occurred in individuals with CKD in England in 2009 to 2010 relative to age- and gender-matched controls.[28] Most

patients with stage 3 to 5 CKD have mixed dyslipidaemia with a highly atherogenic lipid profile.[2] 

In addition to those risk factors described above, other risk factors for CVD include:[2,11,29-34] 

- increased age 

- male gender 

- other markers of hypercholesterolaemia and dyslipidaemia, e.g. 

   - elevated levels of total cholesterol, very low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, Lp(a), non-HDL-C (used to estimate the total number of atherogenic particles e.g. LDL-C and very low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in the blood), and ApoB 

   - low levels of low HDL-C and apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1) 

   - abnormal ApoB/ApoA1 and total cholesterol/HDL-C ratios 

- smoking 

- hypertension 

- physical inactivity and increased body mass index (BMI) 

- family history of CHD 

## **Effects of CVD on patients, carers, and society** 

CVD is the largest cause of death in the UK.[35] Although age-standardised UK mortality rates from CVD have fallen over recent years, the mortality burden associated with CVD remains substantial.[36] In the UK, CHD and stroke accounted for the first and third most common causes of premature mortality in 2013, respectively.[37] In total, a third of all deaths in the UK in 2013 (approximately 192,000 annually or 500 per day) were estimated to be attributable to CVD, including approximately 99,000 due to CHD and 34,000 due to IS.[37] The Department of Health CVD Outcomes Strategy (2013) recognised that England underperforms when compared with similar countries in terms of CV mortality.[35] Preventing premature mortality due to CVD therefore remains a national priority area and is a key indicator in the Department of Health’s NHS Outcomes Framework (2015-2016) and Public Health Outcomes Framework (2013-2016).[38,39] With an ageing population and current levels of obesity, without improvements in CV prevention, previous improvements in CV mortality will not be sustained.[35] 

Non-fatal major CV events can lead to serious long-term consequences such as functional disability, impaired HRQoL, and increased risk of subsequent CV events.[4,40,41] A survey conducted to assess HRQoL of stable patients with CHD showed that HRQoL in patients with CHD is lower than that of the general population, with those having a history of CV events or diabetes experiencing the greatest decrements in HRQoL.[41] Having a history of stroke or experiencing a recurrent CV event were significant predictors of reduced HRQoL.[41] Survivors of CV events may also require support from informal caregivers, which can lead to a detrimental impact on the quality of life of individuals providing such support.[42] 

CVD represents not only a substantial patient burden, but also a considerable direct cost to society that is increasing over time. In 2009, CVD was responsible for 6% (approximately £7 billion) of total healthcare expenditure in the UK, of which CHD accounted for approximately £1.5 billion.[43] Two key drivers of this expenditure are hospitalisations and CVD-related procedures (such as revascularisation), representing 54% of direct costs associated with 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 103 -->

CVD and 56% of direct costs associated with CHD.[43] Per-patient costs associated with CV events (revascularisation, MI, IS, unstable angina, and TIA) are substantial and range from £1,570 to £6,000 in the first 6 months following the event, and up to approximately £1,000 annually thereafter.[44] Between 2014 and 2020, the total healthcare expenditure on CVD in the UK is estimated to rise from approximately £10 billion per year to approximately £12 billion per year,[45] underlying the importance of making available new therapeutic options to reduce the incidence and long-term costs of CVD. 

## **Aims of lipid-lowering therapies** 

The evidence supporting LDL-C as a therapeutic target and surrogate for CV outcomes comes from epidemiological studies, genetic variants (both gain-of-function and loss-offunction), and interventional studies with LDL-C-lowering therapies.[8,46-59] . A meta-analysis of 26 statin trials (169,138 individuals with a median follow-up of 4.9 years) conducted by the CTTC showed that for every 1 mmol/L reduction in LDL-C, the annual risk of major CV events was reduced by 22%, with a continued benefit observed even with low LDL-C levels (< 2.0 mmol/L).[47] To date, no lower limit for LDL-C reduction and the associated reduction in CV risk has been identified. 

Interventions to achieve LDL-C control in patients with elevated LDL-C and in those with high CV risk are prescribed to reduce the risk of CV events. Lowering LDL-C levels through lipid-lowering therapy has been shown to reduce the risk of CV events irrespective of the type of intervention, as noted in NICE technology appraisal (TA) 132.[60-64] A log-linear relationship between LDL-C and CV risk exists with the risk of CHD reduced by approximately 1% for every 1% reduction in LDL-C.[65] This log-linear relationship was independent of the method by which LDL-C was lowered (i.e. by lifestyle modifications, drug treatment, or other therapy).[60,61] Multiple meta-analyses have demonstrated that LDL-C lowering with non-statin therapies is also associated with reductions in CV events, including CHD mortality.[63,66-70] A meta-analysis of 58 trials (including 148,321 patients) of lipidlowering therapies showed that a reduction in LDL-C of 1.0 mmol/L reduced the risk of CHD events by up to 36% over 6 or more years of treatment, regardless of initial CV risk.[70] Another meta-analysis specifically assessed the relationship between LDL-C and CHD risk using data from 81,859 patients enrolled in nine trials of non-statin treatments (bile acid sequestrants, surgery, and diet) and 10 statin trials over 5 years of treatment. The analysis showed that larger reductions in LDL-C were associated with greater reductions in CHD risk. A one-to-one relationship between LDL-C lowering and CHD and stroke reduction was observed over 5 years of treatment, with no difference between the statin and non-statin trials.[63] Results from the large, multinational IMProved Reduction of Outcomes: Vytorin Efficacy International Trial (IMPROVE-IT) show that, in patients with a recent history of ACS, ezetimibe added to simvastatin further lowered LDL-C and significantly reduced the occurrence of a composite endpoint of CV death, MI, unstable angina requiring hospitalisation, coronary revascularisation, or stroke compared with statin alone (p = 0.016).[64] IMPROVE-IT further confirms the relationship between LDL-C reduction and the reduction in risk of CV events, and demonstrates the incremental benefit of adding a non-statin lipid-lowering therapy to a statin.

## **Description and limitations of current treatment options** 

Management of primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia comprises a combination of lifestyle interventions (e.g. diet modification and weight loss, smoking cessation, and alcohol reduction) and lipid-lowering therapies including statins, ezetimibe, bile acid sequestrants, nicotinic acid, fibrates, and, in exceptional circumstances, LDL apheresis. A list of lipid-lowering therapies licensed for use in the UK and listed on the British National Formulary is provided in Appendix II. 

## _Statins_ 

Statins provide an effective first-line treatment option for lowering LDL-C levels by inhibiting the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG CoA) reductase, a key mediator in the production of cholesterol in the liver. Statins are considered the cornerstone of therapy to reduce LDL-C levels, and are generally the most frequently used first-line therapy for highrisk patients. Statins can be dosed at different intensities, which offer differing magnitudes of LDL-C reduction (Table 3-1). Recent studies have shown that more intensive statin therapy (and, consequently, greater LDL-C reduction leading to lower LDL-C levels) is more effective at reducing CV events than less intensive statin therapy.[71] However, on average, the maximum dose of high-intensity statin licensed in the UK achieves a maximal LDL-C reduction of up to 55% (Table 3-1). Moreover, the bulk of LDL-C reduction occurs with the initial selected statin dose;[72,73] doubling the statin dose results in only a 6% incremental reduction in LDL-C levels on average.[70,74-76]

Further, a subset of patients with hypercholesterolaemia (approximately 10% to 20%) is statin intolerant and develop signs or symptoms associated with statin use, including muscle-related symptoms (e.g. myalgia) that can lead to partial or complete intolerability.[78] Statin dose titration will often be accompanied by an increase in these muscle-related adverse events.[72] Such adverse events could lead to treatment discontinuation or dose reduction, thereby limiting the ability of statins to lower LDL-C and prevent major CV events.[79] Statins also have well-documented drug-drug interactions, and thus in patients receiving certain medications (e.g. fibrates and cyclosporine), statin use may be contraindicated or not clinically appropriate.[80-82] 

## _Ezetimibe_ 

Ezetimibe selectively blocks cholesterol absorption in the intestine, and is licensed for use in combination with statins for patients with total cholesterol or LDL-C not adequately controlled by statins alone at their maximally-tolerated dose. The Ezetimibe and Simvastatin in Hypercholesterolemia Enhances Atherosclerosis Regression (ENHANCE), and IMPROVE-IT studies demonstrated significant reductions in LDL-C levels with statin plus ezetimibe combination therapy compared with a statin alone.[64,83] However, these incremental reductions are modest (e.g. 17% in the ENHANCE study)[83] and are accompanied by a correspondingly modest reduction in CV events as shown in the IMPROVE-IT study in which the 7-year composite CV event rate primary endpoint for ezetimibe/statin versus statin monotherapy was 0.94 (p = 0.016).[64] Ezetimibe is also licensed for use as a monotherapy in patients for whom statins are not tolerated or contraindicated, but offers similar modest reductions in LDL-C (17% to 22%).[84] 

## _Additional pharmacological lipid-lowering therapies_ 

Additional lipid-lowering therapies (bile acid sequestrants, fibrates, and nicotinic acid) are also available alone or in combination with statins, but are similarly associated with highly limited LDL-C reductions, as well as various adverse effects (Table 3-2).

## _LDL apheresis_ 

LDL apheresis is a regular process similar to haemodialysis that involves extracting LDL-C from circulating blood over a period of 2 to 4 hours. In some exceptional cases, patients with severe HeFH (Table 3-3) may require apheresis, although this does not offer a long-term solution for patients because the reduction in LDL-C is transient, and LDL-C begins to reaccumulate after each apheresis session. Additionally, apheresis costs are substantial, with an estimated annual cost of between £26,000 to £62,000 for treatment every 1 to 2 weeks (based on a cost of £1,000 to £1,200 per session[78,79] ), and the treatment is performed at hospitals or specialised centres (of which there are only 6 in England and Wales) due to the type and cost of equipment required. Apheresis is also burdensome for patients, and often requires extended travel time due to the limited number of centres, in addition to the long duration of the procedure, which requires substantial time away from work and social activities.[21,86,87] ‘Market research data showed that patients undergoing apheresis felt that an effective new therapy that would avoid or reduce the need for apheresis would improve their QoL.[88] 

## _Unmet need in LDL-C reduction_ 

Data from a retrospective study of over 20,000 patients in the CPRD hospitalised for a first CV event between 2006 and 2012 were used to assess LDL-C distribution patterns.[89] The study population consisted of a cohort of patients who were alive and observable in both the CPRD and hospital episode statistics (HES) data as of January 1, 2005, and were hospitalised for a first CV event between January 2006 and March 2012 (end of HES observation period) i.e. all patients had a CV event at the study index date. Patient cohorts were retrospectively classified as CV low/moderate risk, CV high risk, and CV event history. In patients across the low/moderate and high risk cohorts, 23% of patients treated with highintensity statins (± other lipid-lowering therapies) had LDL-C levels > 3.0 mmol/L at the time of the index event, despite their lipid-lowering therapy. Similarly, 17% of patients in the CV event history cohort treated with high-intensity statins (± other lipid-lowering therapies) had LDL-C levels > 3.0 mmol/L at the time of the index event, despite their lipid-lowering therapy. 

Further, data from the National Audit of Familial Hypercholesterolaemia show that 62% of patients with diagnosed HeFH in the UK have elevated LDL-C levels > 3.0 mmol/L (median 3.3 mmol/L, minimum 0.8 mmol/L to maximum 12.7 mmol/L), despite wide availability of lipid-lowering therapies.[90] 

An overview of LDL-C distribution patterns in patients based on the UK CPRD study and data from the National Audit of Familial Hypercholesterolaemia described above is provided in Figure 3-1. 

Existing treatment options adequately reduce LDL-C levels in most patients; however, there remains a cohort of high-risk patients (e.g. patients with non-familial hypercholesterolaemia at high residual risk due to presence of additional risk factors, and patients with HeFH) for whom existing treatment options are inadequate and who remain particularly vulnerable to CV events. These patients have a substantial unmet medical need.

## **Summary of clinical guidelines, guidance and the UK treatment pathway** 

## _NICE CG and TA guidance_ 

Seven current NICE CGs and one TA providing guidance on lipid modification therapy for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia were identified (Appendix II). CG181, CG71, and TA132 are most relevant to this appraisal (because all others refer to, or are superseded by, this guidance): 

- CG181 provides specific recommendations on lipid-lowering therapy for the primary and secondary prevention of CVD.[77] 

- CG71 provides specific recommendations on management of patients with HeFH, including lipid-lowering therapy.[91] 

- TA132 provides guidance about the use of ezetimibe for the treatment of primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial).[62] 

An overview of the UK treatment pathway based on these guidelines and TA guidance is provided in Figure 3-2, with detailed recommendations provided in Table 3-3. 

**Primary prevention:** CG181 recommends use of a risk assessment tool (QRESEARCH Cardiovascular Risk Algorithm; QRISK2) to assess CVD risk in patients up to and including age 84 years for primary prevention. Atorvastatin 20 mg is recommended for patients who have a ≥ 10% 10-year risk of developing CVD assessed using the QRISK2 assessment tool. A risk assessment tool should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus or CKD (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m[2] and/or albuminuria). 

**Secondary prevention:** CG181 specifies that a risk assessment tool should not be used in patients with existing CVD. When lipid-lowering therapy is required, high-intensity statin therapy (e.g. atorvastatin 80 mg) is the recommended first-line treatment. 

**Familial hypercholesterolaemia:** CG71 specifies that risk estimation tools should not be used given this patient population is already at high risk of premature CVD. Therefore, appropriate control of cholesterol should be based on individualised risk assessment by a clinician. Lipid-lowering therapy is recommended with high-intensity statins as a first-line treatment. Patients with FH are deemed very high risk if they have established CHD, a family history of CHD or two or more other CV risk factors (e.g. male gender, current smoker, hypertension, and diabetes). 

**Statin intolerance:** CG71 and TA132 define statin intolerance as the presence of clinically significant adverse effects (e.g. myalgia or alterations of liver function tests) that are considered to represent an unacceptable risk to the patient or that may result in compliance with therapy being compromised. CG181 specifies that statin intolerance should be defined clinically as the inability to tolerate any dose of three different statins.[92] 

**Ezetimibe and other lipid-modifying therapies** : TA132 provides guidance recommending ezetimibe as an option in patients (familial and non-familial hypercholesterolaemia) achieving inadequate LDL-C reduction with statins. Ezetimibe is recommended for use as combination treatment with statins, or monotherapy in patients with contraindications or intolerance to statins. CG71 recommends that patients with HeFH may further receive

## _Additional UK relevant guidelines_ 

Other available relevant UK guidelines and recommendations published by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network, Joint British Societies, and HEART-UK LDL Apheresis Working Group are generally consistent with the guidance issued by NICE with respect to use of statins as a cornerstone lipid-lowering therapy for prevention of CVD in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia. There are some minor differences with respect to definition patient populations requiring lipid-lowering therapy, and recommendations about specific lipidlowering therapies. See Appendix II for further details. 

## _ESC and EAS Guidelines_ 

The ESC and EAS issued guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias in 2011.[2] These guidelines recommend the assessment of total CVD risk and stratify patients into 4 risk groups (low, moderate, high and very high) based on clinical characteristics (Table 3-4). Patients classified as very high risk and high risk include those with existing CVD, diabetes mellitus (all type 2 and type 1 patients with target organ damage), moderate to severe CKD, and markedly increased individual risk factors such as familial dyslipidaemias. Patients with a 10-year risk of fatal CV events using the Systemic Coronary Risk Estimation (SCORE) above defined thresholds are also considered very high risk (≥ 5%) and high risk (≥ 5% and < 10%). The ESC/EAS guidelines recognise that patients at very high risk and high risk should receive immediate drug intervention when LDL-C levels are > 1.8 mmol/L and > 2.5 mmol/L, respectively.

## _Issues relating to current clinical practice, including any variations or uncertainty about established practice_ 

As described earlier in this section, CV risk is a composite of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Consequently, all current CGs for the prevention of CVD recommend the assessment of total CV risk (e.g. using QRISK2 or SCORE) in clinical practice. Patients with existing CVD are routinely deemed to be at high risk, and therefore undergo closer clinical management to reduce the risk of a recurrent CV event. In the UK, NICE guidelines recommend that CVD risk assessment tools should not be used in patients with existing CVD, as well as those with other clinical conditions which are routinely deemed to place patients at high CV risk (e.g. diabetes mellitus, CKD and FH). This approach is consistent with the ESC/EAS guidelines where patients with existing CVD, diabetes mellitus or moderate to severe CKD are automatically deemed to be very high risk (Table 3-4). Furthermore, risk predictions models are not generally used by clinicians to support their overall assessment of CV risk. Therefore, absolute CV risks (e.g. 10-year risk of > _X_ % of a recurrent fatal or non-fatal CV event) are not used as a starting rule for the management of hypercholesterolaemia with lipid-lowering therapies in these specific populations. Instead, high-risk patients, for example, those with existing CVD and in whom LDL-C levels remain unacceptably high are managed closely to optimise lipid profiles given the contribution of hypercholesterolaemia to overall CV risk. This is an important consideration for the clinicaland cost-effectiveness assessment of evolocumab within its anticipated MA in patients with existing CVD or HeFH for the purposes of this appraisal. 

## **Proposed positioning of evolocumab within the treatment pathway and patient populations** 

Although evolocumab would be beneficial for many patients whose LDL-C remains inadequately controlled by maximally-tolerated doses of statins or who are statin intolerant/contraindicated (per its anticipated MA), the priority for use of evolocumab is in those patients who are at the highest residual risk and are most vulnerable to CV events, where evolocumab represents both a clinically- and cost-effective treatment option for the NHS. These include: 

- Patients without existing CVD but at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (based on QRISK2 score) 

- Patients with existing CVD at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (e.g. diabetes mellitus or CKD) 

- Patients with HeFH

_Overview of positioning of evolocumab in patients without existing CVD but at high residual risk_ 

QRISK2 is recommended by NICE as a risk assessment tool for patients without existing CVD who are ≤ 84 years of age (Table 3-3). It is recognised that NICE CG181 does not recommend risk assessment for patients without existing CVD but with type 1 diabetes or CKD (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m[2] and/or albuminuria) before initiating treatment with statins. 

It is proposed that evolocumab is positioned as a treatment option for patients without existing CVD but at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (based on QRISK2 score) according to severity of hypercholesterolaemia. 

_Overview of positioning of evolocumab in patients with existing CVD at high residual risk due to additional risk factors_ 

NICE CG181 recommends that a risk assessment tool should not be used in patients with existing CVD. Further, currently-available risk scores (e.g. QRISK2 and SCORE) are not intended for use in patients with existing CVD. Therefore, in order to identify patients with existing CVD at high residual risk due to additional risk factors, various sources of evidence were assessed: 

- ESC/EAS 2011 guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias 

- a targeted literature review of recurrent CVD risk equations 

- consultation with UK clinicians 

**ESC/EAS guidelines:** The ESC/EAS guidelines classify patients with existing CVD, patients with diabetes mellitus, patients with moderate to severe CKD, and patients with a calculated 10-year risk SCORE for fatal CVD ≥ 10%, as being at ‘very high’ CV risk (Table 3-4). It is reasonable to assume therefore that patients with existing CVD and either moderate to severe CKD or diabetes mellitus will be at high residual risk of future events. The 10-year risk SCORE is not intended for use in patients with existing CVD, and risk estimation is not recommended for patients with existing CVD in NICE CGs (e.g. CG181), so 10-year risk SCORE ≥ 10% was discounted as a relevant patient characteristic for defining patients with existing CVD at high residual risk. 

**Risk equations for recurrent events:** Of the four risk equation publications identified,[26,93-95] a publication based on the REACH registry was deemed to be the most relevant as it assessed CV risk using a broad definition of CV events.[26] Data from the REACH registry highlighted several additional patient characteristics that were significant predictors of recurrent CV events (both fatal and non-fatal) including age, male gender, diabetes mellitus, number of vascular beds affected, atrial fibrillation, and congestive HF. Other factors were also found to significantly impact risk of recurrent CV events, but were either modifiable patient characteristics (current smoker and BMI < 20 kg/m[2] ) or not clinical patient characteristics (statin use, aspirin use, geographic location) and were consequently discounted as relevant characteristics for defining patients with existing CVD at high residual risk. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 118 -->

**Expert UK clinical opinion:** UK clinical experts were used to validate the risk factors assessed as being relevant for identifying patients with existing CVD at high residual risk based on ESC/EAS guidelines and data from the REACH registry. In addition, this expert opinion suggested that presence of progressive CVD (evidenced by two or more documented acute ischaemic CV events or revascularisation procedures) is a highly clinically relevant risk factor and should be used as an additional characteristic to define patients with existing CVD at high residual risk. Clinicians suggested that patients with progressive CVD had a risk of recurrent events equivalent to or greater than the risk associated with presence of diabetes mellitus. Further, clinicians highlighted the importance of high levels of Lp(a) as a relevant identifier of patients with existing CVD at high residual risk, though no threshold was specified by the clinicians. A ESC/EAS current opinion publication relating to Lp(a) as a CV risk factor[34] highlights the Copenhagen City Heart Study, which showed that multifactorially adjusted HRs for MI for elevated Lp(a) levels were as high as 1.9 (95% CI 1.2, 3.0) for the 90[th] –95[th] centile (77–117 mg/dL), and 2.6 (95% CI 1.6, 4.1) for levels > 95[th] centile (> 117 mg/dL), respectively, versus levels < 22[nd] centile (trend p < 0.001).[96,97]

_Overview of positioning of evolocumab in patients with HeFH_ 

It is proposed that evolocumab is positioned as a treatment option in all patients with HeFH given that these patients have lifelong exposure to elevated LDL-C which renders affected individuals extremely vulnerable to the consequences of severe atherosclerotic disease, such as MI and stroke (Section 3). 

## _Detailed positioning of evolocumab in high-risk patients_ 

Based on the above, and where evolocumab is both clinically- and cost-effective, it is proposed that evolocumab is positioned as a treatment option specifically in the following patient populations at high CV risk as described below: 

1. Adults with primary hypercholesterolaemia (non-familial) or mixed dyslipidaemia without existing CVD but at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (based on QRISK2 score) according to severity of hypercholesterolaemia 

2. Adults with primary hypercholesterolaemia (non-familial) or mixed dyslipidaemia and existing CVD with: 

- LDL cholesterol ≥ 3.5 mmol/L (or equivalent non-HDL-cholesterol ≥ 4.3 mmol/L) and at high residual risk due to the presence of one or more of the following: 

   - Diabetes mellitus 

   - Moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60mL/min/1.73m2) 

   - ACS in the past year 

   - Progressive CVD evidenced by ≥2 documented acute ischaemic CV events or revascularisation procedures 

   - 3 vascular beds affected 

   - Elevated plasma Lp(a) ≥ 77 mg/dL (≥ 90% centile) 

   - Other CV conditions that significantly elevate risk of further CV events: atrial fibrillation 

- LDL cholesterol ≥ 3.0 mmol/L (or equivalent non-HDL-cholesterol ≥ 3.8 mmol/L) and at high residual risk due to the presence of two or more of the following: 

   - Diabetes mellitus 

   - Moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60mL/min/1.73m[2] ) 

   - ACS in the past year 

   - Progressive CVD evidenced by ≥2 documented acute ischaemic CV events or revascularisation procedures 

   - ≥2 vascular beds affected 

   - Elevated plasma Lp(a) ≥ 77 mg/dL (≥ 90% centile) 

   - Other CV conditions that significantly elevate risk of further CV events: heart failure and atrial fibrillation 

Age and gender should also be taken into consideration. 

3. Adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia

## **Life expectancy of patients with the disease** 

Although there are no specific data on absolute life expectancy of patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia, the key consequence of this condition (i.e. CVD) leads to substantial premature mortality. In England and Wales in 2012, more than 35,000 premature deaths (deaths in people < 75 years of age) were caused by CVD, of which approximately 20,000 were caused by CHD.[98] It is estimated that the typical CV event shortens a person’s life by 17 years.[99]

**4 Clinical effectiveness** 

- A SLR identified four high quality (low risk of bias) relevant RCTs, involving the treatment of almost 3,500 patients and representing a robust evaluation of evolocumab versus ezetimibe and versus placebo in relevant patient populations. 

- In these four RCTs, evolocumab 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM provided clinicallyequivalent, consistent and intensive reductions of up to approximately 72% compared with placebo and up to approximately 46% compared with ezetimibe, in addition to any background lipid-lowering therapies patients were receiving (e.g. statins). 

   - Evolocumab reduced LDL-C by an additional 69.1% to 71.8% relative to placebo and 43.3% to 45.5% relative to ezetimibe at the mean of weeks 10/12 in LAPLACE-2 (patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia receiving background moderate- to high-intensity statin therapy). 

   - Evolocumab reduced LDL-C by an additional 61.3% to 66.2% relative to placebo at the mean of weeks 10/12 in RUTHERFORD-2 (patients with HeFH receiving stable background lipid-lowering therapy [statin ± other lipid lowering therapies]). 

   - Evolocumab reduced LDL-C by an additional 38.1% to 39.2% relative to ezetimibe at the mean of weeks 10/12 in GAUSS-2 (patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia with statin intolerance). 

   - Evolocumab reduced LDL-C by an additional 59.3% relative to placebo at week 52 weeks in DESCARTES (patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia receiving stable background lipid-lowering therapy). 

- Pre-specified and post-hoc subgroup analyses show that these reductions in LDL-C are consistent across patient subgroups, including subgroups according to presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia. 

- Evolocumab was also superior to placebo and to ezetimibe in improving other lipid parameters, including non-HDL-C, ApoB, and Lp(a). 

- Supplementary evidence from ongoing, long-term extension studies (OSLER and OSLER-2) show that reductions in LDL-C are maintained for more than 2 years. 

- Analyses of the safety and tolerability data from the evolocumab studies show that evolocumab has a favourable safety and tolerability profile. In an integrated safety analysis (of 6,026 patients, representing 7,235 patient-years of exposure), as well as across populations and therapeutic settings in individual studies, adverse events were overall balanced between treatment groups. Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity, with serious adverse events and adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation infrequently reported and generally similar across treatment groups. 

- The type and incidence of adverse events observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations < 0.6 mmol/L and < 1.0 mmol/L were generally similar to those observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations ≥ 1.0 mmol/L. 

- Anti-evolocumab antibodies were infrequent, non-neutralising, and not associated with clinically relevant adverse events. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 122 -->

- An exploratory safety analysis of recent data from the integrated long-term extension studies showed a significant 53% reduction in 1-year adjudicated CV event rates from 2.18% in the SoC group to 0.95% in the evolocumab plus SoC group (HR: 0.47, p = 0.003). This is in the direction, and of the magnitude, that would be expected given the magnitude of LDL-C lowering associated with evolocumab. 

- The robust and long-term effects of evolocumab on LDL-C and other lipids, combined with its favourable safety and tolerability profile, demonstrate that evolocumab represents a significant medical advance, and a revolutionary stepchange in the management of primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia. Evolocumab will, for the first time, enable clinicians to provide high-risk patients who would otherwise remain vulnerable to CV events (because of inadequate LDL-C reduction with existing therapies) with consistent and intensive LDL-C reductions to reduce their risk of major CV events.

## _Alignment of the SLR with the decision problem_ 

To address the information needs of the decision problem as outlined in the final scope for this appraisal, additional exclusion criteria were applied in a second stage of screening to further align the SLR with the decision problem, and to identify all relevant RCTs that could potentially be used for data synthesis in the absence of sufficient head-to-head data to address the information needs of the decision problem. These additional exclusion criteria included: 

- study not in a population relevant to the decision problem (e.g. HoFH, Japanese population) 

- study assessed neither relevant intervention nor relevant comparator defined in the decision problem 

   - evolocumab alone or in combination with a statin with or without ezetimibe, or in combination with ezetimibe 

   - ezetimibe in combination with a statin (when optimised statin therapy does not appropriately control LDL-C) or ezetimibe alone (when statins are contraindicated or not tolerated) 

- study did not include outcome defined in the decision problem 

   - plasma lipid and lipoprotein levels, including LDL-C, non-HDL-C, ApoB, and Lp(a) 

   - requirement of procedures including LDL apheresis and revascularisation 

   - fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events 

   - mortality 

   - adverse effects of treatment 

   - HRQoL. 

All publications excluded at this second stage of the screening process were documented along with the reasons for exclusion (Appendix III). The remaining publications were considered as potentially relevant for data synthesis. 

## _Identification of studies most relevant for inclusion in the submission_ 

In a third and final filtration step to identify RCTs most relevant for inclusion in this submission, further exclusion criteria were applied: 

- exclusion of studies that did not assess evolocumab 

- exclusion of phase 2 studies if an equivalent phase 3 study in the same population had been conducted. 

All publications excluded at this third stage of the screening process were documented along with the reasons for exclusion (Appendix III).

Finally, following application of further exclusion criteria to identify RCTs most relevant for inclusion in this submission, 22 publications reporting 4 studies were identified. ## _**4.2 List of relevant randomised controlled trials**_ 

The SLR identified four Amgen-sponsored relevant phase 3 RCTs assessing the efficacy and safety of evolocumab, reported in 22 publications. 

Two of these studies provide direct head-to-head evidence for relevant interventions versus relevant comparators as defined in the decision problem: 

- LAPLACE-2: evolocumab (plus background statin therapy) versus ezetimibe (plus background statin therapy) in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia 

- GAUSS-2: evolocumab monotherapy versus ezetimibe monotherapy in statin-intolerant patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia. 

Two of these studies were placebo-controlled studies, with prespecified stratification factor and covariate subgroup analyses providing comparative data for relevant interventions versus relevant comparators as defined in the decision problem: 

- RUTHERFORD-2: evolocumab (plus stable background lipid-lowering therapy [statin ± other lipid-lowering therapy]) versus placebo (plus stable background lipid-lowering therapy [statin ± other lipid-lowering therapy]) in patients with HeFH 

- DESCARTES: evolocumab (plus background lipid-lowering therapy) versus placebo (plus background lipid-lowering therapy) in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia.

Although excluded from the SLR due to the mixed patient populations enrolled in them, interim results from two ongoing, long-term, extension studies (OSLER and OSLER-2) are also reported in this submission to provide additional evidence on the long-term effects of treatment with evolocumab for up to an additional 124 weeks of follow-up. OSLER is an ongoing, phase 2, multicentre, randomised, controlled, open-label, 5-year extension study that enrolled patients who completed a range of phase 2 RCTs, and represents the longest PCSK9 study to date. OSLER-2 is an ongoing, phase 3, multicentre, randomised, controlled, open-label, 2-year extension study that enrolled patients who completed a range of phase 3 RCTs, including all of the relevant RCTs defined in Table 4-2. In both extension studies, patients were randomly assigned to receive evolocumab plus SoC (based on local guidelines and which may include other lipid-lowering therapy) or SoC alone during the first year. Patients randomised to evolocumab plus SoC received evolocumab 420 mg QM (OSLER) or 140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM at patients’ choice (OSLER-2). An overview of the design and methodology of OSLER and OSLER-2 is provided in Appendix IV. 

## _**4.3 Summary of methodology of the relevant randomised controlled trials**_ 

The relevant RCTs were international, multicentre, phase 3 RCTs of 12 weeks’ (LAPLACE2, RUTHERFORD-2, and GAUSS-2) and 52 weeks’ (DESCARTES) duration involving the treatment of almost 3,500 patients. 

**LAPLACE-2** was a 12-week RCT designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of evolocumab compared with placebo or ezetimibe, when administered in combination with moderate- to high-intensity statin therapy in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia. Prior to randomisation, patients entered a screening period to determine eligibility, which included a requirement for LDL-C ≥ 2.1 mmol/L (if taking an intensive statin at screening), ≥ 2.6 mmol/L (if taking a non-intensive statin at screening), or ≥ 4.5 mmol/L (if not taking a statin at screening). During screening, SC administration of placebo was performed to confirm tolerability of SC administration prior to randomisation. After the screening period, eligible patients were randomised to one of five open-label statin cohorts (atorvastatin 10 mg or 80 mg, rosuvastatin 5 mg or 40 mg, or simvastatin 40 mg) for a 4-week lipid stabilisation period. After the lipid-stabilisation period, patients within the atorvastatin cohorts were randomised to one of six treatment groups: placebo Q2W plus ezetimibe OD, placebo Q2W plus placebo OD, evolocumab 140 mg Q2W plus placebo OD, placebo QM plus ezetimibe OD, placebo QM plus placebo OD, evolocumab 420 mg QM plus placebo OD, while continuing background statin therapy. Patients who received rosuvastatin or simvastatin were randomised into one of four treatment groups: placebo Q2W, evolocumab 140 mg Q2W, placebo QM, or evolocumab 420 mg QM, while continuing background statin therapy. Patients were asked to maintain a stable diet and exercise regimen throughout LAPLACE-2. 

**RUTHERFORD-2** was a 12-week RCT designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of evolocumab compared with placebo in patients with HeFH (as per Simon Broome criteria) who did not achieve adequate LDL-C control (i.e. LDL-C levels ≥ 2.6 mmol/L) after receiving a stable dose of an approved statin ± stable dose(s) of allowed lipid-regulating drugs for ≥ 4 weeks before LDL-C screening. Prior to randomisation, patients entered a screening period during which SC administration of placebo was performed to confirm tolerability of SC 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 131 -->

administration. Patients who completed the screening period and met final eligibility criteria were randomised into 4 treatment groups: placebo Q2W, evolocumab 140 mg Q2W, placebo QM, and evolocumab 420 mg QM, while continuing background lipid-lowering therapy. Patients were asked to maintain a stable diet and exercise regimen throughout RUTHERFORD-2. 

**GAUSS-2** was a 12-week RCT designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of evolocumab compared with ezetimibe in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia unable to tolerate any statins or a statin dose high enough to control their LDL-C levels. Statin intolerance was defined as present in patients who had tried two or more statins and were unable to tolerate any statin dose or an increase in dose above a total weekly maximum dose because of intolerable myopathy, with symptoms resolving or improving with statin discontinuation or dose reduction. Prior to randomisation, patients entered a screening period during which SC administration of placebo was performed to confirm tolerability of SC administration prior to randomisation. Depending on a patient’s risk category (based on NCEP adult treatment panel [ATP] III treatment goals), patients must have had LDL-C levels at screening ranging from ≥ 2.6 mmol/L (patients with CHD or CHD risk equivalent) to ≥ 4.9 mmol/L (patients without diagnosed CHD or CHD risk equivalent, with no additional risk factors). Patients who completed the screening period and met final eligibility criteria were randomised into 4 treatment groups: ezetimibe plus placebo Q2W, evolocumab 140 mg Q2W plus placebo OD, ezetimibe plus placebo QM, and evolocumab 420 mg QM plus placebo OD. Patients were asked to maintain a stable diet and exercise regimen throughout GAUSS-2. 

**DESCARTES** was a 52-week RCT designed to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of evolocumab compared with placebo, when added to background lipid-lowering therapy in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia. Eligible patients with screening LDL-C values ≥ 1.9 mmol/L were instructed to follow the NCEP ATP III Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes diet and were assigned to one of the following four background lipid-lowering therapies for a 4-week stabilisation period based on their screening LDL-C levels and its distance from the goal stipulated by NCEP ATP III risk category. These background therapies were diet, diet plus atorvastatin 10 mg, diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg, or diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg plus ezetimibe. At the end of the 4-week stabilisation period, patients who still exceeded the NCEP ATP III risk category LDL-C goal underwent background therapy up-titration to the next therapy level and entered an additional 4-week stabilisation period after which study eligibility based on LDL-C was reassessed. A maximum of two up-titrations were permitted. Patients who were on maximal background therapy were eligible if their LDL-C was ≥ 2.0 mmol/L at the end of the stabilisation period. Patients on maximal background therapy whose LDL-C was < 2.0 mmol/L at the end of the stabilisation period could undergo a single background therapy down-titration to diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg and enter an additional 4-week lipid stabilisation period, after which study eligibility based on a final LDL-C blood draw was reassessed. Patients whose eligibility was confirmed were randomised into two treatment groups: placebo QM and evolocumab 420 mg QM, while continuing background lipidlowering therapy. Patients were asked to maintain a stable diet and exercise regimen throughout DESCARTES. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 132 -->

The determination of efficacy in each study was based on changes in LDL-C and other lipid parameters at select time points. In the relevant RCTs of 12 weeks’ duration (RUTHERFORD-2, LAPLACE-2, and GAUSS-2), the co-primary endpoints were the percent change in LDL-C from baseline at week 12, to address regulatory precedence, and the mean percent change in LDL-C from baseline at the mean of weeks 10 and 12. The rationale for assessing LDL-C at the mean of weeks 10 and 12 is that it represents the average between peak and trough levels for the QM dose. At week 12, the LDL-C lowering effect begins returning toward baseline due to clearance of the antibody and ongoing hepatic PCSK9 production. Obtaining LDL-C levels at weeks 10 and 12 provides a time-averaged efficacy estimate between peak and trough effects. In addition, the week 10/12 data is helpful to clinicians since they won’t necessarily time lipid draws to the dosing cycle. 

In DESCARTES, the primary endpoint was the percent change in LDL-C from baseline at week 52. 

Analyses of LDL-C in the relevant RCTs utilised ultracentrifugation LDL-C, a reflexive approach, and calculated LDL-C. Ultracentrifugation LDL-C values were used to achieve the most rigorous and accurate LDL-C assessment possible, but are not widely available or routinely used in clinical practice. Ultracentrifugation LDL-C was used as the primary analysis method in DESCARTES. A reflexive testing approach was evaluated to assess whether calculated LDL-C concentrations could be used in place of ultracentrifugation LDL-C concentrations in the primary analysis. For analyses of the relevant RCTs of 12 weeks’ duration (RUTHERFORD-2, LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2), a reflexive approach was used as the primary analysis method, where the calculated LDL-C was employed unless the calculated LDL-C was < 1.0 mmol/L or triglycerides were > 4.5 mmol/L, in which case ultracentrifugation LDL-C was determined and utilised. This approach was chosen to provide a robust, conservative, and accurate assessment of LDL-C in the rigorous environment of a controlled clinical study. Data were also evaluated using calculated LDL-C because this method of LDL-C measurement is widely available and is the predominant way in which LDL-C is assessed in clinical practice. 

A summary of key aspects of trial methodology including trial design, eligibility criteria, study settings and locations, study drugs and concomitant medications, and outcome measures is provided in Table 4-3, Table 4-4, and Table 4-5.

## _**4.5 Participant flow in the relevant randomised controlled trials**_ 

## **CONSORT participant flow diagrams** 

Consort participant flow diagrams are provided for each of the relevant RCTs below: 

- LAPLACE-2 (Figure 4-2 and Figure 4-3) 

- RUTHERFORD-2 (Figure 4-4) 

- GAUSS-2 (Figure 4-5) 

- DESCARTES (Figure 4-6). 

An overview of baseline characteristics and baseline/screening/study entry and postbaseline/on-study lipid-lowering therapy use are provided for each of the relevant RCTs in Table 4-7 (LAPLACE-2) and Table 4-8 (RUTHERFORD-2, GAUSS-2, and DESCARTES). Characteristics were generally well-balanced across treatment groups. 

More detailed information on patient disposition, baseline characteristics, and lipid-lowering therapy use is available in the CSRs of each of the relevant RCTs.

## _**4.6 Quality assessment of the relevant randomised controlled trials**_ 

Quality assessment was conducted using the criteria specified in the NICE User Guide for Company Submission of Evidence, adapted from the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination guidance for undertaking reviews in healthcare.[115] 

The risk of bias was assessed as low across all domains of each of the relevant RCTs. Participants randomised and allocation concealment was achieved using interactive voice/web response system, suggesting a low risk of both randomisation and allocation concealment bias. Patients and all trial personnel were blinded to treatment assignment. In addition, an independent data monitoring committee reviewed all data so as to further reduce the risk of bias. All randomised patients who received ≥ 1 dose of investigational product (IP) were included in the analysis in a modified intention-to-treat approach. Data were also reported for all outcomes identified as assessed in the trial methods, suggesting that the risk of selective reporting was low. There were no unexpected imbalances in dropouts between groups across all four trials. 

A summary of the risk of bias assessment is provided in Table 4-9.

## _**4.7 Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant randomised controlled trials**_ 

## **Details of evidence presented** 

All pre-specified primary, secondary, and tertiary efficacy outcomes for all relevant RCTs (defined in Section 4.2) are provided in the main submission and submission appendices. Table 4-10 summarises details of those pre-specified efficacy outcomes presented in detail within the main submission. For the supplementary long-term extension studies, only mean percent change in LDL-C from parent study baseline is presented in the main submission to support evaluation of long-term efficacy, with additional outcomes available in the interim clinical study reports and relevant study publications. A more detailed rationale for the presentation of outcomes from the relevant RCTs in the main submission versus the submission appendices is provided in Appendix V. 

Only LDL-C outcomes using the calculated approach to LDL-C assessment are provided in the main submission. This is in order to best reflect UK clinical practice (where LDL-C is routinely assessed by this method) and to align with the evolocumab’s SmPC (which also cites calculated LDL-C values). Data for LDL-C outcomes using the primary LDL-C assessment method for each relevant RCT, i.e. reflexive in LAPLACE-2, RUTHERFORD-2, and GAUSS-2, and ultracentrifugation in DESCARTES are provided in Appendix V. See Section 4.2 for further details on the LDL-C assessment methods utilised in the relevant RCTs.

## **Results of the relevant randomised controlled trials** 

_LAPLACE-2 (evolocumab versus placebo and versus ezetimibe over 12 weeks in patients - - with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia receiving moderate to high intensity background statins_ 

_**LDL-C percent change from baseline (individual statin cohorts):**_ Evolocumab 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM demonstrated statistically significant mean percent reductions in calculated LDL-C (from baseline at the mean of weeks 10/12) compared with placebo in each statin cohort, with treatment differences of -69.1% to -78.1% across statin cohorts in the Q2W group and -64.5% to -78.0% across statin cohorts in the QM group (p < 0.001 for all treatment differences) (Figure 4-7, Table 4-11, and Table 4-12). Compared with ezetimibe, treatment with evolocumab also resulted in statistically significant mean percent reductions in calculated LDL-C (from baseline at the mean of weeks 10/12) in each atorvastatin cohort, with treatment differences of -40.8% to -48.0% across atorvastatin cohorts in the Q2W group and -45.2% to -46.0% across atorvastatin cohorts in the QM group (p < 0.001 for all treatment differences) (Figure 4-7, Table 4-11, and Table 4-12). These results were consistent when the mean percent change in LDL-C was measured at week 12 (Figure 4-7, Table 4-11, and Table 4-12) and when LDL-C was measured using the reflexive approach to LDL-C assessment at both the mean of weeks 10/12 and at week 12 (Appendix V).

## _**LDL-C percent change from baseline versus placebo (pooled statin cohorts):**_ 

Supportive analyses were conducted to pool treatment effects across all statins (evolocumab versus placebo, prespecified) and across the atorvastatin cohorts (evolocumab versus ezetimibe, ad-hoc). 

For the comparison versus placebo, all patients in the FAS except those randomised to ezetimibe were included in the analyses. For the comparison versus ezetimibe, all patients in the FAS randomised to the atorvastatin cohorts were included in the analyses. Pooling of treatment effects was conducted using fixed and random effects meta-analysis models. Each statin cohort was treated as a separate study in the study level random effects model, and measures of heterogeneity in treatment effects across statin dose cohorts were provided. 

Results from these supportive analyses are in accordance with the main study analyses. Evolocumab Q2W and QM were associated with statistically significant reductions compared with placebo and with ezetimibe in mean percent change in LDL-C from baseline at both the mean of weeks 10/12 and at week 12, irrespective of statin cohort (comparison versus placebo) or atorvastatin cohort (comparison versus ezetimibe), in both the fixed effects and random effects model (Table 4-13 and Table 4-14).

## **Consistency of LDL-C-lowering treatment effect across the relevant RCTs** 

Efficacy results of the relevant RCTs in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia consistently demonstrated superiority of evolocumab in reducing LDL-C compared with placebo or ezetimibe, irrespective of study population and evolocumab dosing regimen (140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM) (Figure 4-11).

## **Results of the supplementary randomised, controlled, open-label extension** 

## **studies** 

_OSLER (evolocumab plus SoC versus SoC in patients from qualifying phase 2 parent - studies for up to 1 year; open label evolocumab in year 2+_ 

**LDL-C percent change from baseline:** At the time of data cutoff (01 April 2014), an analysis of the treatment differences between treatment groups showed that evolocumab 420 mg QM plus SoC (N = 882) significantly reduced mean (standard error [SE]) calculated LDL-C (from parent study baseline) compared with SoC alone (N = 442), with a treatment difference of -54.6% (1.2%) at week 12 and -51.4% (1.5%) at week 52 (p < 0.001 for both treatment differences).[119] Patients who received control in the parent study had unchanged LDL-C levels if they remained on control (SoC alone) during OSLER, but had LDL-C reductions from parent study baseline of approximately 60% at OSLER week 52 if they switched to evolocumab. Conversely, patients who received evolocumab in the parent study maintained consistent LDL-C reductions from parent study baseline at OSLER week 52 if they remained on evolocumab in OSLER, but LDL-C levels returned to approximate parent study baseline by OSLER week 12 if they switched to SoC alone. Detailed results are provided in Appendix V. 

Patients who received evolocumab plus SoC during year 1 and continued to receive evolocumab plus SoC during year 2+ of OSLER had sustained mean percent reductions in calculated LDL-C to week 124. Patients who received SoC alone during year 1 of OSLER and switched to evolocumab plus SoC during year 2+ had a mean (SE) percent change (from parent study baseline) in LDL-C of -54.1% by the first visit after switching to evolocumab plus SoC (week 64), with these reductions sustained to week 124. Detailed results are provided in Appendix V. 

OSLER-2 (evolocumab plus SoC versus SoC in patients from qualifying phase 3 parent - studies for up to 1 year; open label evolocumab in year 2+) 

**LDL-C percent change from baseline:** At the time of data cutoff (01 April 2014), an analysis of the treatment differences between groups showed that evolocumab 140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM plus SoC (N = 1951) significantly reduced mean calculated LDL-C (from parent study baseline) compared with SoC alone (N = 977), with a treatment difference (SE) of -64.5% (1.5%) at week 12 and -59.6% (1.7%) at week 24 (p < 0.001 for both treatment differences).[120] As data were only available for a few patients beyond week 24 (N = 7) at the time of data cutoff, these data are not shown, but are available in the OSLER-2 interim CSR. Patients who received control in the parent study had unchanged LDL-C levels if they remained on control (SoC alone) during OSLER-2, but had LDL-C reductions from parent study baseline of approximately 53.5% at OSLER-2 week 12 if they switched to evolocumab. Conversely, patients who received evolocumab in the parent study maintained consistent LDL-C reductions from parent study baseline at OSLER-2 week 24 if they remained on evolocumab in OSLER-2, but LDL-C levels returned to approximate parent study baseline by OSLER-2 week 12 if they switched to control (SoC alone). Detailed results are provided in Appendix V.

**LDL-C percent change from baseline:** At the time of data cutoff for an integrated analysis of data from OSLER and OSLER-2 (31 October 2014), results showed that by week 12 of the OSLER studies, reductions in calculated LDL-C (from parent study baseline) were 60.9% in patients receiving evolocumab plus SoC (N = 2,976) relative to SoC alone (N = 1,489, p < 0.001 for treatment difference).[121] These reductions were maintained for 48 weeks.

## _Overview of the subgroup analysis_ 

Pre-specified subgroup analyses, controlling for stratification factors and other baseline covariates (including subgroups for screening and baseline LDL-C levels, subgroups for CVD risk, and subgroups for use of lipid-lowering therapies), were conducted for the relevant RCTs (defined in Section 4.2). The analyses were conducted for the coprimary/primary efficacy endpoints of each relevant RCT only (i.e. percent change from baseline in LDL-C at the mean of weeks 10/12 and at week 12 [LAPLACE-2, RUTHERFORD-2, GAUSS-2] or at week 52 [DESCARTES]). An overview of these subgroups and subgroup criteria is provided in Table 4-18. The statistical approach of the stratification factor and other baseline covariate subgroup analyses followed those of the primary efficacy analyses conducted for the overall trial populations (previously described in Section 4.4). Treatment effect differences among subgroups, which represent subgroup by treatment interactions, were estimated and tested based on statistics from the subgroup repeated measures models.
