## _Results of the pre-specified subgroup analyses_ 

Evolocumab 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM were consistently effective relative to placebo and to ezetimibe in lowering LDL-C (mean percent change from baseline at the mean of weeks 10/12 and at week 12 [RUTHERFORD-2, LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2] or at week 52 [DESCARTES]) in all stratification factor and baseline covariate subgroups in each study, with no notable differences between subgroups. 

Forest plots providing detailed results for each prespecified stratification factor and baseline covariate subgroup in each individual relevant RCT are provided in Appendix VI. 

Of particular relevance to the NICE decision problem: 

- Evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to placebo (RUTHERFORD-2 and DESCARTES [QM only]) and to ezetimibe (GAUSS-2) irrespective of baseline and background lipid-lowering therapies. 

   - In RUTHERFORD-2, evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C irrespective of whether or not the statin used as part of the background lipid-lowering therapy was intensive or non-intensive. This is of relevance to the decision problem as NICE recommends use of high-intensity statins as a first-line treatment option for patients with HeFH. Further, evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C, irrespective of whether ezetimibe was used as part of the background lipid-lowering therapy strategy. This is of relevance to the decision problem as the decision problem includes evolocumab in combination with statin and ezetimibe as a relevant intervention, and statin in combination with ezetimibe as a relevant comparator (comparison provided in the ezetimibe use ‘yes’ stratification factor subgroup). 

   - In GAUSS-2, evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to ezetimibe irrespective of whether or not statins were used at baseline. This is of relevance to the decision problem given that some patients considered intolerant to statins under NICE guidelines may continue to receive suboptimal doses of statins in clinical practice in England and Wales. Further, evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to ezetimibe irrespective of whether non-statin lipid-lowering therapy (including bile acid sequestrants or stanols), statins, or neither were used at baseline. This is of relevance to the decision problem given that some patients considered intolerant or contraindicated to statins under NICE guidelines may receive non-statin lipidlowering therapies other than the randomised ezetimibe intervention in clinical practice in England and Wales. 

   - In DESCARTES, evolocumab QM was consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to placebo irrespective of whether background lipid-lowering therapy was diet alone, diet plus atorvastatin 10 mg, diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg, or diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg plus ezetimibe. This is of relevance to the decision problem as (i) NICE recommends use of high-intensity statins as a first-line treatment option for primary and secondary prevention of CVD in patients who qualify for lipidmodification therapy under current NICE guidelines, as well as for the treatment of HeFH (reflected by the diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg stratification factor); and (ii) the decision problem includes evolocumab in combination with a statin and ezetimibe as a relevant intervention and statin plus ezetimibe as a relevant comparator 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 186 -->

(comparison provided in the diet plus atorvastatin 80 mg plus ezetimibe stratification factor subgroup). 

- Evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to placebo (RUTHERFORD-2, LAPLACE-2, and DESCARTES [QM only]) and to ezetimibe (LAPLACE-2 and GAUSS-2) irrespective of whether baseline LDL-C was greater or less than the median. Evolocumab Q2W and QM were also consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to placebo (RUTHERFORD-2) and to ezetimibe (GAUSS-2) irrespective of whether screening LDL-C was greater or less than 160 mg/dL (RUTHERFORD-2) or 180 mg/dL (GAUSS-2). This is of relevance to the decision problem as (i) subgroups according to severity of hypercholesterolaemia are defined as relevant subgroups in the decision problem and (ii) minimum LDL-C thresholds for initiation of treatment with evolocumab in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia are proposed, although it is noted that these thresholds are not fully aligned with the cut-offs used for these subgroup analyses. 

- Evolocumab Q2W and QM were consistently effective at lowering LDL-C relative to placebo (LAPLACE-2, RUTHERFORD-2, and DESCARTES [QM only]) and to ezetimibe (LAPLACE-2 and GAUSS-2) irrespective of whether or not patients had two or more baseline CHD risk factors, were categorised as high-risk according to NCEP guidelines, or whether or not patients had specific CV risk factors (e.g. family history of premature CVD, diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, and smoking). This is of relevance to the decision problem as subgroups according to the risk of CVD are defined as relevant subgroups in the decision problem.

This is of relevance to the decision problem as the ‘Europe’ region subgroup might be considered more representative of patients in England and Wales than the ‘North America’ and ‘other’ region subgroups.

## **Post-hoc subgroup analyses** 

_Overview of the post-hoc subgroup analyses_ 

The prespecified stratification factor/baseline covariate and high-risk subgroups discussed earlier adequately address subgroups of patients according to risk of CVD. 

Additional post-hoc subgroup analyses were conducted to further assess the following with respect to the LDL-C-lowering effect of evolocumab in the relevant RCTs, in accordance with subgroups defined in the decision problem: 

- the impact of presence of CVD using a broader definition of CVD than in the ‘Secondary Prevention’ prespecified high-risk subgroup discussed earlier (angina, MI, coronary artery bypass graft [CABG], percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI], stroke/cerebral infarction, carotid or vertebral artery disease, or peripheral arterial disease) 

- the impact of severity of hypercholesterolaemia (by baseline LDL-C quartile). 

The analysis methods for these post-hoc subgroups followed the analysis principles of the primary analyses of the overall populations for the individual studies. Treatment effect differences among subgroups, which represent subgroup by treatment interactions, were estimated and tested based on statistics from the subgroup repeated measures models for the CVD subgroups; no interaction testing was carried out for the LDL-C quartile subgroups. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765]

_Results of the post-hoc subgroup analyses_ 

Evolocumab 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM were consistently effective relative to placebo and to ezetimibe in lowering LDL-C in each post-hoc subgroup assessed for each relevant RCT, with treatment differences in mean percent change (from baseline at the mean of weeks 10/12 and at week 12 [RUTHERFORD-2, LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2] or at week 52 [DESCARTES]) in calculated LDL-C similar to those observed in the overall trial populations. 

Detailed results for each subgroup are provided in Appendix VI. 

## _**4.9 Meta-analysis**_ 

A meta-analysis was not conducted as it was not deemed necessary for the purposes of this appraisal. 

## _**4.10 Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons**_ 

LAPLACE-2 and GAUSS-2, the phase 3 RCTs which comparing evolocumab (140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM) with ezetimibe have been described in Section 4.2. There were no head-tohead RCTs evaluating evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin in patients with HeFH. Therefore, in order to address the decision problem set out in this submission, network meta-analysis techniques using direct and indirect evidence were evaluated to assess the feasibility of synthesising comparative efficacy for evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin in this population based on the studies identified as being potentially useful for data synthesis in the clinical efficacy SLR (Section 4.1and Appendix III). 

82 publications for 24 trials were identified in the SLR as being potentially useful for data synthesis (Section 4.1 and Appendix III). Of these studies, additional exclusion criteria were applied to identify studies that could potentially useful to synthesise comparative efficacy data for evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin in patients with HeFH: 

- exclusion of studies not specifically in patients with HeFH 

- exclusion of studies that do not include either evolocumab plus statin or ezetimibe plus statin as a treatment arm 

- exclusion of phase 2 studies if an equivalent phase 3 study in the same population had been conducted. 

8 publications reporting data for 2 studies were identified as being potentially useful for synthesising comparative efficacy for evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin in patients with HeFH (Figure 4-12). All publications excluded were documented along with the reasons for exclusion (Appendix III).

One of the two included studies was RUTHERFORD-2,[102] and the other (ENHANCE),[83] assessed ezetimibe in combination with simvastatin versus simvastatin alone in patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia. The primary outcome of ENHANCE was to assess the change from baseline in ultrasonographic measurement of the mean carotid-artery intimamedia thickness. The ENHANCE publication reported LDL-C levels at baseline and at endof-study (2 years). Patients were washed out of prior lipid-lowering therapy before the randomisation and were then randomised to either simvastatin and placebo or simvastatin and ezetimibe. As such, the baseline LDL-C measurements were not comparable between ENHANCE and RUTHERFORD-2 given the patients in ENHANCE were untreated for a minimum of 6 weeks prior to baseline whereas the patients in RUTHERFORD-2 were being treated with stable dose(s) of a statin and lipid-regulating drugs for at least 4 weeks prior to screening and continued to be treated with these therapies on study. Because of the difference in the baseline LDL-C measurements, the percent change from baseline within each patient was not comparable between ENHANCE and RUTHERFORD-2 either, which meant the difference in percent change from baseline between the two studies could not be derived.Therefore, a network meta-analysis to synthesize comparative efficacy data was deemed neither appropriate nor feasible.

## **Summary of methodology of the relevant non-randomised and non-controlled evidence** 

TAUSSIG is an ongoing long-term, open-label phase 2/3 study, which enrols patients who completed study 20110233 (TESLA, a phase 2/3 study in patients with HoFH) as well as de novo patients with FH, including either HoFH or HeFH.[123] 

After being assessed for inclusion and exclusion criteria (Table 4-21), and after providing informed consent, patients received open-label evolocumab 420 mg. Patients not undergoing apheresis at enrolment or within the prior 8 weeks (‘non-apheresis patients’) initiated treatment with 420 mg QM and patients undergoing apheresis at enrolment (‘apheresis patients’) initiated treatment with evolocumab 420 mg Q2W.

|---|---|

Patients visited the site QM (non-apheresis patients) or Q2W (apheresis patients) until week 24, after which they received a 12-week supply of evolocumab if they decided to self-administer evolocumab. Beyond week 24, these patients visited the site every 12 weeks for central laboratory tests. Patients who decided to continue to receive evolocumab at the study centre continued to visit the site QM or Q2W. At week 12, patients with < 5% LDL-C reduction from baseline and serum unbound PCSK9 < 100 ng/mL could discontinue evolocumab. If serum unbound PCSK9 was ≥ 100 ng/mL with QM dosing, the patient could switch to evolocumab 420 mg Q2W treatment at week 12. Patients undergoing apheresis with ≥ 5% LDL-C reduction from baseline and serum unbound PCSK9 < 100 ng/mL with Q2W treatment could switch to QM dosing at week 12. Patients will continue to receive open-label evolocumab for up to 5 years or until evolocumab becomes commercially available in the relevant patient population, whichever occurs first.[123] 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 193 -->

The prespecified primary endpoint in TAUSSIG was the incidence of treatment emergent adverse events during the extension period. Pre-specified secondary endpoints at each scheduled visit within each study period were:[123] 

- percent change in LDL-C from baseline 

- percent change in non-HDL-C from baseline 

- percent change in Lp(a) from baseline 

- percent change in ApoB from baseline 

- percent change in total cholesterol/HDL-C ratio from baseline 

- percent change in ApoB/ApoA1 ratio from baseline 

- response rate of patients with ≥ 15% reduction in LDL-C. 

## **Statistical analysis of the relevant non-randomised and non-controlled** 

## **evidence** 

Statistical analyses in TAUSSIG were descriptive in nature. No statistical inference or missing-value imputation was planned.[123] 

The interim analysis included in the submission includes data collected to 01 July 2014. Analysis sets for this interim analysis included: 

- interim analysis set: all patients enrolled in this study at the time of the data cutoff date who received ≥ 1 dose of evolocumab in TAUSSIG 

- HoFH interim analysis set: all patients who received ≥ 1 dose of evolocumab in TAUSSIG and either met the clinical criteria of HoFH or who had supportive genetic information 

- severe FH interim analysis set: all patients who received ≥ 1 dose of evolocumab in TAUSSIG and were not included in the HoFH interim analysis set. 

As patients with HoFH are not relevant to the decision problem, only patients included in the severe FH interim analysis set (all of whom had severe HeFH, with a mean baseline calculated LDL-C of 4.9 mmol/L) will be discussed further in this submission. 

## **Participant flow in the relevant non-randomised and non-controlled evidence** 

As of the 01 July 2014 data cutoff date, a total of 142 patients with severe HeFH were enrolled in TAUSSIG, including 16 apheresis patients and 126 non-apheresis patients, and were included in the severe FH interim analysis set. Approximately half of the patients (61%) were male, the majority were of white race (96%) and the majority were not of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity (96%). The mean (standard deviation) age of patients at baseline was 54 (12) years and mean (standard deviation) calculated LDL-C was 4.9 (1.6) mmol/L. Approximately 54% of patients had a prior diagnosis of coronary artery disease, 18% had a prior diagnosis of cerebrovascular disease or peripheral arterial disease, and approximately 11% had diabetes mellitus type 2.[123] 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765]

## **Clinical efficacy results of the relevant non-randomised and non-controlled** 

## **evidence** 

## _Details of evidence presented_ 

Similar to clinical efficacy results for the relevant RCTs presented in Section 4.7, of the prespecified efficacy outcome, the only prespecified efficacy outcome presented in the main submission is percent change from baseline in calculated LDL-C. Results for other prespecified efficacy outcomes are available in the interim CSR.[123] 

As requirement of apheresis is included as an outcome of interest in the decision problem, results from an analysis of apheresis requirements prespecified in the statistical analysis plan (SAP) are also presented.[124] 

## _Clinical efficacy results_ 

Treatment with evolocumab led to consistent mean percent reductions (from baseline to 36 weeks) in calculated LDL-C of approximately 50% in patients with severe HeFH (Table 4-22). Reductions at weeks 48 to 108 were generally consistent with those at the other visits, but the small number of patients who provided data at these visits limits interpretation of the results.[123] 

In the prespecified analysis of apheresis requirements, of the 16 patients with severe HeFH undergoing apheresis, 5 (31%) had stopped or reduced the frequency of apheresis at the time of data cut-off. This included 4 patients (25%) who stopped apheresis altogether, and 1 subject who was able to decrease apheresis frequency from two-weekly to monthly.[124]

## **Integrated safety data** 

_Overview of integrated safety analyses_ 

Integrated analyses of safety data were conducted for the purposes of regulatory assessment, including data from 16 phase 2 and phase 3 studies:[126,125] 

- 12 studies that were ~12 weeks in duration and four studies that were long-term studies (one 52-week completed study and three ongoing extension studies) 

- two of the 16 studies were conducted in patients with HoFH, and data from these studies are not integrated or presented in this submission as patients with HoFH are excluded from the decision problem. 

Three integrated analysis sets are used to describe the data from the primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia studies: 

- the integrated parent analysis set comprises integrated data from the parent studies (the 12-week studies in addition to the 52-week study) 

- the integrated extension SoC-controlled period analysis set comprises integrated data from year 1 (the controlled period) of the long-term extension studies 

- the integrated extension all-IP period analysis set comprises integrated data from year 2+ (the all-IP period) of the long-term extension studies. 

Details of these analysis sets, and studies contributing to each, are provided in Table 4-24.

_Overview of adverse events in the integrated safety analyses_ 

Exposure to evolocumab in the clinical program was extensive and provides for a robust and comprehensive assessment of the overall safety of evolocumab. A total of 6,026 patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia have been administered evolocumab (alone or in combination with a variety of statins and other lipid-lowering therapies), placebo, or any control (including SoC) in phase 2 and 3 studies, representing 7,235 patient-years of exposure, including 5,246 patient years exposure to evolocumab. Of the 5,115 patients who received any dose of evolocumab, 709 have received more than 2 years of treatment. 

In the integrated parent studies, the incidence of adverse events was balanced between treatment groups (any evolocumab 51.1%, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, any control 49.6%) (Table 4-25). Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity (grade 1 and grade 2), and serious adverse events and adverse events leading to discontinuation of IP were infrequently reported and generally similar across treatment groups. Serious adverse events were reported in 2.8% of patients in the any evolocumab group and 2.1% of patients receiving any control (Appendix VII). XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX 

The incidence of adverse events in the long-term extension studies, which is higher than that in the integrated parent studies, cannot be directly compared with the parent studies due to the long exposure periods in the extension studies and different controls utilised. In the year 1 SoC-controlled period of the extension studies, the patient incidence of adverse events was 65% in the evolocumab plus SoC group and 61% in the SoC group. A potential bias toward reporting more adverse events in the evolocumab group than the control group may be due to the greater number of protocol-specified visits for the evolocumab group than the control group and the open-label study design. In year 1, adverse events leading to discontinuation of IP in the evolocumab plus SoC group was 2.3%. Serious adverse events were balanced between the evolocumab plus SoC group (6.6%) and the SoC alone group

## _Common adverse events in the integrated safety analyses_ 

The common adverse events in the integrated parent studies and those in the extension studies were similar to those seen in the individual studies in the evolocumab trial program. There were no differences in the safety profile of evolocumab at varying doses and dosing intervals, including the 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM doses. The most common adverse events reported during the integrated parent studies for evolocumab were nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, and back pain (Table 4-26). In the extension studies (year 1 SoCcontrolled and year 2+ open-label periods), similar common adverse events were reported (Appendix VII).

_Adjudicated cardiovascular events and noncoronary revascularisations in the integrated safety analyses_ 

The number of positively adjudicated CV events (including revascularisation procedures), was small and similar between evolocumab and controls during the parent studies. In the extension studies, preliminary empirical evidence from safety analyses suggests that long-term use of evolocumab to lower LDL-C may be associated with reduced risk of CV events (including revascularisation procedures). In the extension studies, the proportion of patients in the evolocumab plus SoC group who experienced an adjudicated CV clinical event XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (Table 4-27). Adhoc analyses of more recent integrated data from the extension studies (21 January 2015 data cutoff date) showed a larger difference, with rates of CV events at 1 year being reduced from 2.18% in the SoC group to 0.95% in the evolocumab plus SoC group (HR in the evolocumab group, 0.47; 95% CI 0.28, 0.78; p = 0.003).[121] 

To date, the observed event reduction is similar to, if not even better than, the event reduction predicted from the CTTC relationship between LDL and CV outcomes. As discussed earlier in Section 4, reductions of approximately 50% to 60% in LDL-C concentrations were observed and maintained with long-term administration of evolocumab plus SoC compared with SoC alone during the year-long controlled treatment periods of the extension studies. It is estimated that the average absolute reduction in LDL-C with evolocumab plus SoC was 1.85 mmol/L in OSLER/OSLER-2 during weeks 12 to 48.[121] If the relationship, as described by the CTTC between reduction in LDL-C and relative risk of major CV events for the statins, were to apply to evolocumab (risk ratio per 1 mmol/L reduction in LDL-C = 0.78), the estimated risk of major CV events in the evolocumab arm is anticipated to be 0.63 (0.78[1.85] ) x the risk in the SoC arm. 

Although it is acknowledged that these data are preliminary and the trials are not powered to detect a difference in major CV events, the point estimates provided are in the direction and of the magnitude that would be expected, and are consistent with similar ad-hoc analyses with another PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab).[114] These results are also consistent with a meta-analysis of safety data from randomised clinical trials of PCSK9 inhibitors.[128] This meta-analysis showed that, compared with no PCSK9 inhibitor, use of PCSK9 inhibitors resulted in a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality (OR = 0.45; 95% CI 0.23, 0.86]; p = 0.015), a reduction in CV mortality (OR = 0.50; 95% CI 0.23, 1.10]; p = 0.084), and a significant reduction in the rate of MI (OR = 0.49; 95% CI 0.26, 0.93; p = 0.030). 

No patterns or changes in electrocardiogram parameters were observed.

## _Adverse events of interest in the integrated safety analyses_ 

No safety issues were noted for adverse events associated with other lipid-lowering therapies (i.e. diabetes, liver, and muscle events), events associated with other injectable protein therapies (i.e. hypersensitivity events, injection site reactions), or events that could theoretically be associated with PCSK9 inhibition/LDLR upregulation (i.e. hepatitis C events). 

**Muscle and creatine kinase:** Using the standard MedRA query (SMQ) narrow search strategy for potential muscle-related adverse events, XXXXXX were reported in any evolocumab-treated patients during the parent studies and year 1 SoC-controlled period of the extension studies; XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX was reported during year 2+ of the extension studies. 

The incidence of creatine kinase (CK) > 5 x upper limit of normal (ULN) or > 10 x ULN in the integrated parent and the integrated extension analyses was similar and was also comparable across treatment groups within the analysis periods. In the integrated parent studies, 0.7% of patients in both the any evolocumab group and the any control group had CK > 5 x ULN at any postbaseline visit. For CK > 10 x ULN, the incidence was also the same between the groups: 0.2% of patients in both the any evolocumab group and the any control group. In the year 1 SoC-controlled period of the extension studies, 0.6% of patients in the evolocumab plus SoC group, and 1.2% of patients in the SoC alone group had CK > 5 x ULN at any postbaseline visit. For CK > 10 x ULN, the incidence was also similar between the groups: 0.2% of patients in the evolocumab plus SoC group and 0.6% of patients in the SoC alone group. In the year 2+ openlabel period of the extension studies, XXXX of patients had CK > 5 x ULN and XXXX patients had CK > 10 x ULN at any postbaseline visit. 

**Liver enzymes:** The incidence of liver function test abnormalities was similar in the parent and extension studies, and was also comparable across treatment groups within the three safety analysis sets. In the integrated parent studies, the incidence of aspartate aminotransferase or alanine aminotransferase > 5 x ULN at any postbaseline visit was 0.2% and 0.3% in the any evolocumab and any control groups, respectively. The incidence of aspartate aminotransferase or alanine aminotransferase > 5 x ULN remained low in the extension studies. 

**Diabetes:** Using the SMQ narrow search strategy for potential diabetes events, the incidence of diabetes events was low in the integrated parent studies (any evolocumab 0.9%; any control 0.8%), the year 1 SoC-controlled period of the extension studies (evolocumab plus SoC 2.2%; SoC alone 2.1%), and the year 2+ open-label period of the extension studies XXXX. Changes in haemoglobin A1c and fasting blood glucose in the integrated parent and the long-term extension studies were similar and were also comparable across treatment groups within the analysis periods. There were no differences in adverse events, haemoglobin A1c levels, fasting blood glucose levels, or proteinuria in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome, or neither type 2 diabetes mellitus nor metabolic syndrome at baseline.

period of the extension studies XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and the year 2+ openlabel period of the extension studies XXXX.  Hepatitis C infection was infrequent across all periods, with a total of XXXX patients in the clinical development program who were hepatitis C virus RNA positive. 

**Neurocognitive events:** Overall, no important findings were noted from a review of the Nervous System or Psychiatric Disorders system organ class in the three integrated safety analysis sets. Upon medical review of the neurocognitive events, no overall pattern related to time to onset, resolution, or outcome was identified. The majority of events occurred in patients who had risk factors (medical history and/or concomitant medications) for potential neurocognitive events. Neurocognitive events were not increased with evolocumab compared with control during the integrated parent studies. In the year 1 SOC-controlled period of the extension studies, the rate of neurocognitive events was low (< 1%) and consisted primarily of amnesia and memory impairment. In ad-hoc analyses of more recent integrated data from the extension studies (31 October 2014 data cutoff date), more neurocognitive events were observed with evolocumab plus SoC compared with SoC alone (0.9% vs: 0.3%).[121] The potential effect of variable visit schedules between arms is unknown. In the open-label extension studies, primarily with OSLER, scheduled clinic visits occurred more frequently for patients receiving evolocumab plus SoC than for patients receiving SoC alone in order for patients to receive protocol-specified in-clinic evolocumab administrations. Notably, the incidence of neurocognitive events did not appear to be related to on-treatment LDL-C. A substudy of the ongoing FOURIER outcomes study (EBBINGHAUS) will provide a robust assessment of cognitive function (Section 4.14). 

**Hypersensitivity and injection site reactions:** Using the SMQ narrow search strategy with multiple preferred terms possibly associated with hypersensitivity, the incidence of hypersensitivity was low in the integrated parent studies (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX), the year 1 SoC-controlled period of the extension studies (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX), and the year 2+ open-label period (XXXX). Most events were mild to moderate in severity. Rash and urticaria were determined to be adverse drug reactions with evolocumab use. The incidence of injection site reactions with evolocumab was also low and similar between treatment groups in the integrated parent studies (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX), the year 1 SoC-controlled period of the extension studies (evolocumab plus SoC 4.1%; SoC alone did not receive injections), and the year 2+ open-label period of the extension studies (XXXX). Most events were mild to moderate in severity. Injection site reactions were determined to be adverse drug reactions with evolocumab use. The most common injection site reaction adverse events were erythaema, pain, and bruising. 

**Immunogenicity:** Anti-evolocumab antibodies were infrequent; the cumulative incidence of binding antibodies after ≥ 1 dose of evolocumab was 0.3% (13 out of 4,915 patients) in the integrated phase 2 and phase 3 studies (as of 01 July 2014). No neutralising anti-evolocumab antibodies have been detected in any patient. Based on a review of adverse events for the patients with binding antibodies, there were no adverse events (i.e. hypersensitivity) determined

to be due to the presence of a binding antibody. No serious adverse events were temporally associated with a positive antibody result. 

**Adverse events in patients with low LDL-C:** Evolocumab represents a novel treatment that significantly reduces LDL-C levels with total reductions of magnitudes not previously demonstrated with statins and/or ezetimibe. Because cholesterol is critical to and involved in many aspects of membrane function and is a precursor for several classes of steroid hormones, adverse events potentially associated with low levels of LDL-C were explored. In the integrated parent studies, the type and incidence of adverse events observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations < 0.6 mmol/L and < 1.0 mmol/L were generally similar to those observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations ≥ 1.0 mmol/L. Adverse events were reported in 826 (51%) patients in the any evolocumab group who achieved LDL-C < 0.6 mmol/L and 1308 (51%) patients in the any evolocumab group who achieved LDL-C < 1.0 mmol/L compared with 696 (52%) patients in the any evolocumab group with ≥ 1.0 mmol/L and 1018 (50%) patients in the any control group with LDL-C ≥ 1.0 mmol/L. However, few patients in the any control group achieved LDL-C < 0.6 mmol/L; therefore, meaningful comparisons with the control group could not be made. No safety signal was identified for neurocognitive adverse events with evolocumab regardless of LDL-C level. Analyses of vitamin E and steroid analytes were performed by LDL-C subgroup, and the analyses were consistent across subgroups in the extension studies. Overall, no pattern in adverse events was noted with further reduction of LDL-C when evolocumab was administered long term. 

## **Safety and tolerability conclusions** 

Analyses of the safety and tolerability data from the evolocumab studies show that evolocumab has a favourable safety and tolerability profile in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia. In an integrated safety analysis (of 6,026 patients, representing 7,235 patient-years of exposure), as well as across populations and therapeutic settings in individual studies, adverse events were overall balanced between treatment groups. Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity, with serious adverse events and adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation infrequently reported. The most common adverse events reported during the integrated parent studies for evolocumab were nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, and back pain. Exploratory safety data from the long-term extension studies suggest that evolocumab is associated with a reduction in CV events of approximately 50%, which is consistent with that predicted (per CTTC) given the magnitude of its LDL-C lowering. No safety issues were detected for events of interest associated with other lipid-lowering therapies (i.e. diabetes events, liver events, muscle events), those associated with other injectable protein therapies (i.e. hypersensitivity events, injection site reactions), those that could theoretically be associated with PCSK9 inhibition/LDLC receptor upregulation (i.e. hepatitis C events). Anti-evolocumab antibodies were infrequent, non-neutralising, and not associated with clinically relevant adverse events.

## _**4.13 Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence**_ 

## **Summary of the principal findings from the clinical evidence base** 

## _Benefits_ 

A side-by-side analysis of efficacy across the relevant studies included within this submission support the following key efficacy conclusions. 

- Evolocumab consistently reduced LDL-C by up to approximately 72% compared with placebo and up to approximately 46% compared with ezetimibe, in addition to any background lipid-lowering therapy patients were receiving (e.g. statins), with reductions sustained with long-term therapy. 

- Evolocumab 140 mg Q2W and 420 mg QM dosing regimens are clinically equivalent, with no clinically meaningful differences in efficacy or safety observed between the two doses. 

- Reductions in LDL-C are consistent across patient populations and patient subgroups (including subgroups according to presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia). 

- Reductions in LDL-C are consistent irrespective of presence and type of background lipidlowering therapy. 

In summary, results from evolocumab clinical studies provide substantial evidence that inhibition of the PCSK9 pathway with evolocumab translates into consistent and intensive reductions in serum LDL-C concentrations. 

## _Risks_ 

The results of the analyses conducted in the primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia integrated safety analysis set for evolocumab support the following key safety conclusions. 

- Adverse events were overall balanced between groups in all three periods of the integrated safety data set, as well as across populations and therapeutic settings. 

- Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity, and serious adverse events and adverse events leading to discontinuation of IP were infrequently reported and generally similar across treatment groups. 

- No safety issues were detected for adverse events of interest associated with other lipidlowering therapies (i.e. diabetes events, liver events, muscle events) and those that could theoretically be associated with PCSK9 inhibition/LDL-C receptor upregulation (i.e. hepatitis C events). 

- Presence of anti-evolocumab antibodies was infrequent, non-neutralising, and not associated with clinically relevant adverse events. 

- The type and incidence of adverse events observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations < 0.6 mmol/L and < 1.0 mmol/L were similar to those observed in patients with LDL-C concentrations ≥ 1.0 mmol/L. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 212 -->

## _Benefit:risk conclusions_ 

The robust and long-term effects of evolocumab on LDL-C and other lipids, combined with its favourable safety and tolerability profile, demonstrate that evolocumab represents a major clinical advancement and revolutionary step-change in the management of primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia. Evolocumab will, for the first time, enable clinicians to provide high-risk patients who would otherwise remain vulnerable to CV events (because of inadequate LDL-C reduction with existing therapies) with consistent and intensive LDL-C reductions to reduce their risk of major CV events. 

## **Strengths and limitations of the clinical evidence base** 

## _Internal validity_ 

The clinical evidence base for evolocumab included in this submission includes data from relevant large, international phase 3 RCTs, the highest quality evidence for presenting and evaluating clinical efficacy. All of the relevant RCTs included in this submission were determined to be high quality (low risk of bias) following completion of an SLR, as described in Section 4.6. 

The relevant RCTs and subgroup analyses consistently demonstrate superiority of evolocumab in reducing LDL-C compared with placebo and ezetimibe, irrespective of: 

- patient population and patient characteristics (including presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia) 

- evolocumab dosing regimen (Q2W or QM) 

- presence and type of background lipid-lowering therapy. 

This consistent LDL-C-lowering effect was sustained for more than 2 years, demonstrating durability of effect. 

Analyses of safety and tolerability have been conducted based on a total of 6,026 patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia who have been administered evolocumab (alone or in combination with a variety of statins), placebo, or any control (including SoC) in phase 2 and 3 studies, representing 7,235 patient-years of exposure. This safety dataset provides a robust estimate of the safety and tolerability of evolocumab, and shows that evolocumab is generally well tolerated with a favourable safety profile. 

## _External validity_ 

All of the relevant RCTs included in this submission included patient populations that are consistent with the overall patient population defined in the decision problem i.e. patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia for whom lipid-lowering therapies would be considered in line with current NICE guidance. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 213 -->

## **Patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia (NICE CG71, CG181 and TA132)** 

Evidence supporting the efficacy of evolocumab in this patient population comes from the 12week relevant RCT LAPLACE-2, the 52-week relevant RCT DESCARTES, and the ongoing supplementary long-term extension studies OSLER and OSLER-2. 

## LAPLACE-2 

**Population:** LAPLACE-2 enrolled patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia receiving moderate- to high-intensity background statin therapy. The clinical characteristics of patients enrolled in LAPLACE-2 were consistent with those of patients in realworld clinical practice in the UK (Appendix VIII). Pre-specified and post-hoc subgroup analyses provided in Section 4.8 provide clinical efficacy data for patient subgroups defined in the decision problem, including presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia. **Intervention:** LAPLACE-2 included an assessment of evolocumab used in accordance with its MA (i.e.140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM) (Appendix I). 

**Comparator:** The comparators in LAPLACE-2 were placebo and ezetimibe, the latter of which was administered in accordance with its UK SmPC (i.e. 10 mg OD]). The background moderateto high-intensity statin therapies used in LAPLACE-2 were generally consistent with those recommended in NICE guidance and used in UK clinical practice (Appendix VIII). In the context of the background statin therapy, comparisons can be made between (i) evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin (relevant intervention and comparator in the decision problem) and (ii) evolocumab plus statin versus statin alone (relevant intervention, but not comparator). 

## DESCARTES 

**Population:** DESCARTES enrolled patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia receiving background lipid-lowering therapy. The clinical characteristics of patients enrolled in DESCARTES were consistent with those of patients in real-world clinical practice in the UK (Appendix VIII) Pre-specified and post-hoc subgroup analyses provided in Section 4.8 provide clinical efficacy data for patient subgroups defined in the decision problem, including presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia. 

**Intervention:** DESCARTES included an assessment of evolocumab used in accordance with its MA (i.e. 420 mg QM) (Appendix I). 

**Comparator:** This was a placebo-controlled study in patients receiving background lipidlowering therapies. The background lipid-lowering therapies used in DESCARTES were generally consistent with those recommended in NICE guidance and used in UK clinical practice (Appendix VIII). Using the pre-specified background therapy stratification factor subgroups, comparisons can be made between (i) evolocumab plus statin plus ezetimibe plus diet versus statin plus ezetimibe plus diet (relevant intervention and relevant comparator); (ii) evolocumab plus statin plus diet versus statin plus diet (relevant intervention but not comparator); and (iii) evolocumab plus diet versus diet alone (not relevant intervention or comparator). 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 214 -->

## OSLER/OSLER-2 

**Population:** OSLER and OSLER-2 included a heterogeneous population which completed a range of parent phase 2 and phase 3 studies, respectively. Although this diversity might be viewed as a strength in terms of the generalisability of the findings, some of the included parent studies enrolled patients (i) at low CV risk who did not receive statin therapy at baseline; or (ii) were from a Japanese patient population, which may not represent the population that would ultimately receive evolocumab in clinical practice in England and Wales. 

**Intervention:** OSLER and OSLER-2 included an evolocumab plus SoC intervention arm during the 1-year randomised, controlled period. OSLER and OSLER-2 included an assessment of evolocumab used in accordance with its MA (420 mg QM in OSLER and 140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM in OSLER-2) (Appendix I). 

**Comparator:** The comparator in OSLER and OSLER-2 was SoC. The definition of SoC was based on local guidelines, but the majority of patients were using statins and ezetimibe at the start of each of these studies. 

## **Patients with HeFH (NICE CG71 and TA132)** 

Patients with HeFH are defined as a relevant subgroup in the decision problem. Evidence supporting the efficacy of evolocumab in this patient population comes from the 12-week relevant RCT RUTHERFORD-2 and the ongoing non-randomised, non-controlled TAUSSIG study. 

## RUTHERFORD-2 

**Population:** RUTHERFORD-2 enrolled patients with HeFH unable to achieve adequate LDL-C control despite stable lipid-lowering therapy (statin ± other lipid-lowering therapy). The inclusion criteria for this study specified that patients needed to have a clinical diagnosis of HeFH according to Simon Broome criteria, which is consistent with the recommended diagnostic method specified in NICE CG71. The clinical characteristics of patients enrolled in RUTHERFORD-2 were consistent those of patients with HeFH in real-world clinical practice in the UK (Appendix VIII). Pre-specified and post-hoc subgroup analyses provided in Section 4.8 provide clinical efficacy data for patient subgroups defined in the decision problem, including presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia. 

**Intervention:** RUTHERFORD-2 included an assessment of evolocumab used in accordance with its MA (i.e.140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM) (Appendix I). 

**Comparator:** This was a placebo-controlled study patients receiving stable background lipidlowering therapy (statins ± other lipid-lowering therapies). The stable background lipid-lowering therapies received by patients in RUTHERFORD-2 were generally consistent with those recommended in NICE guidance and used in UK clinical practice (Appendix VIII). Using the prespecified ezetimibe use (yes/no) stratification factor subgroups, it is possible to make a comparison between: (i) evolocumab plus statin plus ezetimibe versus statin plus ezetimibe (relevant intervention and comparator); and (ii) evolocumab plus statin versus statin (relevant intervention, but not relevant comparator). However, due to the design of the trial, it is not 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 215 -->

possible to make a comparison between evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin (a relevant intervention and comparator in the decision problem). Many patients with HeFH unable to control LDL-C with statins alone may already be receiving additional lipid-lowering therapies such as ezetimibe (62% of patients in RUTHERFORD-2 were receiving ezetimibe at baseline), and it would not have been ethical to discontinue ezetimibe use for washout prior to randomisation to IP in RUTHERFORD-2 in these high-risk patients. Further, given the uncertainty of the treatment effect of evolocumab, it would not have been ethical to enrol patients with HeFH who had not already been offered optimal treatment with currently available therapies e.g. ezetimibe. Following a review of studies identified in the SLR as being potentially useful to synthesize comparative efficacy data for evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin, a network meta-analysis was deemed neither appropriate nor feasible (Section 4.10). Further, no comparison of evolocumab monotherapy versus ezetimibe monotherapy (a relevant intervention and comparator in statin intolerant or contraindicated patients) in the HeFH population in RUTHERFORD-2 is possible given that all patients were required to be on stable doses of statins, and subgroups of patients according to history of intolerance to statins were not investigated. Given the consistency of treatment effect of evolocumab across multiple studies in different populations, it is reasonable to assume that the relative efficacy of evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin (based on LAPLACE-2) and relative efficacy of evolocumab monotherapy versus ezetimibe monotherapy in statin intolerant or contraindicated patients (based on GAUSS-2) are generalisable to the HeFH population. This is supported by the economic evaluation of ezetimibe that was utilised in NICE TA132, in which an assumption was made that the treatment effect of ezetimibe in non-HeFH patients was generalisable to patients with HeFH, in the absence of HeFH-specific efficacy data.[62] 

## TAUSSIG 

**Population:** TAUSSIG included patients with severe HeFH (mean baseline LDL-C 4.9 mmol/L), which is relevant to patients in England and Wales who also have severe forms of this disease (Figure 3-1). 

**Intervention:** Patients in TAUSSIG received evolocumab 420 mg QM (non-apheresis patients) or 420 mg Q2W (apheresis patients). The QM dose is in accordance with evolocumab’s MA for patients with HeFH but the Q2W dose is not (Appendix I). Generalisability across the two doses of evolocumab is limited as patients could discontinue, or switch between the two doses, pending achievement of defined LDL-C levels. 

**Comparator:** Not applicable. 

## **Patients for whom statins are not tolerated or are not clinically appropriate (NICE CG181 and TA132)** 

Patients with statin intolerance are defined as a relevant subgroup in the decision problem. Evidence supporting the efficacy of evolocumab in this patient population comes from the 12week relevant RCT GAUSS-2. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 216 -->

**Population:** The clinical characteristics of patients enrolled in GAUSS-2 were consistent with those of patients in real-world clinical practice in the UK (Appendix VIII). GAUSS-2 enrolled patients with previous intolerance to two or more statins, defined as inability to tolerate any dose or increase the dose above the smallest tablet strength because of intolerable muscle-related side effects. The use of muscle symptoms as a key identifier of statin intolerance is consistent with the definition of statin intolerance provided in NICE CG71 and TA132. CG181 specifies that statin intolerance should be defined clinically as the inability to tolerate 3 different statins,[92] which is more than the minimum number of statins patients were required to be intolerant to in GAUSS-2, though > 50% patients enrolled in GAUSS-2 were intolerant to ≥ 3 statins (Section 4.5). The definition of statin intolerance used in GAUSS-2 is also consistent with clinical practice in the UK, where respondents to a clinician survey reported that 74% and 66% of patients with potential statin intolerance and established statin intolerance (following e.g. statin rechallenge, statin regimen modification, and CK/transaminase testing), respectively, presented with muscle symptoms.[129] Further, 75% of respondents indicated that they would try two or more statins before considering a patient statin intolerant. Pre-specified and post-hoc subgroup analyses provided in Section 4.8 provide clinical efficacy data for patient subgroups defined in the decision problem, including presence or risk of CVD and severity of hypercholesterolaemia. Although GAUSS-2 did not include any patients contraindicated to statins, it is reasonable to assume that the treatment effect of evolocumab in GAUSS-2 is representative of this patient population in the absence of specific evidence in statin-contraindicated patients. 

**Intervention:** GAUSS-2 included an assessment of evolocumab used in accordance with its MA (i.e.140 mg Q2W or 420 mg QM) (Appendix I). 

**Comparator:** The comparator in GAUSS-2 was ezetimibe, which was administered in accordance with its MA (i.e.10 mg OD); this comparator is consistent with the relevant comparator in the decision problem for this population (i.e. ezetimibe monotherapy). A minority (18%) of the patients enrolled in GAUSS-2 remained on low-dose statin at baseline. This is reflective of clinical practice in the UK where statin-intolerant patients may continue to be prescribed statins (Appendix VIII). 

## **Outcomes** 

The current evidence base does not include an assessment of the incidence of CV events as an efficacy outcome (although a CV outcomes study, FOURIER, is ongoing [Section 4.14]), the evidence supporting LDL-C as a therapeutic target and validated surrogate for CV outcomes is multi-faceted, as discussed in Section 3. Epidemiological and interventional studies demonstrate a proportional and continuous relationship between LDL-C and CV outcomes irrespective of treatment mechanism, whilst genetic variants that are associated with variations in LDL-C demonstrate the expected impact on CVD risk. This is recognised in NICE guidance (TA132).[62] Further, exploratory safety data from the long-term extension studies suggest that evolocumab is associated with a reduction in CV events of approximately 50%, which is consistent with that predicted (per CTTC) given the magnitude of its LDL-C lowering. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 217 -->

## **Interpretation of clinical efficacy and safety evidence conclusions** 

The clinical evidence base included in this submission includes robust, high-quality evidence (with low risk of bias) on the consistent, intensive, and long-term efficacy of evolocumab with respect to lowering LDL-C across various patient populations and therapeutic settings, as well as its favourable safety and tolerability profile. The evidence base adequately addresses the decision problem, provides data in relevant patient populations and versus relevant comparators, and is generalisable to patients who will ultimately receive evolocumab in clinical practice in England and Wales. 

## _**4.14 Ongoing studies**_ 

Amgen is currently conducting studies intended to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of evolocumab in LDL-C lowering, the effect of evolocumab in reducing CV morbidity/mortality (FOURIER) and coronary atherosclerosis using intravascular ultrasound (GLAGOV), the effect of evolocumab in special populations (e.g. patients with statin intolerance [GAUSS-3] and paediatric patients with FH [HAUSER]), and the effect of evolocumab on neurocognitive function (EBBINGHAUS). Table 4-28 summarises all ongoing studies of evolocumab. 

Within 12 months of this submission (i.e. through July 2016), we anticipate that the following will be published: 

- a 52-week analysis of the effects of evolocumab on vitamin E and steroid hormone levels based on the DESCARTES study 

- an analysis of the efficacy and safety of evolocumab in statin-treated, Japanese patients at high CV risk based on the YUKAWA-2 study 

- 52-week results from the ongoing TAUSSIG study 

- results from the FLOREY study, which assessed the impact of evolocumab in combination with atorvastatin on lipoprotein kinetics 

- an analysis of the relationship between long-term reduction in LDL-C and Lp(a).

## **5 Cost effectiveness** 

- A _de novo_ cost-effectiveness Markov model analysis was developed for the economic evaluation and undertaken in accordance with the NICE reference case. A lifetime analysis was performed (cycle length of one year; half-cycle correction used). Costs and outcomes were discounted at 3.5% per annum. 

- Drug costs were taken from the NHS Drug Tariff. The acute and long-term care costs of CV events were based on a retrospective longitudinal observation cohort study using CPRD and HES data. 

- Health state utilities were based on NICE CG181 for acute and long-term CVD states. 

- Baseline characteristics from the relevant phase 3 evolocumab RCTs were used for the populations under assessment to inform baseline CV risk using Framingham Heart Study and Reach registry risk equations. 

- Baseline CV rates were calibrated based on estimations for patients with and without existing CVD and HeFH using CPRD and FH registry data. 

- LDL-C reductions from the relevant phase 3 evolocumab RCTs were used for evolocumab and ezetimibe to model the translation between LDL-C and CV events for the treatment strategies, based on the CTTC meta-analysis for LDL-C reduction and major CV events. 

- Populations: The following populations have been considered in the context of NICE guidance for whom lipid-lowering therapies would be considered; patients with and without existing CVD at high residual risk due to additional risk factors, and patients with HeFH. 

- Evolocumab and ezetimibe (comparator) were considered in accordance with their MAs. 

- Parameter uncertainty was assessed in a series of scenario analyses, deterministic sensitivity analyses and probabilistic sensitivity analysis. 

- Threshold analyses indicate the evolocumab represents a cost-effective treatment option compared with ezetimibe in patients without existing CVD and at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (based on QRISK2 score) according to the severity of hypercholesterolaemia. 

- Base case deterministic results show that when age and gender are taken into consideration, the incremental cost per QALY gained is less than £30,000 in patients with existing CVD and at high residual risk due to the presence of one or more additional risk factors (e.g. diabetes mellitus or CKD) according to the severity of hypercholesterolaemia. 

- The incremental cost per QALY gained is approximately £XXXXX to £ XXXXX for evolocumab versus ezetimibe in patients with HeFH when assessed across the four treatment scenarios. 

- The cost-effectiveness results were robust to a number of scenario analyses, univariate sensitivity analyses and probabilistic sensitivity analysis conducted to assess uncertainty.

## _**5.1 Published cost-effectiveness studies**_ 

## **Identification of studies** 

A SLR was conducted to systematically identify, critically review, and summarise studies evaluating the cost-effectiveness of evolocumab, statins, and ezetimibe for LDL-C reduction in adults with hypercholesterolaemia. The review of model structures was used to inform the cost-effectiveness model used for this appraisal. The SLR was conducted in accordance with general guidelines for conducting systematic reviews published by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD).[130] 

## _Information sources_ 

The search included peer-reviewed journal articles, HTA documents, and data from relevant conference proceedings (i.e. published studies only) identified through the systematic search process described below. 

## _Databases_ 

The literature review was conducted on 31 December 2014, and the following electronic databases were searched: 

- MEDLINE 

- Embase 

- Econlit 

- National Health Service Economic Evaluations Database (NHS EED). 

MEDLINE, Embase, and Econlit were accessed via the Ovid gateway, and NHS EED was accessed via the CRD website. The search was limited to articles with abstracts written in the English language and published between 2000 and 2014. 

Searches before 2000 were not performed because no relevant economic evaluations were expected to be published before that date. Furthermore, estimates of resource use and unit costs published more than 15 years ago would be outdated; the resource use quoted in older articles would not be reflective of current clinical practice and unit costs may not represent current prices. 

The search strategy used was formulated using terms focussing on (i) LDL-C, (ii) lipidlowering therapy, and (iii) economic evaluations. Appendix F of the NICE lipid modification CG (CG181)[131] was used to inform the search terms for the lipid-lowering therapy, health conditions, and excluded publication types. Medical Subject Headings and keyword searches were used and edited in line with the appropriate search syntax for the different databases used. All search strategies are provided in Appendix IX. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 223 -->

## _Conference proceedings_ 

In the conference proceedings search, conference abstracts published in 2013 and 2014 from the following congresses were reviewed: 

- International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research (ISPOR) 

- American College of Cardiology (ACC) 

- American Heart Association (AHA) 

- European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 

- European Atherosclerosis Society (EAS). 

The 2-year timeframe for the conference abstract search was selected as full publications were anticipated following this period. The conference proceeding search used the same strategy as the Embase search strategy. All conferences were indexed in Embase except ESC 2014, EAS 2014, and EAS 2013. The websites of the conferences not indexed by Embase were searched manually for relevant abstracts. Conference abstracts presented at ESC 2014 were indexed via www.congress365.escardio.org, and abstracts presented at EAS 2014 were indexed via www.atherosclerosis-journal.com. There was no website available for the EAS 2013 conference abstracts. All search strategies are provided in Appendix IX. 

## _HTA documents_ 

In addition, HTA documents assessing economic evaluations of lipid-lowering drug therapies were identified through a manual search of the HTA websites of the UK (including NICE, All Wales Medical Strategy Group, and the SMC), Spain, Sweden, France, Australia, Canada, Netherlands, Belgium, Austria, Ireland, Portugal, Poland, Hungary, Slovenia, Mexico, and Brazil. Economic evaluations of lipid-lowering therapies reported in HTA submissions between 2000 and 2014 were selected. Searches before 2000 were not performed because no relevant economic evaluations were expected to be published beyond the time horizon of the past 15 years. All search strategies are provided in Appendix IX. 

## _Other sources_ 

Reference sections of review articles identified in search results were hand searched for original relevant articles fitting the identified search criteria of economic studies, describing a health condition in cardiovascular diseases, evaluating lipid-lowering therapies, and published in the English language between 2000 and 2014.

## **Validity assessment** 

After the literature had been obtained from the databases, the conference proceedings, and HTA searches, a three-stage process was used to identify relevant articles for extraction. In the first stage, titles and abstracts from the peer-reviewed literature and HTA documents were reviewed for eligibility against inclusion/exclusion criteria. The articles and documents meeting the criteria were selected for full-text review (stage 2). The first two stages of the literature review were carried out by two researchers independently. If a study did not meet the eligibility criteria, the reason for exclusion was noted in a data extraction form. Articles considered eligible after full-text review were selected for data extraction, which constituted the third stage of the review process. 

## **Description of identified studies** 

The database literature search (in MEDLINE, Embase, Econlit, and NHS EED) identified 882 citation results. Of these, 107 articles were duplicates and subsequently removed from the review for a total of 775 unique articles that could proceed to phase 1 selection. A list of the duplicate studies can be found in Appendix IX. Of the unique articles, 645 were excluded after a review of titles/abstracts (stage 1). During stage 1 of the review process, one additional hand-searched article was identified, for a total of 131 articles retrieved for full-text review (stage 2). After full-text review, during which a further 35 studies were excluded, a total of 96 studies from the database search were included for data extraction. A full list of the 35 excluded studies from stage 2, can be found in Appendix IX. 

The PRISMA flow chart of the inclusion and exclusion of the studies from the database search is presented in Figure 5-1.

For the final data extraction, 108 studies were included (96 identified through database searches, 11 HTA documents, and one conference proceeding). A full list of studies reporting relevant economic evaluations and the main items included during data extraction are presented in Appendix IX. This table is composed of publications from the database search (n = 96; highlighted green), HTA documents (n = 11; highlighted orange), and conference proceedings (n = 1; highlighted blue). 

The data extraction was focussed on the population consisting of adults with hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia for whom lipid-lowering therapies would be considered. This population is eligible for treatment with evolocumab and of interest for the cost-effectiveness model, as described in more detail in section 5.2. Most of the papers presented results based on models with a UK focus (n = 28). A further two studies were from Argentina, seven from Australia, two from Belgium, 11 from Canada, two from Finland, two from Greece, three from Ireland, two from Japan, two from Korea, five from Netherlands, two from Spain, four from Sweden, 19 from the USA, and 10 were conducted in multiple countries. Additionally, single studies were identified that focussed on Austria, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, France, Hungary, Italy, Philippines, Portugal, Tanzania. 

Of the 108 extracted studies, most used a Markov model (n = 66) and 53 (approximately 50%) studies modelled a lifetime time horizon (25 years or more). None of the identified publications presented an economic evaluation of evolocumab. 

_Economic evaluation summary data extraction tables._ 

Table 5-2 highlights the data extracted from studies with a UK focus that present a Markov model with a lifetime time horizon. A full overview table, providing details from all studies that underwent data extraction is provided in Appendix IX.

One of the publications presented in Table 5-2 is NICE CG181. The economic evaluation was based on a Markov model with a lifetime time horizon and 1-year cycle length from a UK NHS perspective. The model was used to investigate the effect of low-, medium-, and highintensity statin therapy on the occurrence of CV events in adults without CVD, with diabetes and without CVD, and with existing CVD in England and Wales. The model inputs used are extracted from the SLR. 

## **Quality assessment** 

Quality assessments for the extracted studies were conducted using the Drummond and Jefferson instrument (1996).[143] The Drummond and Jefferson instrument comprises 36 items that assess the comprehensiveness of cost-effectiveness studies. An example quality assessment form and the completed quality assessment forms are presented in Appendix IX. Of the 108 studies extracted, 19 (17.6%) were deemed to be of low quality (scored < 75%), 63 (58.3%) to be of average quality (scored 75-89%), and 26 (24.1%) to be of high quality (scored ≥ 90%). Studies were not selected or excluded from the review based on quality assessment. 

## _**5.2**_ **De novo** _**analysis**_ 

## **Patient population** 

The overall patient populations included in the economic evaluation reflect both the anticipated indication for evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia and the patient populations evaluated in the relevant phase 3 studies. 

In the context of existing NICE CG and TA guidance for the management of hypercholesterolaemia with lipid-lowering therapies, the economic evaluation considered evolocumab in combination with a statin and/or other lipid-lowering therapies in the following specific patient populations according to severity of hypercholesterolaemia (as outlined in the decision problem): 

- presence or risk of CVD 

- patients with HeFH 

- patients with statin intolerance or for whom a statin is contraindicated. 

For the assessment of patients with presence or risk of CVD, the patient population from LAPLACE-2 was used on the basis of baseline characteristics for CVD history in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia. For patients without existing CVD, analyses were conducted on the basis of baseline LDL-C (severity of hypercholesterolaemia) to establish the 10-year CVD risks (measured using a risk assessment tool such as QRISK2) at which treatment with evolocumab in accordance with its MA would be deemed a cost-effective use of NHS resources. 

For the assessment of patients with HeFH, the patient population from RUTHERFORD-2 has been used since it specifically enrolled patients with HeFH (Simon Broome criteria) who did not achieve adequate LDL-C control (i.e. LDL-C ≥ 2.6 mmol/L). 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 235 -->

GAUSS-2 enrolled patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia unable to tolerate any statins or a statin dose high enough to control their LDL-C levels. However, for the purposes of the economic evaluation, the patient populations from LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 were used since statin intolerance or contraindication is considered a subgroup of the primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia, and HeFH populations. Furthermore, there is no RCT assessing evolocumab in a HeFH population with statin intolerance. LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 were used instead of GAUSS-2, since patients that are intolerant or contraindicated to statins are anticipated to have a greater severity of hypercholesterolaemia as they cannot achieve adequate LDL-C control with lipid-lowering therapies (e.g. low dose statin or alternative lipid-lowering therapy). Baseline LDL-C levels were 2.7 mmol/L to 2.9 mmol/L, 3.9 mmol/L to 4.2 mmol/L, and 5.0 mmol/L to 5.1 mmol/L in LAPLACE-2, RUTHERFORD-2 and GAUSS-2, respectively. Therefore, the LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 patient populations were used with additional cost-effectiveness analyses based on severity of hypercholesterolaemia (baseline LDL-C) to represent populations that are intolerant or contraindicated to statins. 

## **Model structure** 

A _de novo_ cost-effectiveness Markov model was developed for the economic evaluation of evolocumab in accordance with its MA. The model was developed to capture the lifetime progression of CVD among adults with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia. A Markov modelling approach was chosen because it adequately captures the scope of the disease and clinical practice of CVD. Furthermore, this approach is commonly applied in other published economic evaluation studies evaluating the cost-effectiveness of drugs for LDL-C reduction in hypercholesterolaemia.[62,77,134,140,142,144-148] Figure 5-2 illustrates the core model structure with possible transitions indicated by arrows between the model health states. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765]
