of evolocumab added to statins versus statins was computed in a 1-year time horizon, matching the duration of OSLER. A rate ratio of 0.48, meaning a 52% percent reduction in fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events and revascularisations, was obtained from the model. This compares favourably to the hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.28, 0.78; p = 0.003), meaning a 53% reduction in outcomes, presented in OSLER. The reduction in CV events in the economic model and OSLER are therefore well aligned. 

## _**5.15 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence**_ 

The economic evaluation considered patient populations that are consistent with the overall patient population defined in the decision problem, i.e. patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia for whom lipid-lowering therapies would be considered in line with current NICE guidance. Although evolocumab provides a consistent and intensive LDL-C lowering treatment effect in all patient populations indicated and in line with current NICE guidance, the priority for use of evolocumab is in those patients who are at the highest residual risk and are most vulnerable to CV events. 

In patients without existing CVD, 10-year CVD risk threshold analyses were conducted to identify the minimum 10-year risk required for evolocumab to be cost-effective at different willingness-to-pay thresholds. Although QRISK2 is the risk assessment tool recommended in NICE CG181 for patients without existing CVD, 10-year CVD risks based on the Framingham study (primary prevention) and REACH registry (recurrent events) were used in the economic evaluation for patients without existing CVD, for the reasons outlined in Section 5.3. However, to align with NICE guidance, the absolute minimum 10-year risks expressed as QRISK2 scores are proposed as criteria for initiation of treatment with evolocumab in this population. This can be considered a conservative approach, given that the Framingham study includes a narrower definition of CVD events (i.e. any given risk based on the Framingham definition of CVD will be be higher than that of QRISK2 in any given patient). 

To date, no other economic evaluations have specifically assessed the cost-effectiveness of lipid-lowering therapies in patients with existing CVD and at high residual risk due to the presence of additional risk factors. NICE CG181 recommends that a risk assessment tool should not be used in patients with existing CVD. Further, currently-available risk assessment tools (e.g. QRISK2 and SCORE) are not intended for use in patients with existing CVD. Therefore, threshold analyses based on 10-year CVD risk as conducted for patients without existing CVD would not be appropriate in the context of current clinical practice and guidelines. To enable the identification of patients at high residual risk due to additional risk factors, various sources of evidence were assessed, i.e. ESC/EAS 2011 guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias, a targeted literature review of recurrent CVD risk equations and consultation with UK clinicians. Based on this assessment, patient characteristics relevant for identifying patients with existing CVD at high residual risk were identified where the clinical and cost-effectiveness of evolocumab will be optimal in accordance with recognised willingness-to-pay thresholds. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 346 -->

There are a number of strengths in the economic evaluation. Firstly, the clinical evidence underpinning the economic evaluation is based on robust, high-quality evidence (with low risk of bias) on the consistent and sustained effectiveness of evolocumab with respect to lowering LDL-C across various patient populations and therapeutic settings. Secondly, UK observational data (CPRD, HES, and Office of National Statistics) has been used to quantify the acute and long-term CV baseline rates for patient populations of interest and the costs of CV events of interest. These sources are supplementary to previously conducted economic evaluations in the UK. This provides certainty that the anticipated benefits and costs are relevant and reflect the decision problem for this appraisal. Thirdly, evidence for the baseline risk in the HeFH population was identified in a systematic manner (including assessment of bias) in order to estimate the rate ratio for CV event in these high-risk populations. Fourthly, the _de novo_ model included additional combined CVD states in order to attenuate the memory-less attribute of a Markov model to appropriately associated CVD history for risk, costs, and utilities. This has been attempted indirectly previously in economic evaluations by associating differential utility weights based on number of CV events. 

There are some weaknesses associated with the economic evaluation. Firstly, there are limited long-term data on clinical effectiveness and safety evidence for evolocumab requiring the extrapolation of LDL-C treatment effect over the lifetime horizon. However, supplementary evidence from ongoing, long-term extension studies (OSLER and OSLER-2) indicates that the reduction in LDL-C is maintained for more than 2 years and that evolocumab has a favourable safety and tolerability profile (data representing 7,235 patientyears of exposure to date). Secondly, in the absence of long-term clinical effectiveness data for CV events, we have translated changes in surrogate outcomes (LDL-C) to reductions in CV events based on established findings from the CTTC meta-analysis of 26 statin trials with 129,138 individuals. This relationship is based on evidence from observational, clinical, and genetic data. It is anticipated that the long-term efficacy of evolocumab with respect to reduction of CV events will be demonstrated in a fully-enrolled ongoing study assessing the impact of evolocumab on CV morbidity/mortality (FOURIER). In the interim, supplementary evidence from ongoing, long-term extension studies (OSLER and OSLER-2) show that the reduction in LDL-C is maintained for more than 2 years and that evolocumab is associated with a reduction in CV events of approximately 50%, which is consistent with that predicted as per the CTTC. Additionally, the external validity assessment indicates that the predictions from the model are consistent with the findings from the CTTC in terms of LDL-C reduction to CV events and the findings of OSLER/OSLER-2. Thirdly, there is a lack of direct evidence of evolocumab versus ezetimibe in patients with HeFH. In the absence of this, head-to-head evidence for the relative treatment effect from LAPLACE-2 and GAUSS-2 are used in the HeFH population since the treatment effect of evolocumab was consistent regardless of patient population and patient characteristics, evolocumab dosing regimen, and presence and type of background lipid-lowering therapy. 

Further research and analyses for HRQoL data representing disabilities associated with the CVD health states used in the economic evaluation use a number of assumptions to model the changes associated with events. As for risks and costs, evidence is required for differences in short- and long-term changes in HRQoL associated with individual events and any potential difference in HRQoL associated with primary or subsequent events.

## **Current treatment options and market share** 

The current treatment option in the relevant populations is ezetimibe (NICE TA132) for those in whom LDL-C is not adequately controlled with statin therapy, or for those that are intolerant to statins. It is assumed that the absolute market share for ezetimibe will remain constant over time and is estimated at 15% and 37% in patients with and without existing CVD, and patients with HeFH, respectively.[211] The uptake of evolocumab was assumed to increase over time as an alternative to ezetimibe. ## **Additional treatment costs** 

The costs of monitoring and training have been included in addition to drug acquisition costs. 

## **Unit costs** 

The following unit costs have been considered for the budget impact analysis. 

- Drug acquisition costs for evolocumab and ezetimibe were based on the respective dosing regimens, cost per pack, and total doses per year (Table 5-21). The cost of ezetimibe was based on the NHS Drug Tariff.[204] 

- Monitoring costs for evolocumab and ezetimibe were based on healthcare resource use from NICE CG181 and unit costs from NHS Reference Costs 2013/2014[206] and PSSRU (Table 5-22).[202,205] 

## **Resource savings** 

Between 2014 and 2020, the estimated direct cost of CVD is expected to rise from approximately £10 billion per year to approximately £12 billion per year, underlying the importance of making available new therapeutic options to reduce the incidence and longterm costs of CVD (Section 3). The costs associated with acute and long-term management of CV events are based on those described in Table 5-23. The introduction of evolocumab is anticipated to result in a significantly greater reduction of CV events due to substantially greater magnitude of LDL-C reduction relative to ezetimibe. These were based on a CPRD study for healthcare resource use and unit costs from NHS Reference Costs 2013/2014[206] and PSSRU Unit Costs of Health and Social Care 2013.[205]

## **Single Technology Appraisal (STA)** 

## **Evolocumab for treating primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia ID765** 

## Dear XXX 

The Evidence Review Group, the School of Health and Related Research (ScHARR) at the University of Sheffield, and the technical team at NICE have now had an opportunity to take a look at the submission received on the 22[nd] of July 2015 by Amgen. In general terms they felt that it is well presented and clear. However, the ERG and the NICE technical team would like further clarification relating to the clinical and cost effectiveness data. 

Both the ERG and the technical team at NICE will be addressing these issues in their reports. 

We request you to provide a written response to this letter to the Institute by **5pm** , **Tuesday 25 August** . Two versions of this written response should be submitted; one with academic/commercial in confidence information clearly marked and one from which this information is removed. 

Please underline all confidential information, and separately highlight information that is submitted under ‘commercial in confidence’ in turquoise, and all information submitted under ‘academic in confidence’ in yellow. 

If you present data that is not already referenced in the main body of your submission and that data is seen to be academic/commercial in confidence information, please complete the attached checklist for in confidence information. 

Please do not ‘embed’ documents (i.e. PDFs, spreadsheets) within your response as this may result in your information being displaced or unreadable. Any supporting documents should be uploaded to NICE Docs/Appraisals. 

If you have any further queries on the technical issues raised in this letter then please contact Ahmed Elsada, Technical Lead (ahmed.elsada@nice.org.uk). Any procedural questions should be addressed to Lori Farrar, Project Manager (lori.farrar@nice.org.uk) in the first instance. 

Yours sincerely 

Dr Frances Sutcliffe Associate Director – Appraisals Centre for Health Technology Evaluation

## **A: Clarification on clinical-effectiveness data** 

## **A1 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Appendix III, Section 2, pages 5–26. The ERG notes that the clinical effectiveness searches do not include terms for dyslipidaemia/mixed dyslipidaemia. Please clarify the reasons for this.** 

A decision was made during development of the systematic literature review (SLR) that the use of the terms ‘hypercholesterolaemia’ and ‘hyperlipidaemia’ would be sufficient to identify all relevant studies given that all patients with mixed dyslipidaemia (i.e. hypercholesterolaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia) have hypercholesterolaemia. Dyslipidaemias other than hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia are outside of the licensed indication for evolocumab. 

The only studies that are relevant to the decision problem are those assessing evolocumab (either alone or in combination with statins with or without ezetimibe) or ezetimibe (either alone or in combination with statins). All clinical studies of evolocumab conducted to date are Amgen-sponsored, and all of these enrolled patients with either ‘hypercholesterolaemia’ or ‘hypercholesterolemia or mixed dyslipidaemia’, meaning they would have been identified using the original search terms alone. Ezetimibe is specifically indicated for hypercholesterolaemia (not mixed dyslipidaemia), so addition of a ‘dyslipidaemia’/‘mixed dyslipidaemia’ search term is unlikely to have identified additional relevant studies in its licensed indication. Nevertheless, to assess the impact of excluding a ‘dyslipidaemia’/‘mixed dyslipidaemia’ search term from the SLR search strategies on identification of relevant ezetimibe studies, targeted searches using a search term for ‘dyslipidaemia’ were conducted in Medline, Medline in Process, Embase, CENTRAL, CDSR, and DARE (search strategies provided in Appendix I of this document). These searches yielded no relevant ezetimibe studies in addition to those already identified in the original SLR. 

## **A2: Appendix III Section 2.1, page 7. An RCT filter has been applied to the results of the clinical effectiveness Medline search. The ERG notes that this filter has been modified from the version published by Lefebvre et al. Please explain why the filter has been modified and the basis for the changes made.** 

The only amendment to the original filter was the addition of truncation to the word random$ in line 56 of the strategy to increase the sensitivity and to pick up terms such as ‘randomised’ and ‘randomisation’. In line with recommendations made by Lefebvre et al.,[1] the original source filter was clearly referenced with an indication that the filter had been amended (i.e. use of the phrase ‘Based on’). 



<!-- page 441 -->

## **A3 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 4.11, page 130. Please clarify what search was performed to identify relevant non-RCT evidence, and which inclusion/exclusion criteria were applied. Please also provide details of the identified non-RCT studies that were excluded and the reasons for their exclusion.** 

Given the robust evidence base derived from relevant randomised controlled trials (RCTs) which adequately addresses the decision problem, no systematic search was performed to identify non-RCT evidence. 

The ongoing, Amgen-sponsored TAUSSIG study enrols patients who completed study 20110233 (TESLA, a phase 2/3 study in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia [HoFH]) as well as de novo patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH), including either HoFH or heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HeFH).[2,3] Data from the TAUSSIG ‘Severe FH interim analysis set’ (i.e. patients with HeFH) were included as supplementary information given that: 

- subgroups according to severity of hypercholesterolaemia are defined as relevant subgroups in the decision problem. This study provides clinical efficacy data for evolocumab in patients with severe HeFH (mean baseline calculated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C] 4.9 mmol/L) 

- TAUSSIG provides data on the effect of evolocumab on requirement of apheresis (a relevant outcome in the decision problem) 

- TAUSSIG provides longer-term follow-up data in the HeFH population than RUTHERFORD-2. 

## **A4: Section 5.1 and Appendix IX, Tables IX-1 and IX-2. The cost-effectiveness searches on Medline and EMBASE use a filter to identify economic evaluations. However, this contains some errors (for example, pharmaco?economic* – the “?” character cannot be used to find hyphens or spaces in Ovid). Please explain why a validated filter, such as those developed by SIGN (http://sign.ac.uk/methodology/filters.html#econ), has not been used.** 

We sought to update the previously conducted cost-effectiveness study SLR in NICE CG181 by replicating the search strategy. Thank you for identifying this error. As a result, the searches were re-run in Ovid for MEDLINE and EMBASE using validated filters as developed by SIGN, and NHS EED and Econlit.  The search was run for the same period as the previous SLR (January 2000 to December 2014) and de-duplicated. Full details of the updated search stragtegies are provided in Appendix II. All the cost-effectiveness studies from the previous SLR were identified.The publications were screened at the first (title and abstract) level and second level (full-text) by two reviewers as per the methods outlined in the evidence submission (Section 5.1). 

Of the additional 272 abstracts, two were identified for full-text screening; of these only one was identified (Fitch et al., 2009)[4] for inclusion and selected for data extraction.  Fitch et al.,[4] was a cost-effectiveness study based on a three-year event forecast model with a US focus (refer to Appendix II for study data extraction). 



<!-- page 442 -->

**A5: Section.5.4 pages 206–207. The submission states that bibliography checking has been used to identify records for the systematic literature review of health-related quality of life. Please clarify whether this method has also been used to identify studies for the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness reviews, and whether the process involved citation searching to locate references forwards as well as backwards.** 

For the clinical efficacy and cost-effectiveness SLRs, the reference lists in retrieved articles and relevant systematic reviews were checked to identify additional studies. Forward citation searching was not part of the methods for these SLRs. 

**A6 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 4.2, page 67. The population described in the decision problem relates to people with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidemia, whose low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is not controlled by statins or cannot have statins (contraindicated or not tolerated), and who would therefore currently receive ezetimibe (with or without a statin). Relevant subgroups are people with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HeFH), presence or risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and severity of hypercholesterolaemia. Please clarify how the populations in the trials LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2 and DESCARTES correspond to the population defined in the final scope, including details of any deviations. Please also clarify whether HeFH patients were eligible for inclusion in these trials.** 

As described in Table A-1, LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2, and DESCARTES are generalisable to the populations described in the decision problem, though it is acknowledged there are some deviations given that these studies were global in nature and not designed specifically to meet the needs of the decision problem. 

HeFH status was not assessed in LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2, and DESCARTES, and was not an exclusion criterion in these studies.[5-11] Therefore, it is likely that some patients with HeFH were enrolled in these studies, which is supported by patient level data that show that some patients had substantially elevated LDL-C at baseline, indicative of FH.

## **A7: Section 4.2, page 67. RUTHERFORD-2 considers a specific subgroup of interest (HeFH). Please clarify whether the population in this trial had uncontrolled LDL-C levels on statins or were intolerant to statins.** 

All patients in RUTHERFORD-2 had uncontrolled LDL-C levels (≥ 2.6 mmol/L) despite treatment with stable doses of statins ± other lipid-lowering therapies, as specified in the inclusion criteria column of Table 4-4 in the evidence submission (‘Summary of eligibility criteria in the relevant RCTs’):[5,6] 



<!-- page 445 -->

- On a stable dose of an approved statin ± other allowed lipid-lowering therapy (e.g. ezetimibe, resins, stanols, or niacin) for ≥ 4 weeks before screening and, in the opinion of the investigator, not requiring uptitration 

- Fasting LDL-C ≥ 2.6 mmol/L at screening. 

In the RUTHERFORD-2 full analysis set (FAS), 76% of patients were receiving stable doses of high-intensity statins and 22% were receiving stable doses of moderate-intensity statins (per American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association statin intensity definition, which is generally consistent with NICE CG181) for ≥ 4 weeks before screening.[16,19,20] It is therefore reasonable to assume that these patients were not statin intolerant, though no information on history of intolerance to statins was collected in the study. 

**A8 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 4.1 and Table 4-1. RUTHERFORD-2 considers a specific subgroup of interest (HeFH), but is a placebo-controlled trial. This does not accord with the decision problem and its criteria relating to comparators, as specified under Section 4.1 (and Table 4-1) of the company’s submission, which requires trials of evolocumab compared with ezetimibe. Section 4.13 explains that subgroup analyses relating to exposure to ezetimibe could not be performed. Please clarify and explain the inclusion of this trial in the systematic review of clinical effectiveness.** 

Section 4.13 of the evidence submission does not state that subgroup analyses relating to exposure to ezetimibe could not be performed: 

_‘ - Using the pre specified ezetimibe use (yes/no) stratification factor subgroups, it is possible to make a comparison between: (i) evolocumab plus statin plus ezetimibe versus statin plus ezetimibe (relevant intervention and comparator); and (ii) evolocumab plus statin versus statin (relevant intervention, but not relevant comparator). However, due to the design of the trial, it is not possible to make a comparison between evolocumab plus statin versus ezetimibe plus statin (a relevant intervention and comparator in the decision problem).’_ 

RUTHERFORD-2 meets the inclusion criteria of the clinical-effectiveness SLR by providing data for a relevant intervention (evolocumab plus statin plus ezetimibe) versus a relevant comparator (statin plus ezetimibe) defined in the decision problem, though it is acknowledged in the submission that this study does not provide data for another relevant intervention (evolocumab plus statin) versus the same comparator. Many patients with HeFH unable to control LDL-C with statins alone may already be receiving additional lipid-lowering therapies such as ezetimibe (62% of patients in the RUTHERFORD-2 FAS were receiving ezetimibe at baseline),[6] and it would not have been ethical to discontinue ezetimibe use for washout prior to randomisation to IP in RUTHERFORD-2 in these high-risk patients. Further, given the uncertainty of the treatment effect of evolocumab, it would not have been ethical to enrol patients with HeFH who had not already been offered optimal treatment with currently available therapies e.g. ezetimibe. 

Further, RUTHERFORD-2 is the only phase 3 RCT that assessed evolocumab specifically in the HeFH population. Exclusion of this study would therefore not allow for evaluation of evolocumab in accordance with its full marketing authorisation (primary hypercholesterolaemia [heterozygous familial or non-familial] or mixed dyslipidaemia). 



<!-- page 446 -->

## **A9: Regarding the methods and processes of systematic review:** 

- Section 4-1, page 62. Please clarify the number of reviewers who conducted the study screening process and the procedures followed to minimise potential errors in study selection. 

- Section 4.2. Please clarify the number of reviewers who conducted data extraction and the procedures followed to minimise potential errors. 

- Section 4.6, page 100. Please clarify the number of reviewers who conducted the critical appraisal of the included trials and what procedures were followed to minimise potential errors or differences of interpretation. 

During the screening process, trials were independently selected for inclusion by two reviewers. Any discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or the intervention of a third reviewer. 

Data extraction and quality assessment were performed by one reviewer and independently checked for errors against the original trial report by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or through the intervention of a third reviewer.

## **A11: Sections 4.1, 4.10, 4.11 and 4.12 apply different inclusion criteria. Sections 4.1 and 4.10 explicitly source included studies from the same search. Please clarify the exact criteria applied in Sections 4.1 and 4.10 at the process stages to reduce the numbers of citations from 666 to 196 and from 196 to 82.** 

The reduction in number of citations from 666 to 196 was at assessment of eligibility of full text articles for the broad SLR. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for the broad SLR are detailed in Table 4-1 of the evidence submission and are provided again in Appendix IV of this document. 

As described in Section 4-1 of the evidence submission, additional exclusion criteria were applied in a second stage of screening to further align the SLR with the decision problem, and to identify all relevant RCTs that could potentially be used for data synthesis in the absence of sufficient head-to-head data to address the information needs of the decision 



<!-- page 448 -->

problem. This second stage of screening reduced the number of citations from 196 to 82. The additional exclusion criteria were: 

- study not in a population relevant to the decision problem (e.g. HoFH, Japanese population) 

- study assessed neither relevant intervention nor relevant comparator defined in the decision problem 

   - evolocumab alone or in combination with a statin with or without ezetimibe, or in combination with ezetimibe 

   - ezetimibe in combination with a statin (when optimised statin therapy does not appropriately control LDL-C) or ezetimibe alone (when statins are contraindicated or not tolerated) 

- study did not include outcome defined in the decision problem 

   - plasma lipid and lipoprotein levels, including LDL-C, non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (non-HDL-C), apolipoprotein B (ApoB), and lipoprotein (a) (Lp[a]) 

   - requirement of procedures including LDL apheresis and revascularisation 

   - fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events 

   - mortality 

   - adverse effects of treatment 

   - Health-related quality of life (HRQoL).

**A13: Section 4.7, Table 4-17, page 117 and subsequent results; executive summary; Section 1.3 and Table 1-3. Please clarify whether the provided pooled estimates across all treatment groups in the DESCARTES trial include a subgroup of patients treated with ezetimibe 10mg/day. In Section 4.13 (page 152), relevant subgroup comparisons are stated, including** _**“(i) evolocumab plus statin plus ezetimibe plus diet versus statin plus ezetimibe plus diet (relevant intervention and relevant comparator).”**_ **Please provide estimates of treatment effect for this subgroup.** 

The four assigned background lipid-lowering therapy regimens in DESCARTES (stratification factor subgroups) were:[10,11] 

- Diet alone 

- Diet + atorvastatin 10 mg 

- Diet + atorvastatin 80 mg 

- Diet + atorvastatin 80 mg + ezetimibe 

The study level treatment effects provided in Section 1.3 and Section 4.7 of the evidence submission include patients in all of these background therapy stratification factor subgroups. 

A prespecified subgroup analysis of the diet + atorvastatin 80 mg + ezetimibe stratification factor subgroup is provided in the CSR and shows a treatment difference in mean percent change from baseline in LDL-C at week 52 of -49.3% (p < 0.001) for evolocumab versus placebo (Table A-3).[18] Results were consistent across background therapy subgroups (interaction p=0.089).

One reviewer conducted the data extraction and quality assessment of each study using the Drummond and Jefferson (1996) instrument.[22] A second reviewer conducted a review of a sample (30%) of the abstracted studies to ensure complete extraction of relevant data and accurate quality assessments. ## **B5 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 4.13, page 155. The current evidence base discussed in the submission does not include any evidence relating to the effect of evolocumab on CVD events. Please provide the study protocol of the FOURIER study, and further details including any interim results that are currently available.** 

The FOURIER study protocol has been provided in conjunction with this document. No interim data from FOURIER are currently available. 

However, the evidence base included in the submission does include some evidence relating to the effect of evolocumab on cardiovascular disease (CVD) events based on an exploratory safety analysis of data from the integrated long-term extension studies OSLER and OLSER-2 (Section 4-10 of the evidence submission). These data showed a significant 53% reduction in 1-year adjudicated cardiovascular (CV) event rates from 2.18% in the standard of care (SoC) group to 0.95% in the evolocumab plus SoC group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.47, p = 0.003).[23] Although it is acknowledged that these data are preliminary and the trials are not powered to detect a difference in major CV events, this is in the direction, and of the magnitude, that would be expected given the magnitude of LDL-C lowering associated with evolocumab. 

**B6 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Executive summary and Section 5.4, pages 27, 28, and 279–282. The submission presents tables reporting ICERs for patients with 1 or 2 additional risk factors. The accompanying text states** _**“The grey cells denote patient profiles where the incremental cost per QALY gained is less than £30,000.”**_ **However, none of the values presented in the tables are below £30,000 per QALY gained. Please clarify whether the text or tables are incorrect.** 

We can confirm that this text is not applicable to the cost-effectiveness results presented for patients with existing CVD and one or two additional risk factors since all the values in the tables are above £30,000 per QALY gained. 

**B7 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 5, page 160. The text states** _**“The incremental cost per QALY gained is approximately £15,119 to £18,200 for evolocumab versus ezetimibe in patients with HeFH when assessed across the four treatment scenarios.”**_ **These ICERs are not mentioned elsewhere in the submission and appear considerably lower than the ICERs presented in Tables 5-27, 5-42, 5-47, 5-62 and 5-63. Please clarify this discrepancy.** 

Thank you for identifying this discrepancy. The cost-effectiveness results summarised in Section 5, page 160 of the evidence submission, should indeed reflect the incremental costeffectiveness ratios (ICERs) presented in Tables 5-27, 5-42, 5-47, 5-62 and 5-63 of the evidence submission.

**B8: Section 5.7, page 240. Please clarify why a threshold of >2.5 mmol/L has been selected to define “high risk” population in the LAPLACE-2 analyses. Please also clarify whether patients in the LAPLACE-2 trial were stratified according to LDL-C at baseline (LDL-C≤2.5 mmol/L and LDL-C>2.5 mmol/L). Also, please provide baseline characteristics for those with LDL-C>2.5 mmol/L by treatment group (with p values).** 

A LDL-C threshold of > 2.5mmol/L was selected to define a high risk population for the economic evaluation based on clinical expert advice regarding the patient population that would be anticipated to be treated with evolocumab in clinical practice. Therefore, this LDL-C threshold was used to allow appropriate baseline CVD risk estimation in alignment with anticipated clinical practice for the purposes of the cost-effectiveness analysis. Patients were not stratified according LDL-C (≤ 2.5 mmol/L and >2.5 mmol/L) at baseline in LAPLACE-2. 

Please find an additional _post hoc_ analysis (Table B-5) of baseline characteristics and lipidlowering therapy use for patients in LAPLACE-2 with LDL-C > 2.5 mmol/L by treatment group (with p-values) as requested. The included characteristics are aligned with the overall study level characteristics presented in Table 4-7 of the evidence submission.

## **B9: Section 5.5, page 229. The model includes only the costs of atorvastatin 20mg/80mg. Please justify why other statins were not included in the model. Please also provide details on how this assumption corresponds to the experience in the evolocumab trials and the high-risk LAPLACE-2 population included in the model.** 

As described in the evidence submission, NICE CG181[14] and CG71[13] provide the following recommendations for lipid modification therapy for primary and secondary prevention of CVD and treatment of HeFH: 

- Offer atorvastatin 20 mg for the primary prevention of CVD to people who have a 10% or greater 10-year risk of developing CVD (CG181). 

- Start statin treatment in people with CVD with atorvastatin 80 mg (CG181). 

- When a decision is made to prescribe a statin use a statin of high intensity and low acquisition cost (CG181). 

- Healthcare professionals should consider prescribing a high-intensity statin to achieve a recommended reduction in LDL-C concentration of greater than 50% from baseline (that is, LDL-C concentration before treatment) (CG71). 

Therefore, the economic evaluation was based on atorvastatin 20 mg for patients without existing CVD and atorvastatin 80 mg for patients with existing CVD to represent the relevant background statin therapy in accordance with the recommendations from NICE CG181. Atorvastatin 80 mg was also selected in the absence of a recommendation for a specific high-intensity statin agent in patients with HeFH (CG71) for consistency. We acknowledge the availability of a range of different statin agents and have provided additional information to support the selection of atorvastatin alone (20 mg and 80 mg) in the economic evaluation. 

These alternative statin agents and their respective acquisition costs are summarised in Table B-6.

The Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) study discussed in the evidence submission assessed statin treatment patterns in patients at CVD risk or those with history of CVD (evidence submission Appendix XV, Table 12). For example, of patients with existing CVD treated with a statin; simvastatin and atorvastatin represented the majority of statin therapy use (61.7% and 30.5%, respectively). Fluvastatin, pravastatin and rosuvastatin represented only 0.5%, 3.9% and 3.4%, respectively. Notably, the CPRD study enrolled patients from 2005 onwards; therefore, additional data for statin treatment patterns are also provided below, given the potential change in statin treatment patterns over time.

When considering statin prescribing in the context of NICE CG181 recommendations for the use of high-intensity statins (described in Table B-6), atorvastatin 20 mg, 40 mg and 80 mg represent 92.5% of total high-intensity statin use. Simvastatin (80 mg) and rosuvastatin (10 mg, 20 mg and 40 mg) represent 1.6% and 5.9% of high-intensity statin use, respectively (Table B-8). As such, atorvastatin is the most commonly used high-intensity statin (> 90%) and also a low cost statin agent. Therefore, atorvastatin represents the most appropriate choice for background lipid-lowering therapy in the base case analysis and also consistent with the recommendations in NICE CG181.

In LAPLACE-2, the background moderate- to high-intensity statin therapies used were generally consistent with the recommendations in NICE CG181 and used in UK clinical practice (Appendix VIII of the evidence submission). In RUTHERFORD-2, most patients received high-intensity statin therapy which is consistent with NICE CG71.  We acknowledge the differences between the economic evaluation and the experience in the evolocumab RCTs (including the high-risk LAPLACE-2 population) based on the intensity and type of statin agent.  The evolocumab studies were global in nature and not designed specifically to meet the anticipated needs of the decision problem.  We have additionally assessed the impact of alternative costs of background statin therapy and demonstrated the costeffectiveness results are not sensitive to this variable. 

## **B10: Section 5.3, page 196. Please clarify why LDL-C was the only surrogate used for CVD risk. Please clarify whether other markers were considered.** 

LDL-C was the only surrogate considered for CVD risk in the economic evaluation given that the body of evidence supporting LDL-C as a therapeutic target and surrogate for CV outcomes is overwhelming. This evidence comes from a range of studies including epidemiological studies, genetic variants (both gain-of-function and loss-of-function), and interventional studies with LDL-C-lowering therapies.[26-40] In contrast, the relationship between other lipid markers and CV event rates, and whether changing these markers through therapeutic intervention has an effect on CVD risk, is less well-established and understood.  Therefore, other markers were not considered. 

Although evolocumab also has a significant positive effect on other lipid markers (e.g. nonHDL-C and Lp[a]), the primary effects of evolocumab are on LDL-C. We anticipate that improvements in these other markers may contribute to reduction in CV risk, but in the absence of data supporting the impact of altering these markers on CV risk, they were not used in the model as a surrogate. 

**B11 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 5.2, pages 174–181. Please comment on the advantages of using combined health states compared with the approach used in the NICE clinical guideline 181, particularly with respect to the number of assumptions required and the availability of data to inform the outcomes associated with these health states. Please also comment on whether the approach taken, whereby the highest transition probability, lowest utility and highest cost is selected for combined health states, had been used in any of the previous economic analyses identified in the cost-effectiveness review presented in Section 5.1.** 

As acknowledged in NICE CG181; _‘Markov models also do not preserve memory of past events, and so the risk of experiencing a further stroke for someone in the post-stroke state is equal whether they have previously experience one stroke or several strokes’._ As stated in the evidence submission (Section 5.2, pages 176 to 178), the use of combined health states is an approach to overcome the memory-less condition of Markov models, otherwise there may be modelled scenarios in which patients may encounter improvements in health status (or reduction in costs) by having certain recurrent CV events which is not clinically plausible. 

With respect to assumptions, for combined health states involving an acute event, the risks and costs are always based on those of the acute event. Utilities are generally those of the 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 468 -->

acute event, with the exception of ‘acute ACS’, which has a utility higher (0.7700) than the ‘post-IS’ (0.7064) and ‘post-HF’ (0.7222) health states. 

For combined health states involving long-term health states only, the economic model needs to consider a long-term cost, utility, and risk: 

- The health status of a patient can only remain the same or become worse by having further CV events, therefore the minimum utility is used. This is a conservative assumption compared with a memory-less Markov model, as treatment with evolocumab maintains patients in the long-term health states by avoiding more CV events compared with alternative scenarios without evolocumab. 

- The long-term patient costs can only remain the same or increase by having further CV events; therefore, we are taking the maximum individual cost. This is a conservative assumption compared to a memory-less Markov model, as evolocumab keeps patients in the long-term health states by avoiding CV events compared to alternative scenarios without evolocumab. 

- The long-term patient risks are anticipated to remain the same or increase due to further CV events; therefore we are using the maximum risk. 

We are not aware of data availability on costs and risks conditional on CV event recurrence, or whether is it readily available in sources such as CPRD, to enable these assumptions to be assessed. 

We have also further assessed whether this approach has been utilised in previous economic evaluation studies (as identified in the SLR). Four studies were identified presenting multiple health event states (Ara et al., 2009, Ara et al., 2012, Taylor et al., 2009, Wagner et al., 2009).[41-44] Moreover, three studies were identified which included recurrent event states in their model (Khoury et al., 2009, Nagata-Kobayashi et al., 2005, Peura et al., 2008).[45-47] 

The economic evaluations by Ara et al., (2009)[41] and Ara et al., (2012)[42] , used a Markov model with the following health states: 

- Unstable angina (UA) 

- Myocardial infarction (MI) 

- Revascularisation 

- Hospitalisation for UA 

- Non-fatal MI with history of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) 

- Non-fatal stroke with history of ACS 

- Non-fatal MI with history of stroke 

- Non-fatal stroke with history of stroke and ACS 

- Hospitalisation for UA with history of stroke and ACS 

- Non-CVD mortality 

- CVD mortality. 

Most of the health states are combined health states to compensate for memory-less attribute with regards clinical history, and only the costs and health consequences associated with the current health state are applied in a Markov model. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 469 -->

For the combined health states, it was assumed that the transition probabilities for future events will be the highest transition probabilities of the experienced events. In clinical practice, it is plausible that patients can experience a severe CV event followed by a less severe CV event. To represent that in the models developed by Ara et al., (2009) and Ara et al., (2012), costs and utilities of the combined health states were adjusted in such a way that a patient who experienced a subsequent event would not benefit in terms of ongoing costs, health-related quality of life, or subsequent risks compared with previous experienced events. For utilities, based on clinical advice, an additional 10% reduction was applied for subsequent CV events. 

The health states included in Taylor et al., (2009)[43] are divided into: 

- major CV events: MI, stroke, congestive heart failure (CHF), revascularisation, and resuscitated cardiac arrest (RCA); 

- minor CV events: peripheral artery disease [PAD], transient ischaemic attack (TIA), and documented angina; and 

- death. 

The major CV event status can be a single event or a combination of two major events (allowing for all possible combinations of events excluding RCA). Rates of second major events were conditional on the type of the first-event. In order to simplify the model, second major events were considered in the analysis only if they occurred within the first year of the first major event. Utilities and costs were assigned to each health state. Patients in major event states were subjected to long-term utilities and mortality consequences, while minor events resulted only in short-term cost and utility consequences, reflecting the transient nature of these conditions. Patients in the combined major event states were assigned the larger mortality multiplier of the two individual events. 

Wagner et al., (2009)[44] presented a Markov model with a lifetime horizon to predict major and minor CV events, survival, costs, and quality-adjusted life years in the Canadian context for CHD patients. The model comprised of four health states: 

- Stable CHD 

- Single major CV event 

- Double major CV event 

- Death. 

Patients could suffer a single (first) major CV event or suffer two major CV events within the same year. A major CV event was defined as MI, stroke, CHF, RCA, or revascularisation either by coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). A minor CV event (PAD, TIA, or documented angina) could occur at any point in the model but did not cause transition of the patient to a different health state. For patients who experienced a second major event during the same year, the mortality rate of the first event was applied. In the case patients survived two major events in one year; the mortality multiplier of the more severe event was used. 

Khuoury et al., (2009),[45] used a Markov model that modelled patients with diabetes with a prior MI. This model included 5 health states: 

- Well (no history of a CV event) 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 470 -->

- Event history 

- Second event history 

- Event death 

- Other death (i.e. death due to non-CV events). 

Patients in the event history health state were at risk of experiencing a second coronary heart disease (CHD) or stroke event. The risk of having a second event was increased by 2.3 times for CHD and 1.89 times for stroke, to reflect clinical reality. Relative risk ratios for secondary CHD and stroke events were derived from additional literature. Utility decrements were used for CHD (-0.03) and stroke (-0.16). Utility decrements were assumed to be cumulative. 

Nagata-Kobayashi et al., (2005)[46] and Peura et al., (2008)[47] used a Markov model to follow one type of CV-event (MI). Both divided health states into the time before the onset of the CHD (‘CHD free, primary prevention’) and the states when the individual has experienced a MI (‘CHD, secondary prevention’ and ‘recurrent MI’). In both of these studies, no decrement or correction on utilities or correction on costs were applied for recurrent events, as patients could only experience the same CV event again. 

As described, previous economic evaluations have attempted to account for combined health states by ensuring the appropriate application of risks, utilities and costs to prevent patients from benefiting from specific sequences of CV events which would not be clinically plausible. Our economic model has included the full set of possible combined health states and has applied the same principles to introduce memory of prior CV events for risk, utilities, and costs, as implemented only partially in earlier economic evaluation studies. Furthermore, during the economic model development, clinical and economic advisors supported these assumptions as reasonable and conservative in the absence of robust data.

Our evidence submission states that _‘evolocumab represents both a clinically- and costeffective treatment option for the NHS in patients without existing CVD but at high residual risk due to additional risk factors (based on QRISK2 score)’_ . The estimates of the minimum 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 473 -->

baseline CVD risk required for patients without existing CVD are described on the basis of QRISK2 to align with the risk assessment method specified in NICE CG181,[14] although the numbers are based on the Framingham risk equation used in the model. We believe this can be considered a conservative estimate, given that the Framingham study includes a broader definition of CV events (i.e. any estimated CVD risk based on the Framingham definition of CVD will likely be higher than derived from QRISK2). We acknowledge the error in Section 5.15, page 284, where this is incorrectly stated as ‘ _Framingham study includes a narrower definition…_ ’. 

QRISK2 includes a narrower definition of CV events compared with that in economic models designed to model the natural course of CVD. For example, the QRISK2 definition of a first CV event does not include PAD or HF. As such, previous economic evaluations such as that for NICE CG181 have amended the CV risk estimated from QRISK2 to a ‘total CV risk’. For example, a QRISK2 derived absolute 10-year CVD risk of 10% has been calculated as being equivalent to a ‘total CV risk’ of 14.7% (NICE CG181 Appendices, pages 597 to 598[12] ). 

In the absence of evidence to allow calibration of Framingham-based and QRISK2-based risk estimates in the high risk population for the UK, a minimum 10-year CVD risk based on Framingham was adopted. A patient without existing CVD estimated to have an absolute 10year CVD risk of 40% for a primary event using QRISK2 is anticipated to be lower risk in terms of ‘total CV risk’ compared with a patent without existing CVD with the same absolute risk using Framingham, given the narrower definition of events from QRISK2. As such, the estimates in the threshold analyses provide a reasonable conservative estimate of the minimum 10-year risk required in order to demonstrate cost-effectiveness. 

## **B13 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Please clarify why the UKPDS risk engine was not used to assess CV risk in the diabetic population. Please also discuss the limitations of using the Framingham equations in the diabetic population in the CPRD dataset.** 

The UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) risk equation is indeed relevant for estimating risk of a first CV event in a diabetic population without existing CVD. As a diabetic population was not specifically modelled, we did not feel it was necessary to use this risk equation to estimate baseline CV risk. Furthermore, since the proportion of patients with diabetes mellitus (type II) in the high-risk LAPLACE-2 population with existing CVD was approximately 10%, it was also deemed unnecessary to use two different underlying risk equations to estimate risk in the diabetic and non-diabetic populations. 

With respect to the CPRD dataset, studies have previously identified that the Framingham risk equations may be unreliable when applied in diabetic populations. Despite a diabetes specific risk equation not being used, the calibration exercise using CPRD (see response to Question B33) allowed us to ensure the predictions from Framingham matched real-world observed CV rates for the diabetic cohort used as a proxy for primary prevention.

## **B14 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 5.3, page 184. The company’s submission suggests that calibration is necessary irrespective of whether the QRISK2 or Framingham equation is used. If the QRISK2 risk equation was used, why would this require calibration?** 

We believe it is good practice to conduct calibration of predicted events from risk equations to observed events in the population of interest since this supports external validity when modelling different patient profiles. As such, calibration should be conducted irrespective of the risk equation underpinning the estimation of a primary CV event risks (QRISK2 or Framingham). 

There are two primary reasons for this; the definition of predicted primary CV events from QRISK2 (fatal or non-fatal angina, MI, TIA or stroke) is narrower than the CV events than those modelled (and previously modelled, in economic evaluations such as NICE CG181). The broader definition in the economic model better reflects the natural course of the disease and includes CV events such as PAD and HF. Secondly; we have specifically modelled a higher risk population in comparison with the primary cohort in QRESEARCH UK that informs QRISK2. Therefore, calibration is required to ensure the model is not under- or over-predicting the occurrence of CV events using risk equations such as Framingham or QRISK2, compared with observed CV events within the population of interest. This supports the external validity of the cost-effectiveness analyses.

This analysis indicates that the predicted rates of recurrent non-fatal and fatal CV events using the REACH risk equation are consistent irrespective of whether diabetic status was assumed or estimates were based on subgroup data (actual) in males and females (Table B-15).

## **Please clarify the source of these values. Please clarify whether these multipliers were applied to the probability or the rate of each event. Please also clarify whether D’Agostino and the REACH risk equations produce rates or probabilities.** 

In the threshold analysis for patients without existing CVD, all the primary prevention event rates are artificially increased by a multiplier (hard-coded values) in the “Populations” worksheet of the economic model. These multipliers are applied to the rates of events (i.e. they are rate ratios) and are based on the calculated level of risk increase required in order to demonstrate cost-effectiveness according to the willingness-to-pay thresholds. The derivation of the multiplier values can be seen in “Risk Frontier Tracking” worksheet, column A, of the economic model. Based on the clarification request dated 11[th] August 2015, these threshold analyses have been removed from the updated version of the economic model for the NHS list price analysis. 

The D’Agostino (Framingham)[49] and the REACH[50] risk equations are based on Cox proportional hazards models and therefore they produce probabilities. These probabilities have been converted to rates using the formula proposed in NICE CG181 (exponential distribution) whereby, risk = 1 – exp[–rate] .

## **B18: Section 5.3, page 192. Please explain where the data contained in Table 5-9 are applied in the model.** 

Table 5-9 is descriptive and was included to provide context regarding CVD risk for the different populations. The absolute 10-year CVD risk in Table 5-9 is derived from the economic model based on amending the modelled time horizon to 10 years (and converting the predicted rates to probabilities). The baseline LDL-C (mean mmol/L) is based on the patient characteristics from LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 for the relevant populations. 

**B19 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Table 5-10, page 193. The treatment effects used for the combination with statin therapy (from LAPLACE-2) relate to the treatment difference compared with background statin therapy. The treatment effects for monotherapy (from GAUSS-2) relate to the mean percentage change from baseline, which does not account for the change in LDL-C on placebo treatment. Please clarify the evidence for assuming that there will be no change in response in the placebo group, or alternatively, how this issue has been addressed in the cost-effectiveness model?** 

As described in the evidence submission (Section 4.2, Table 4-2), GAUSS-2 assessed evolocumab monotherapy versus ezetimibe monotherapy. There was no placebo alone arm in GAUSS-2 since it would have been unethical to conduct a RCT in patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia with statin intolerance with LDL-C ≥ 2.6 mmol/L (patients with CHD or CHD risk equivalent) to ≥ 4.9 mmol/L (patients without diagnosed CHD or CHD risk equivalent, with no additional risk factors) who had not already been offered optimal treatment with currently available therapies e.g. ezetimibe. Therefore, this is no direct evidence in the evolocumab RCTs for a change in response in a placebo alone population with statin intolerance. 

In the absence of evidence, no assumption was made for a hypothetical placebo response by attempting to attribute a proxy effect based on the observed placebo responses from LAPLACE-2, RUTHERFORD-2 or DESCARTES. 

This was indirectly addressed in the cost-effectiveness analyses based on the univariate sensitivity analysis for both evolocumab and ezetimibe according to the lower and upper 95% confidence intervals of the relative LDL-C reduction treatment effect from GAUSS-2. 

## **B20: Table 5-10, page 193. Please clarify the method for the “post hoc pooled analysis” that was used to provide the pooled treatment effects for ezetimibe 10mg** . 

The _post hoc_ pooled analysis for LAPLACE-2 involved pooling all placebo arms and all ezetimibe arms to generate a pooled treatment difference for ezetimibe versus placebo for the mean percent change from baseline in calculated LDL-C at the mean of weeks 10/12. As there were no placebo arms in GAUSS-2, both ezetimibe arms were pooled to generate a pooled ezetimibe mean percent change from baseline in calculated LDL-C at the mean of weeks 10/12. 

Aside from the pooling of data, this _post hoc_ analysis was conducted using methods in accordance with the main study analyses presented in the submission.

**B21 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 5.3, Figure 5-7 and Table 5-11. Please clarify how the effect of the combination treatment is generated? For example, for scenario 4, treatment effects from LAPLACE-2 are used. For ezetimibe there was a treatment effect of -27% mean change from baseline. For evolocumab there was a treatment effect of -72 % mean change from placebo, or -64 % mean change from baseline. Assuming a baseline LDL-C of B for a given individual, would the calculated LDL-C after treatment be:** 

- **1) B*(1-0.27)*(1-0.64) or** 

- **2) B*(1-0.27-0.64)** 

## **Also, was the evidence from the relevant DESCARTES subgroup (that assessed evolocumab and ezetimibe in combination) considered to inform this treatment effect?** 

The effect of the combination treatment is generated in the economic model based on sequential LDL-C lowering from baseline (background statin therapy) stated above in equation 1. 

We acknowledge the mean percent change from baseline in LDL-C at week 52 was -49.3% (p < 0.001) for evolocumab versus placebo in this subgroup from DESCARTES in the relevant subgroup of (diet + atorvastatin 80mg + ezetimibe). This subgroup level treatment effect from DESCARTES was not used given the overall consistency of LDL-C reduction for evolocumab in addition to background lipid-lowering therapy across the RCTs. 

Additionally, in accordance with our response to question B26, no reduction in CV event rate is associated with LDL-C levels < 1.03 mmol/L after treatment. This conservative assumption based on sequential LDL-C lowering primarily reduces the efficacy of the combination treatment of evolocumab, ezetimibe and statin since patients with baseline LDL-C ≤ 4.5 mmol/L achieve LDL-C levels < 1.03 mmol/L after treatment.

## **B24: Section 5.3, page 193. The relative treatment effects for evolocumab in the statinintolerant population are taken from the GAUSS-2 trial. However, the modelled risk of CVD is based on baseline characteristics from LAPLACE-2 or RUTHERFORD-2. Please clarify why patient-level data from the GAUSS-2 trial have not been used to derive the CVD risk as per the approach used for LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2.** 

As stated in our evidence submission (Section 5.2, page 174), “ _GAUSS-2 enrolled patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia unable to tolerate any statins or a statin dose high enough to control their LDL-C levels. However, for the purposes of the economic evaluation, the patient populations from LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 were_ 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 482 -->

_used since statin intolerance or contraindication is considered a subgroup of the primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia, and HeFH populations_ .” 

Statin intolerance is associated with adverse events such as, muscle-related symptoms, elevation in serum creatine kinase or persistent elevations in transaminase levels. The incidence of these adverse events is typically biochemical in nature and unrelated to patient characteristics used for CVD risk estimation. Patients with statin intolerance are anticipated to be similar to patients without statin intolerance except for baseline LDL-C due to differential background lipid-lowering therapies. Consequently, it was deemed appropriate to use the LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 populations for estimating baseline CVD risk across the primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia and HeFH populations, vary baseline LDL-C (severity of hypercholesterolaemia), and use the GAUSS-2 treatment effects to assess the cost-effectiveness in a statin intolerant population. 

**B25: Section 5.3, Table 5-5, page 183. The number of vascular beds (VB) and proportion of patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) are based on the mean observed in the REACH study. Please comment on the potential biases associated with this. Please also confirm that this information is not available from the LAPLACE-2, DESCARTES, RUTHERFORD-2 or GAUSS-2 trials.** 

The number of vascular beds and proportion of patients with atrial fibrillation were based on the means observed in the REACH registry. The REACH equations are based on a Cox proportional hazards model considering mean-centred risk factors. In the absence of information for these risk factors in the modelled populations, considering the mean value reported in Wilson et al., (2012)[50] means these risk factors have no impact on the CVD risk predictions: 

- Vascular beds: The REACH registry assesses the role of previously diagnosed vascular disease using an ordinal variable to test for the effects of 1, 2, or 3 vascular beds involved. We have conducted an exploratory assessment of patients with existing CVD in LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 on the basis of assuming the number of vascular beds is equivalent to individual peripheral, coronary and cerebrovascular beds. This indicates that the LAPLACE-2 and RUTHERFORD-2 patients with existing CVD have 1.227 and 1.333 vascular beds, respectively, in comparison with 1.212 reported in the REACH registry. This slightly higher estimate from this exploratory assessment would indicate we have undertaken a conservative approach in estimating CVD risk from these RCTs compared with the REACH registry. Further, the number of vascular beds is a dynamic risk factor that could be adjusted on the basis of when a CV event occurs in a new vascular bed (peripheral, coronary or cerebrovascular) if the definitions are assumed to be the same. For simplicity, the number of vascular beds is kept static as we are using a cohort model (as opposed to patient-level simulations), and as such would be conservative when assessing a cohort experiencing recurrent CV events. Counterfactually, we can anticipate that we are over-estimating risk in a population without existing CVD in the short term following a CV event. This population would be anticipated to have 1 vascular bed following a first CV event as opposed to 1.212 based on the REACH registry. 

- Atrial fibrillation (AF): the proportion of patients with AF is based on the REACH registry (11.7%) since patients with uncontrolled serious cardiac arrhythmia (including AF) in the past 3 months prior to randomisation were excluded from the relevant RCTs. Therefore, 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 483 -->

the estimate from the REACH registry was deemed a more appropriate estimate for the purposes of CVD risk estimation. Assessment of the CPRD study indicated that 13.6% of patients with existing CVD had a diagnosis of AF. This would suggest that the REACH registry estimate for this cardiovascular condition could be a reasonable estimate for prevalence in the absence of this from the RCTs due to the exclusion of patients with uncontrolled AF. 

## **B26 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 5.3, page 198. Please clarify why no reduction in CV event rate associated with LDL-C levels when lower than 1.03mmol/L from baseline (equivalent to 40mg/dL) was assumed?** 

None of the studies included in the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists’ Collaboration (CTTC) meta-analysis, used as key data source for translating LDL-C reductions to CV events included an intervention that reduced LDL-C below 1.03mmol/L.[28] Therefore, a conservative approach was adopted in favour of alternative strategies since only patients treated with evolocumab can experience such intensive LDL-C reductions on the basis of different severities of hypercholesterolaemia (baseline LDL-C) thereby achieving LDL-C levels below this threshold. ## **B27: Section 5.4, pages 219–220. Please clarify why utilities from NICE clinical guideline 181 were assumed when the company’s submission includes a new systematic review of health-related quality of life literature.** 

As NICE CG181[19] is a recent clinical guideline including an economic evaluation, it was used to support development of the current economic model. As such, the utilities used in CG181 fit reasonably well and appropriate to the current economic model structure. However, the utility values applied in NICE CG181 were sourced from primary documents that were published between the mid-1990s and mid-2000s. Therefore, we undertook a SLR to check if more recent utility values of equal relevance had been published. 

The SLR identified 173 studies which included potential utility data for one or more healthstates in the economic model. Each of the identified studies was assessed in order to

## **B28: Section 5.5, Table 5-20, pages 227–228. Please clarify why the resource use/cost review focuses only on Markov models with lifetime horizon relating to a UK setting? Please clarify how these studies were used to inform the de novo health economic analysis.** 

Thank you for identifying this typographic error. The table heading summarising the results of resource use/cost review should state _‘Cost summary data extraction of UK studies’_ . No model-based limitations were applied during this review. 

The SLR was broad and covered 13 European countries. In order to present the identified studies most relevant to the current submission, a summary table containing only the UK studies presenting costs from the past 10 years was presented in the evidence submission. A full data extraction table was provided in Appendix XIV, Table XIV-8 of the evidence submission. 

**B29: Section 5.3, Table 5-12, page 197. Please clarify why rate ratio for the “more vs less” is used for non-fatal CV events (based on 5 trials), whereas the rate ratio for all lipid agents (n=26 trials) is used for fatal CV events. Please also clarify why only ischaemic stroke (rather than other forms of stroke) is included in the model.** 

The CTTC meta-analysis for _‘more versus less intensive statin therapy’_ was used since this meta-analysis specifically considered whether larger reductions in LDL-C safely produce further reductions in major vascular events, since several trials have compared more intensive versus less intensive statin regimens.[28] This meta-analysis (2 trials in patients with ACS and 3 trials in patient with stable coronary disease) was deemed to be more representative of the high-risk CV population and clinical intent for patients who would be treated with evolocumab as opposed to the _‘standard versus control’_ meta-analysis which is generally based on studies of lower intensity statins versus placebo. 

The _‘more versus less intensive statin therapy’_ meta-analysis was not used for fatal events for two reasons. Firstly, the rate ratio per mmol/L reduction of LDL-C was not reported for ischaemic stroke (IS) in this meta-analysis; however, it was reported in the _‘standard versus control’_ meta-analysis. Secondly, CV outcomes trials typically assess major vascular events as a composite endpoint (e.g. coronary death, non-fatal MI, coronary revascularisation, or stroke). As such, due to the lower frequency of coronary deaths across the five trials, the _‘more versus less intensive statin therapy’_ reports a non-significant reduction in coronary death (rate ratio per mmol/L reduction in LDL-C of 0.85, 95% CI: 0.62 to 1.15. The authors state that after differences in the absolute reductions in LDL-C were accounted for, the proportional reduction in the incidence of major vascular events per mmol/L was slightly larger (heterogeneity p=0.03) in the trials of _‘more versus less intensive therapy’_ than in 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 489 -->

those of _‘statin versus control’_ . It is reasonable to assume that this would also be the case with more data for coronary death, since there is no clinical reason for a differential finding for this major vascular event. Therefore, to gain alignment with the source for the rate ratio for fatal IS, the rate ratios for fatal events were used from the _‘statin versus control’_ metaanalysis. 

IS was only assessed in the economic model because available evidence from the CTTC meta-analysis indicated that the rate ratio per mmol/L LDL-C reduction for both non-fatal and fatal haemorrhagic strokes were non-significant. 

## **B30: Section 5.3, pages 196–198. The company’s model focuses on patients deemed to be at high risk of CV events (according to baseline LDL, presence of diabetes etc.). The company uses data from the CTTC meta-analysis for all patients irrespective of baseline LDL, risk factors or history of cardiac event. Please comment on the availability of data on CV risk by baseline risk factors.** 

The CTTC meta-analysis assessed the effect of major vascular events by baseline LDL-C concentration and reported that the rate ratio per mmol/L LDL-C reduction is consistent irrespective of baseline LDL-C.[28] We are not aware of data for other risk factors (e.g. diabetes mellitus). 

## **B31: Company’s model. Please clarify why the 10-year risk was calculated for the overall population in the RUTHERFORD-2 trial in the HeFH population; that is, why was the Framingham risk equation applied to patients who have a history of CVD? Why were the primary and secondary prevention populations not evaluated separately?** 

The Framingham equation was only applied for transitions for HeFH patients without existing CVD (i.e. primary prevention).   The primary and secondary prevention populations in HeFH were not evaluated separately to reflect the decision problem. The economic model cannot assess primary and secondary prevention cohorts simultaneously, therefore average cohort patient characteristics from the primary and secondary preventon population from RUTHERFORD-2 are used for the cost-effectiveness analysis. 

The economic model has the flexibility to allow evaluation of these primary and secondary prevention populations separately.  This can be conducted by selection of the relevant RUTHERFORD-2 primary or secondary prevention population in the ‘Main’ worksheet (cell I3). 

We have included the cost-effectiveness analyses in this clarification request for the HeFH primary and secondary prevention populations based on comparison of evolocumab and statin versus ezetimibe and statin (scenario 1) (Table B-24).  These indicate a lower incremental cost per QALY gained versus ezetimibe in the combined cohort compared with the individual primary and secondary prevention population analyses.  This is due to the balance between the costs and benefits accrued in a mixed CVD history population when compared with assessing individual cohorts based on CVD history.

## **B32: Company’s model. Please provide further explanation on how the 10-year risk was adjusted for age in the model, including any assumptions used. In particular, please explain what the calculations in worksheet “Rates & non-CVD Utilities” columns C and E are intended to do.** 

The average 10-year rate of events predicted from patient-level data was annualised ensuring the sum of the first 10 annual rates (from the starting age) presented in “Rates & non-CVD Utilities” worksheet, columns C (males) and D (females) equals the original 10year rate prediction. This was done as the 10-year predicted rates include the effect of aging over the follow-up time in the Framingham study; therefore the rates were corrected to remove this effect and avoid overestimation of event risks.[55] 

The effect of aging was assumed to be equal to the age coefficient from the Cox proportional hazards models that were used to develop the Framingham equation. The effect of age was removed from the predicted event rate by using a correction factor that represented the cumulative effect of aging beyond the first year. This correction factor is presented in ‘Rates & non-CVD Utilities’ worksheet (sum of column E [males] and sum of column F [females]). As the Framingham study included the log of age in the prediction model, its correction factor varied with age. For example, the average 10-year rate for RUTHERFORD-2 (male) patients was predicted to be 0.1699 for a starting age of 49 years old. This equals the sum of the 10 annual rates presented in ‘Rates & non-CVD Utilities’ worksheet (cells C49 to C58). 

The same approach was used to annualise the 20-month rates predicted from the REACH equation. In this case, the correction factor is not age-dependent. 

## **B33 (PRIORITY QUESTION): Section 5.3, pages 187–192. The company attempted to calibrate the 10-year risk estimated from the Framingham algorithm using data from the CPRD (20 months from REACH using the HES data).** 

- Please comment on whether calibration factors are already available in the literature and if so, how these compare with the calibration factors estimated from the CPRD/HES dataset? 

- Please clarify why only patients with diabetes were included in the CPRD dataset for primary prevention. Please comment on the potential biases associated with this approach. 

- The submission states that about half the patients from the CPRD dataset could not be linked (or did not have information). Please comment on the potential biases resulting from this (for example, selection bias). Please also comment on any differences between patients included and excluded (or those who could not be linked). 

- How does this calibration approach compare with the methods used in NICE clinical guideline 181? 

- Please explain why the event rates from the CPRD analysis were not used to directly estimate CV risk (as opposed to using Framingham as per the company’s model)? 

As far as we are aware, there are no published calibration factors for the Framingham or REACH registry risk equations based on comparisons with UK data specific to the populations used in our study. Literature comparing the accuracy of the Framingham risk equation in other countries for the primary prevention population as a whole is available.

However, because the populations in the CRPD study are specific to support assessment of a high-risk population, it would be unexpected to find literature documenting calibration factors for these five specific populations treated with high-intensity statins: prevalent diabetes, prevalent evident CVD, incident ACS, incident IS, and incident HF (in patients with ACS or IS). With respect to REACH, at the time of the CPRD study, we were not aware of any studies that developed calibration factors. This is one of the reasons why we conducted the calibration 

We also compared overall CV event rates from three different countries for these five cohorts. Each study was done with different research organisations, so the results are with slightly different methodologies owing to study design and data. For example, rates from Sweden and the UK are during the first 1500 days, and Spain reflects rates over the entire follow-up period. Also, the exclusion of events within the first 30 days for the incident (ACS, IS, and HF) cohorts is handled differently in the three countries. However, their overall concordance suggests that the CPRD findings are not substantially different from those in other countries (Table B-25 to Table B-29).

Patients with diabetes were selected because they represent the largest group of high-risk primary prevention patients. While there are other risk factors that confer high risk, most do not confer high-risk status in and of themselves, and those that do typically reflect very small subgroups. Therefore, patients with diabetes were selected to represent a large, easily identifiable subgroup of primary prevention patients at high risk of CV events. Most primary prevention risk equations include diabetes as a risk factor, so these equations should appropriately reflect the risk of diabetic patients. As with any risk equation, there may be biases with regards the representativeness of the population used to estimate the risk equation. Even then, the results may not generalise to other countries. Therefore, we developed calibration equations to address this issue. 

High-risk patients with diabetes may have a variety of other complications due to associated microvascular disease, and may have a different distribution of CV events than patients with other risk factors that result in the same risk level. 

We conducted a brief comparison of patients in CPRD who did and did not have linked hospital episode statistics (HES) data, and found there to be no substantial differences (Table B-30). It should be noted that these comparisons were earlier in the cohort finalisation process, so the HES cohort is not exactly the same as the final cohort used in the analyses. This is because these were exploratory analyses at the point where the HES data were merged with the CPRD data. After this step, additional exclusion criteria were applied, including removing patients who died within 30 days after the index event. Based on these analyses, we feel that there is no substantive effect of selection bias in restricting our cohort to patients with HES data.
