## **8 OVERALL CONCLUSIONS** 

The principal efficacy review represents a good quality systematic review of four relevant, good quality RCTs. The trials were generally consistent with the NICE scope. The primary efficacy outcome was mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline, and mean treatment difference across trial arms, at follow-ups of 12 weeks (LAPLACE-2, GAUSS-2, DESCARTES and RUTHERFORD2) and 52 weeks (DESCARTES). 

In the LAPLACE-2 trial, at 12 weeks, patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia on background atorvastatin therapy (intensive and non-intensive doses) had a treatment difference in mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline of -46.9 (95% CI, -53.0 to -40.7, _p_ <0.001) and -42.5 (95% CI, -47.9 to -37.0, _p_ <0.001) for the Q2W and QM doses of evolocumab respectively, compared with ezetimibe (fixed effects model). 

In the GAUSS-2 trial, at 12 weeks, patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia who were statin intolerant had a treatment difference in mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline of -39.3 (95% CI, -45.0 to -33.5, _p_ <0.001) and -38.1 (95% CI, -42.9 to -33.4, _p_ <0.001) for the Q2W and QM doses of evolocumab compared with ezetimibe. 

In the placebo-controlled RUTHERFORD-2 trial, at 12 weeks, patients with HeFH on background statin therapy (intensive and non-intensive doses) had a mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline of -62.7 (95% CI, -66.3 to -59.1) and -56.6 (95% CI, -60.9 to -52.3) for the Q2W and QM doses of evolocumab, respectively. The treatment difference in mean percentage change compared with placebo was -60.6 (95% CI, -66.7 to -54.5, _p_ <0.001) and -60.3 (95% CI, -67.8, -52.9, _p_ <0.001) for the Q2W and QM doses of evolocumab, respectively. The ERG received clinical advice that the HeFH population of the RUTHERFORD trial with a confirmed genetic mutation was higher than might be found in usual clinical practice in the UK, but the implications of this are unclear. The ERG also noted, following clinical advice, that the proportion of patients with CHD was higher in the intervention arms of the RUTHERFORD-2 trial (i.e. 30-36%) compared with what would be expected in clinical practice in a HeFH population, and was higher than the prevalence reported for the other three trials (e.g. LAPLACE-2 trial arm populations ranged from 17% to 24% with CHD characteristics). 

In the placebo-controlled DESCARTES trial, patients with primary hypercholesterolaemia on background statin therapy (intensive and non-intensive doses) had a mean percentage change in LDLC from baseline of -50.6 (95% CI, -53.2 to -48.0) for the QM dose of evolocumab at 52 weeks. The 

141 



<!-- page 761 -->

treatment difference in mean percentage change compared with placebo was -59.3 (95% CI, -63.8 to - 54.9, _p_ <0.001) at 52 weeks. 

The results for other lipid parameters, such as non-HDL-cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a), were consistent with the results for LDL-C, and pre-specified subgroup analyses demonstrated that these results were not sensitive to the different doses of evolocumab, or other key variables, such as LDL-C baseline levels, severity of hypercholesterolaemia or CVD risk factors. The ERG noted that only 12-week evidence was available for the efficacy of the Q2W dose, while the QM dose had some data for 52 weeks. Additional clinical efficacy evidence was provided from a non-RCT study (TAUSSIG) and two open-label, extension trials (OSLER1 and 2). However, the extension studies included some trials with populations and/or comparators that were excluded from the principal review of four RCTs and it is unclear how these trials and the non-RCT study were identified for inclusion in the company’s review. The inclusion of these studies was justified by the company on account of the longer-term evidence both from the extension studies and from TAUSSIG on the HeFH subgroup (36 weeks). An NMA was not performed, although this might have been possible using particular trial evidence from both the primary non-familial hypercholesterolaemia population and the HeFH subgroup. 

The clinical effectiveness review found that evolocumab is efficacious at lowering LDL-C, but in itself this is not a clinically important outcome: its importance is derived from it being a surrogate for CVD. Although there is an established relationship between statin-generated LDL-C reduction and reduced CV events, the impact of evolocumab on CVD has not been demonstrated: there is little or no direct evidence on this relationship. The ongoing FOURIER trial (clinicaltrials.gov identifier NCT02207634) aims to evaluate the impact of evolocumab on CVD outcomes, but only in people who have already had a CV event. The ERG also noted that there was no evidence on the relative efficacy of evolocumab versus ezetimibe in the familial hypercholesterolaemia subgroup, or for evolocumab in combination with ezetimibe in any population, and there was little or no direct trial evidence for evolocumab in terms of health-related quality of life or apheresis. 

The submission of safety evidence was a non-systematic review of good quality RCTs, providing evidence for up to two years. There were no obvious safety concerns, with most AEs being balanced across evolocumab and comparator trial arms, and very small numbers of SAEs. However, the ERG noted that relatively higher 12-week AE rates were reported in patients who had HeFH or who had primary non-familial hypercholesterolaemia and were statin-intolerant. Similarly, these rates were also relatively higher for trials with a longer follow-up duration. This suggests that some patient subgroups might experience more frequent events and that all patients are at risk of AEs over time, though the rates are generally similar to comparators. The ERG noted also that the longer-term 

142 



<!-- page 762 -->

evidence presented was derived from some trials with populations who would not be eligible to receive evolocumab in clinical practice in the NHS (e.g. people who were not on maximum-tolerated doses of statins). More long-term data are therefore needed in relevant UK populations, although it is not clear whether ongoing trials will address this. 

Based on the company model, the probabilistic ICERs for evolocumab against ezetimibe are above £119,000 per QALY gained within the non-familial population and are approximately £49,000 within the HeFH population. However, the ERG has a number of concerns regarding the company’s implemented model; some of these represent major mathematical errors whilst others indicate the improper use of the available evidence. The key concerns identified by the ERG can be separated into four sets of issues: (a) the company’s general modelling approach; (b) the conceptual representation of the condition; (c) the model process and logic; and; (d) model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs. The ERG also expresses concerns regarding the conduct of the analysis for the HeFH population. These conceptual and structural problems are complex and intertwined, and the resolution of individual issues in isolation would not result in an appropriate or credible model. Rather, the ERG considers that the joint resolution of these problems would require a full “rethinking” of the model’s logic. Consequently, the ERG has serious doubts regarding the validity of the results presented within the CS and would advise considerable caution in their interpretation and use in informing decision-making. As such, the expected cost-effectiveness of evolocumab in the nonfamilial and HeFH populations is unclear. 

## **8.1 Implications for research** 

Future research should seek to address the following key areas of uncertainty: 

- The efficacy of evolocumab in reducing the risk of CVD in all populations (adults with familial and non-familial primary hypercholesterolaemia), especially in comparison with ezetimibe. 

- The efficacy of evolocumab in combination with ezetimibe compared with ezetimibe alone in all populations (adults with familial and non-familial primary hypercholesterolaemia). 

- The impact of evolocumab on HRQoL and apheresis in the short- and long-term.

## **Overview:** 

This addendum provides details regarding amendments to the economic model associated with the Evidence Review Group (ERG) clarification request dated 11[th] August 2015 and subsequent ERG report received 25[th] September 2015. 

Based on the amendments to the economic model, the cost effectiveness analyses have been updated for these populations (Appendix): 

- Patients without existing CVD 

- Patients with existing CVD 

- Patients with HeFH 

Notably, due to the challenges in interpretation of the threshold analyses for patients without existing CVD (ERG report page 131 to 132) and the very high levels of CVD risk previously estimated in order to demonstrate cost-effectiveness at willingness-to-pay thresholds of £20,000 and £30,000, these analyses have not been repeated. 

## **1. Model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs - REACH** 

## **Registry Equation** 

The ERG report (page 117) states, “ _the company…assumes that the risk for “next cardiovascular event” predicted by the REACH Registry equation includes only non-fatal events. This is incorrect and was confirmed through correspondence between the ERG and the author of the REACH Registry paper”_ . 

We thank the ERG for identifying this incorrect interpretation of the REACH Registry risk equation based on correspondence with the author. 

We have undertaken the following steps to ensure the correct application of the REACH Registry equation for “next cardiovascular event” in the economic model: 

- Distribution of CV events recalculated based on the original multinomial models so the predicted risk from REACH Registry “next cardiovascular event” is now split among fatal and non-fatal CV events, mirroring the approach used for the for Framingham equation. 

- The new distribution of CV events is highlighted in yellow in worksheet ‘Events Distribution (model)’. 

- Re-estimation of the calibration factors for non-familial populations (from CPRD) by comparing overall CV event rates (fatal and non-fatal) versus predictions from REACH Registry for “next cardiovascular event” (after conversion to rates), mirroring the approach for Framingham equation. The new calibration factors are highlighted in yellow in worksheet ‘Calibration’. 

- Re-estimation of the calibration factors was undertaken since the REACH Registry “next cardiovascular event” was assumed to account for non-fatal events only and was therefore calibrated against CPRD non-fatal events (see updated Appendix 11 - Amgen Study Estimation and calibration of CV event rates). The predicted risk was split using only non-fatal event proportions (adding up to 1) from CPRD. REACH Registry “cardiovascular death” was calibrated against fatal events, and the risk predicted was split using fatal event proportions from CPRD (adding up to 1). 

- The amendments are shown schematically in Figure 1.

## **2. Model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs – Negative transition probabilities** 

The ERG report (page 117) states, “ _Further, since the model estimates the risk of fatal and non-fatal CVD events separately and without constraint, this leads to mathematical inconsistencies when the risk of fatal and non-fatal CVD events is high. Consequently, when the sum of predicted probabilities for fatal and non-fatal CVD events exceeds 1, this leads to a situation whereby some of the transition probabilities and health state populations become negative”,_ and _“The ERG notes that whilst this is a structural problem, the company’s amendment treats this as a parametric issue. The ERG highlights that it should not be possible under any combination of model parameter inputs for transition probabilities or health state populations to be negative, even at the highest levels of predicted CV risk. Despite the company’s amendment to the model, negative probabilities are still possible when different input parameters are used, for example, when the cap for age is increased from 85 to 90 years, or when the adjustment factors for the HeFH population are increased to the upper CI reported within the CS”._ 

We appreciate that the previous amendment was deemed methodologically insufficient by the ERG.  Therefore we have undertaken the following alternative amendment to prevent the occurrence of negative transition probabilities in the economic model: 

- A correction for competing risks (non-CVD mortality versus CV events) has been included in such a way that only patients alive from other causes are at risk of CV events (all transition probabilities have been corrected by a factor representing the probability of the complementary event of non-CVD mortality in each cycle). The correction is performed in worksheet ‘Baseline Risks (model)’. 

- This is represented below: 

**==> picture [481 x 133] intentionally omitted <==**

**----- Start of picture text -----**<br>
p(non-CVD death)<br>Death other causes<br>CVD event<br>(1 - p(non-CVD death)) * p(CVD event)<br>No CVD event<br># = (1 - p(non-CVD death)) * (1 - p(CVD event))<br>**----- End of picture text -----**<br>


## Acute health states: 

For example, ‘No CVD’ to ‘ACS’, worksheet ‘Baseline Risks (model)’, cell C145. = (1-EXP(-'Calibrated Rates (model)'!C145))*'Events Distribution (model)'!E145*(1-'Rates & non-CVD Utilities'!AE145) 

Whereby: 

- Calibrated rate converted to a risk 

- ACS proportion conditional on no previous event (CPRD) 

- Adjustment for competing risks 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765] 




<!-- page 774 -->

## Combined health states: 

Combined health states follow these rules in each cycle to ensure non-negative probabilities regardless the level of risk: 

- If an acute CV event is included in the combined health state, the set of risks is that of the acute health state. 

- In the case of combined health states of post-acute health states only, the set of risks of the post-acute health state with a higher calibrated rate is considered. 

For example, ‘post-ACS + post-IS’ to ‘ACS’, worksheet ‘Baseline Risks (model)’, cell BA145 _._ =IF('Calibrated Rates (model)'!$AV145>'Calibrated Rates (model)'!$AW145,'Baseline Risks (model)'!AB145,'Baseline Risks (model)'!AG145) 

Whereby: 

- Compare the calibrated rates for patients with post-ACS and post-IS history 

- If post-ACS calibrated rate is higher, take post-ACS to ACS risk 

- If post-IS calibrated rates is higher, take post-IS to ACS risk 

As calibrated rates are an aggregate (any CV event), the same decision rule would apply to all transitions to any CV event from ‘post-ACS + post-stroke’ combined health state. 

The same logic applies to the maximum risks rule. For example, ‘ACS’ to ‘ACS’, worksheet ‘Baseline Risks (model)’, cell M145. 

=IF('Calibrated Rates (model)'!$AQ145>'Calibrated Rates (model)'!$AS145,'Baseline Risks (model)'!C145,(1-EXP(-'Calibrated Rates (model)'!M145))*'Events Distribution (model)'!AC145*(1-'Rates & non-CVD Utilities'!AE145)) 

## Whereby: 

- Compare the calibrated rates for patients with no event and ACS history 

- If no event calibrated rate is higher, take no event to ACS risk (this risk has been already applied the event distribution and adjustment of competing risk as per the example above) 

- If ACS calibrated rate is higher, take ACS to ACS rate converted to a risk and apply ACS proportion conditional on previous ACS (CPRD) and the adjustment for competing risks 

Previously, the maximum risk for the individual transitions was used in the economic model. Now, the full set of risks for the CV event with the highest calibrated rate is used instead. This amended approach ensures the sum of probabilities never exceeds 1. The economic model has also been tested for any negative probabilities at the very highest levels of risk. Trackers for negative probabilities have also been included in worksheets ‘Prob_Backbone’ to ‘Prob_3LEvo’, cell B222 for transparency.

## **3. Model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs – LDL-C treatment effects** 

The ERG report (pages 117 to 188) states, _“The company estimates the risk of CVD using baseline characteristics at entry into the LAPLACE-2/RUTHERFORD-2 trials and uses the LDL-C at baseline to represent the risk of CVD for people treated with statins. However, the model then applies the treatment effect (a relative reduction in LDL-C) for ezetimibe and evolocumab calculated from the treatment difference (statins versus ezetimibe or evolocumab) at the mean of weeks 10/12, rather than based on the change from baseline. The ERG believes there is a mismatch as the treatment effect used in the model does not match the baseline LDL-C level from which it is estimated. This leads to a larger treatment effect being used in the model (treatment difference of -71.8% at week 10/12 against statins vs. -64.33% from baseline in the LAPLACE-2 trial)”._ 

We aknowledge the ERG comments and have therefore amended the LDL-C treatment effects (Table 1): 

- Mean percentage change from baseline (instead of versus placebo) used for nonfamilial population based on LAPLACE-2 for evolocumab and ezetimibe 

- Mean percentage change from baseline used for HeFH based on RUTHERFORD-2 (instead of LAPLACE-2) for evolocumab 

- Mean percentage change from baseline from LAPLACE-2 (instead of versus placebo) used for HeFH for ezetimibe in the absence of evidence.

## _**1.5 Sensitivity analyses**_ 

## **Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

The probabilistic sensitivity analysis was run with 1,000 simulations. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis outputs are represented graphically by plotting incremental cost and effectiveness pairs on the cost-effectiveness plane and presenting the likelihood of evolocumab being the optimal strategy across different maximum willingness-to-pay thresholds. The results of the probabilistic sensitivity analysis depicted as scatter plots are presented in the figures below for patients with existing CVD and HeFH based on scenarios 1 and 2 (Figure 1 to Figure 4). The ellipses represent the 95% CI and the gradients represent £20,000 and £30,000 incremental cost per QALY gained on the scatterplots.

## **Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

Deterministic sensitivity analyses were performed by means of one-way sensitivity analyses, where one parameter was varied relative to its base case value. A summary of the results is presented below for patients with existing CVD and patients with HeFH for evolocumab and statin versus ezetimibe and statin. The additional scenarios are not presented as the results were not sensitive to the different treatment strategies covered in scenarios 2 to 4. All parameters where the incremental cost per QALY gained was sensitive by > 1% are presented in Tornado plots (Figure 9 to Figure 10). 

The Tornado plots that indicate the most sensitive parameters for cost-effectiveness of evolocumab versus ezetimibe were: 

- CV event rate ratio (HeFH alone) 

- CPRD ratio ratios (secondary prevention alone) 

- treatment duration 

- effect of LDL-C reduction on CV events 

- ezetimibe treatment effect 

- evolocumab treatment effect 

- ‘ECVD’ and ‘post-ACS’ health state utility multiplier.

## **Additional scenario analyses** 

The following scenario analyses were performed for patients without existing CVD, patients with existing CVD and patients with HeFH. 

**Treatment scenarios for evolocumab:** In the base case, it is assumed that evolocumab with be used either in combination with statin or alone in patients who are statin intolerant or contraindicated. In these scenarios the cost-effectiveness of evolocumab and ezetimibe versus ezetimibe alone (scenario 3), and evolocumab, statin and ezetimibe versus statin and ezetimibe (scenario 4) are assessed. 

**Treatment duration:** In the base case analysis, a lifetime treatment duration (to a maximum age of 100 years) is assumed. In these scenario analyses the treatment duration is shortened to 5, 10, and 20 years. 

**Discounting:** In the base case, discount rates of 3.5% were applied to both costs and health effects. Here the discount rates are changed to (1) 0% for both costs and health effects, and (2) 0% for costs and 6% for health effects. 

**Risk capping at age 75 years:** As CVD patients age, the risk of CV events increases. In this scenario it is assumed that the risk of CV events does not increase any more after patients have reached the age of 75 years (versus 85 years assumed in the base case). 

**CV cost data based on NICE CG181:** In the base case CV, costs were based on the CPRD study. In this scenario the costs for CV events as presented in NICE CG181 are used. 

**Utilities based on TTO study:** In the base case, utilities as presented in NICE CG181 were used. In this scenario analysis, utilities from the TTO study are used. This analysis uses the absolute utility modelling approach, not the multiplicative approach applied in the base case. 

**Nursing time evolocumab self-administration training:** In the base case it is assumed that 1 hour of nurse time will be needed for evolocumab self-administration training. As this is an assumption, the impact of using half and double the time is investigated.

## **1 Introduction** 

The 2009 Pharmaceutical Price Regulation Scheme (PPRS) (www.dh.gov.uk/en/Healthcare/Medicinespharmacyandindustry/Pharmaceutic alpriceregulationscheme/2009PPRS) is a non-contractual scheme between the Department of Health and the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry. The purpose of the 2009 PPRS is to ensure that safe and costeffective medicines are available on reasonable terms to the NHS in England and Wales. One of the features of the 2009 PPRS is to improve patients’ access to medicines at prices that better reflect their value through patient access schemes. 

Patient access schemes are arrangements which may be used on an exceptional basis for the acquisition of medicines for the NHS in England and Wales. Patient access schemes propose either a discount or rebate that may be linked to the number, type or response of patients, or a change in the list price of a medicine linked to the collection of new evidence (outcomes). These schemes help to improve the cost effectiveness of a medicine and therefore allow the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to recommend treatments which it would otherwise not have found to be cost effective. More information on the framework for patient access schemes is provided in the 2009 PPRS 

(www.dh.gov.uk/en/Healthcare/Medicinespharmacyandindustry/Pharmaceutic alpriceregulationscheme/2009PPRS. 

Patient access schemes are proposed by a pharmaceutical company and agreed with the Department of Health, with input from the Patient Access Schemes Liaison Unit (PASLU) within the Centre for Health Technology Evaluation at NICE. 

Patient access scheme submission template – October 2009

## **2 Instructions for manufacturers and sponsors** 

This document is the patient access scheme submission template for technology appraisals. If manufacturers and sponsors want the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) to consider a patient access scheme as part of a technology appraisal, they should use this template. NICE can only consider a patient access scheme after formal referral from the Department of Health. 

The template contains the information NICE requires to assess the impact of a patient access scheme on the clinical and cost effectiveness of a technology, in the context of a technology appraisal, and explains the way in which background information (evidence) should be presented. If you are unable to follow this format, you must state your reasons clearly. You should insert ‘N/A’ against sections that you do not consider relevant, and give a reason for this response. 

Please refer to the following documents when completing the template: 

- ‘Guide to the methods of technology appraisal’ - - - - - - 

- (http://publications.nice.org.uk/guide to the methods of technology - - 

- appraisal 2013 pmg9) 

- ‘Specification for manufacturer/sponsor submission of evidence’ (http://www.nice.org.uk/aboutnice/howwework/devnicetech/singletechnolog yappraisalsubmissiontemplates.jsp) and 

- Pharmaceutical Price Regulation Scheme 2009 

(www.dh.gov.uk/en/Healthcare/Medicinespharmacyandindustry/Pharmaceu ticalpriceregulationscheme/2009PPRS). 

For further details on the technology appraisal process, please see NICE’s ‘Guide to the single technology appraisal (STA) process’ and ‘Guide to the multiple technology appraisal (MTA) process’ 

(http://www.nice.org.uk/aboutnice/howwework/devnicetech/technologyapprais alprocessguides/technology_appraisal_process_guides.jsp). The 

Patient access scheme submission template – October 2009 




<!-- page 809 -->

‘Specification for manufacturer/sponsor submission of evidence’ provides details on disclosure of information and equality issues. 

Make the submission as brief and informative as possible. Only mark information as confidential when absolutely necessary. Sufficient information must be publicly available for stakeholders to comment on the full content of the technology appraisal, including details of the proposed patient access scheme. Send submissions electronically to NICE in Word or a compatible format, not as a PDF file. 

Appendices may be used to include additional information that is considered relevant to the submission. Do not include information in the appendices that has been requested in the template. Appendices should be clearly referenced in the main submission. 

When making a patient access scheme submission, include: 

- an updated version of the checklist of confidential information, if necessary 

- an economic model with the patient access scheme incorporated, in accordance with the ‘Guide to the methods of technology appraisal’ - - - - - - 

- (http://publications.nice.org.uk/guide to the methods of technology - - 

- appraisal 2013 pmg9). 

If you are submitting the patient access scheme at the end of the appraisal process, you should update the economic model to reflect the assumptions that the Appraisal Committee considered to be most plausible. No other changes should be made to the model.

## **3 Details of the patient access scheme** 

- _3.1 Please give the name of the technology and the disease area to which the patient access scheme applies._ 

Technology:  Evolocumab (brand name: Repatha) 

Disease area: Hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia 

- _3.2 Please outline the rationale for developing the patient access scheme._ 

The patient access scheme (simple scheme) has been developed in order to allow demonstration of cost-effectiveness for the technology versus the comparator in the relevant populations in accordance with the Institute’s reference case. 

- _3.3 Please describe the type of patient access scheme, as defined by the PPRS._ 

The patient access scheme is a simple scheme (confidential discount).

## **Sensitivity analyses** 

- _4.9 Please present deterministic sensitivity analysis results as_ 

   - _described for the main manufacturer/sponsor submission of evidence for the technology appraisal. Consider using tornado diagrams._ 

## **Deterministic sensitivity analysis** 

Deterministic sensitivity analyses were performed by means of one-way sensitivity analyses, where one parameter was varied relative to its base case value. The method adopted and the parameters tested are described in the evidence submission (Section 5.6). A summary of the results is presented below for patients with existing CVD and patients with HeFH for evolocumab and statin versus ezetimibe and statin (scenario 1). The additional scenarios are not presented as the results were not sensitive to the different treatment strategies covered in scenarios 2 to 4. All parameters where the incremental cost per QALY gained was sensitive by > 1% are presented in Tornado plots (Figure 1 to Figure 2). 

The Tornado plots indicate that the most sensitive parameters for cost-effectiveness of evolocumab versus ezetimibe were in patients with existing CVD are: 

- effect of LDL-C lowering on CHD death and IS death 

- ezetimibe treatment effect 

- CPRD ratio ratios 

- effect of LDL-C reduction on CV events 

- treatment duration. 

The Tornado plots indicate that the most sensitive parameters for cost-effectiveness of evolocumab versus ezetimibe were in patients with HeFH are: 

- effect of LDL-C lowering on CHD death 

- CVD event rate ratio (HeFH alone) 

- effect of LDL-C reduction on CV events 

- ezetimibe treatment effect 

- treatment duration 

- evolocumab treatment effect.

## **Evolocumab for treating primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed dyslipidaemia: A Single Technology Appraisal** 

**Critique of company’s addendum 2 and accompanying PAS application** 

Mr Rachid Rafia, Research Fellow, ScHARR, University of Sheffield, Regent Court, 30 Regent Street, Sheffield, S1 4DA 

Dr Paul Tappenden, Reader in Health Economic Modelling, ScHARR, University of Sheffield, Regent Court, 30 Regent Street, Sheffield, S1 4DA 

Dr Christopher Carroll, Reader in Health Technology Assessment, ScHARR, University of Sheffield, Regent Court, 30 Regent Street, Sheffield, S1 4DA 

8[th] October 2015 



<!-- page 864 -->

## **1. Introduction** 

In response to the critique presented in the Evidence Review Group (ERG) report,[1] the company submitted a further amended health economic model at the fact check stage which addresses some of the concerns raised by the ERG. The changes made by the company and their impact upon the economic analyses using the list price for evolocumab are documented within the company’s addendum 2.[2] The impact of the model amendments together with the Patient Access Scheme (PAS) for evolocumab are presented in the company’s PAS submission.[3] The key changes made by the company relate to: 

- (i) The use of the REACH Registry risk equations[4] within the health economic model (and reestimation of calibration factors in the CPRD/HES datasets[5] ). 

- (ii) The addition of constraints which are intended to prevent the model from generating negative transition probabilities. 

- (iii) The use of treatment effects calculated from baseline (instead of the treatment differences compared with statins at the mean of week 10/12) and amendments to the treatment effect estimate used for the HeFH population. 

- (iv) The inclusion of a PAS for evolocumab. 

This document provides a brief summary and critique of the changes made by the company within their model. Owing to time constraints, the ERG advises caution in that this critique is based on the limited information provided by the company within addendum 2 and only a brief examination of the company’s revised model. 

## **2. ERG critique of amendments in company’s addendum 2** 

## _2.1 Model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs - REACH registry equations_ 

The company appears to have corrected the model implementation error whereby the risk equation for the next cardiovascular (CV) event reported by Wilson _et al_[4] was interpreted as the risk of the next non-fatal CV event, thereby leading to double counting of fatal CV events in the company’s original submitted model. The company’s amended model now uses only the risk equation for “next cardiovascular event” from the REACH Registry.[4] 

Briefly, this amendment has been implemented as follows. The company’s model first estimates the risk (probability) of any CVD event using the REACH equation for next CV event using baseline patient characteristics for the subset of patients within the LAPLACE-2 trial with baseline LDLC>2.5mmol/L (non-familial population) and the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population from the RUTHERFORD-2 trial (HeFH population). The aggregate risks (probability) are then transformed into aggregate rates and further transformed into age-specific rates for any CV event (according to history of CV events). The resulting CV event rates are then adjusted by a series of calibration factors 



<!-- page 865 -->

estimated from the CPRD/HES data, and transformed back into probabilities which are then separated into fatal (coronary heart disease [CHD] death and ischaemic stroke [IS] death) and non-fatal events (established CVD [ECVD], acute coronary syndromes [ACS], myocardial infarction [MI] and heart failure [HF]). 

The ERG is generally satisfied with the company’s amendment. The ERG notes however that the description provided in the company’s addendum 2 is sometimes misleading and a number of changes to the model structure have been made (notably the addition of a further worksheet named “Calibrated Rates (model)” in the model). Whilst not justified by the company, the ERG notes that the company’s amended model uses the risk for post-event states for patients with ECVD rather than the risk associated with the acute event. In the absence of any justification of this within the company’s addendum 2, the ERG is unclear whether this assumption was made intentionally or whether this is a programming error. 

The ERG reiterates that whilst the company has attempted to resolve this issue within their existing model structure, the overall approach to using calibrated risk equations is convoluted and circular; the ERG would have preferred a model which calculates transition probabilities based on CV events directly observed within the CPRD/HES datasets. This would reduce the number of assumptions and adjustments made by the company. The impact of this alternative approach on the ICER for evolocumab is unclear. 

_2.2 Model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs – negative transition probabilities_ In response to concerns raised within the ERG report[1] about the presence of negative transition probabilities, the company has added a number of constraints to prevent the model from generating negative values. Some of these constraints appear somewhat arbitrary and the logic underpinning them is difficult to follow from the information provided in the company’s addendum 2. Within addendum 2, the company provides only a limited description of the constraints added to the amended model. Following scrutiny of the model, the ERG notes the following changes: 

- The adjustment of the probabilities of CV events for all individual event health states (acute and post-acute) for the proportion of patients that die from other causes. The ERG is generally satisfied with this amendment. 

- The addition of constraints for all individual event health states (acute and post-acute), such that the estimated risk of an event cannot be greater than the risk of the first CV event in patients without a history of CVD. The ERG believes that these constraints are inappropriate and arbitrary as the model attempts to compare two different risks: (a) the event risk in patients with a history of CVD and (b) the event risk in patients without a history of CVD. This is not described in addendum 2. 



<!-- page 866 -->

- For the composite health states which include one acute event (i.e. whereby patients have experienced an acute event in the previous model cycle), the risk of CV events associated with the previous acute event is used to represent the future risk of the next CV event. The ERG notes that this is different to the approach used in the company’s original model, whereby the highest risk was used. The company’s addendum 2 states that this approach was used to prevent the sum of probabilities from exceeding 1.0. The ERG considers these adjustments to be arbitrary and notes that the use of composite health states adds complexity to the model and relies on assumptions that are not informed by evidence. 

- For the composite health states which do not include an acute event, the highest probability is used. The approach has been slightly amended compared with the original submitted model. 

The ERG notes that under the base case assumptions, the transition probabilities remain positive in all three main populations included within the company’s model. However, if the user sets the HeFH calibration factors to very high (clinically implausible) values e.g. 1,000, then several transition probabilities in the “Prob_Backbone” (statins/no treatment) worksheet become negative. Correspondence from the company indicates that a possible reason for the occurrence of these negative values is due to software precision limitations within Microsoft Excel. Whilst the ERG cannot verify this without a full check of the amended model, the ERG believes the company’s explanation to be reasonable. 

_2.3 Model implementation and misspecification of evidence inputs – LDL-C treatment effects_ In response to comments made within the ERG report (see ERG report, Section 5.3, point 7), the company has amended the treatment effect estimates used in the model. The key changes are as follows: 

- For the non-familial population (statin tolerant), use of the treatment effect from the LAPLACE-2 trial for evolocumab and ezetimibe from baseline (rather than the treatment difference compared with statins at the mean of weeks 10/12). 

- For the HeFH population (statin tolerant), use of the treatment effect from the RUTHERFORD-2 trial for evolocumab and from the LAPLACE-2 trial for ezetimibe (rather than using the treatment effect from the LAPLACE-2 trial for both arms). 

For patients who are unable to take statins, no change has been made and the treatment effect from the GAUSS-2 trial is used. 

Overall, the ERG is satisfied with these amendments. 



<!-- page 867 -->

## _2.4 Additional amendments to the economic model_ 

## _2.4.1 Implementation of the PAS_ 

The PAS appears to have been implemented correctly within the company’s new model. This is applied as a simple price discount per pack of evolocumab. The ERG was able to replicate the summary results presented in Table 58 of the company’s PAS submission using the company’s new model. The ERG was also able to generate similar probabilistic results to those presented within the PAS submission.[3] 

## _2.4.2 Inclusion of statin indicator variable_ 

As suggested within the ERG report,[1] the company’s amended model includes a statin indicator variable for the REACH registry equations to account for differential CV event risk in patients who are or are not able to take statins. However, as per the company’s original analyses, this variable is set to “yes” for all analyses presented using the corrected model. Consequently, this amendment has no impact on the company’s new analyses. The ERG considers that this variable should have been set to “no” for all analyses in which patients are unable to take statins. 

## **3. Summary of results presented within the company’s PAS submission** 

## _3.1 Base case cost-effectiveness results (deterministic)_ 

Table 1 summarises the deterministic cost-effectiveness results presented within the company’s addendum 2. For the sake of brevity, and in line with the final NICE scope, results are presented only for the comparison of evolocumab (with or without statins) versus ezetimibe (with or without statins). The ERG notes that whilst the inclusion of the PAS reduces the incremental costs of evolocumab, the amendments to the company’s model described above result in a noticeable reduction in the incremental estimates of QALYs gained for evolocumab in most of the company’s analyses. All results presented here are based on the PAS submission[3] and re-analyses of the company’s amended model including the PAS price. 

## _Non-familial primary prevention population (analyses A and B)_ 

As discussed in the ERG report,[1] during the clarification stage of the appraisal, the ERG identified a serious programming error within the company’s model whereby it was possible for many of the transition probabilities, and hence the health state populations in the Markov trace, to be negative. Consequently, NICE submitted a request to the company to rectify the error. In response, the company submitted an amended model and an addendum detailing revised results produced using this amended model (company’s addendum 1).[6] Within addendum 1, the company’s threshold analyses for evolocumab within the non-familial primary prevention population were considered to be “invalid” and re-analyses within this population using the first corrected model were not presented. The company’s addendum 2 and PAS submission do not include any further threshold analyses in the non- 



<!-- page 868 -->

familial primary prevention population. Instead however, the PAS submission, which is based on the second amended version of the model, presents a cohort-based analysis for this population. It should be noted that the company’s addendum 2 and PAS submission do not present probabilistic sensitivity analyses for the primary prevention population, hence results presented here are based on re-analyses undertaken by the ERG. All results are presented separately for those patients who are able to take statins (denoted ST) and for those patients in whom statins are contraindicated or not tolerated (denoted SI). 

Within the non-familial primary prevention ST population (analysis A), the company’s base case analysis suggests that evolocumab plus statins is expected to produce an additional 0.32 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe plus statins; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £74,331 per QALY gained. The probabilistic ICER is higher at £76,446 per QALY gained. The probability that evolocumab produces more net benefit than ezetimibe is approximately zero at a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained. Within the non-familial primary prevention SI population (analysis B), the company’s base case analysis suggests that evolocumab monotherapy produces an additional 0.30 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe monotherapy; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £78,879 per QALY gained. The probabilistic ICER is higher at £80,688 per QALY gained. The probability that evolocumab produces more net benefit than ezetimibe is approximately zero at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained. 

_Non-familial secondary prevention population (analyses C and D)_ 

Within the non-familial secondary prevention ST population (analysis C), the company’s base case analysis suggests that evolocumab plus statins is expected to produce an additional 0.39 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe plus statins; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £46,005 per QALY gained. The probabilistic ICER is higher at £47,079 per QALY gained. The probability that evolocumab produces more net benefit than ezetimibe is approximately zero at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained. Within the non-familial secondary prevention SI population (analysis D), the company’s base case analysis suggests that evolocumab monotherapy produces an additional 0.37 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe monotherapy; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £49,278 per QALY gained. The probabilistic ICER is higher at £50,321 per QALY gained. The probability that evolocumab produces more net benefit than ezetimibe is approximately zero at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained. 

## _HeFH primary/secondary prevention population (analyses G and H)_ 

Within the HeFH primary/secondary prevention ST population (analysis G), the company’s base case analysis suggests that evolocumab plus statins is expected to produce an additional 0.86 QALYs at an 



<!-- page 869 -->

additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe plus statins; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £22,902 per QALY gained. The probabilistic ICER is higher at £23,504 per QALY gained. The probability that evolocumab produces more net benefit than ezetimibe is approximately 0.08 at a WTP threshold of £20,000 per QALY gained, and approximately 0.96 at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained. Within the HeFH primary/secondary prevention SI population (analysis H), evolocumab monotherapy is expected to produce an additional 0.82 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* as compared against ezetimibe monotherapy; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £23,927 per QALY gained. The probabilistic ICER is higher at £24,604 per QALY gained. The probability that evolocumab produces more net benefit than ezetimibe is approximately 0.05 at a WTP threshold of £20,000 per QALY gained, and approximately 0.91 at a WTP threshold of £30,000 per QALY gained.

_3.2 Scenario analysis results – evolocumab in combination with ezetimibe_ 

Table 2 summarises the results of the company’s scenario analyses in which evolocumab is given in combination with ezetimibe (with/without concomitant statins). Probabilistic analyses were not presented for these populations and have not been repeated by the ERG. 

## _Non-familial secondary prevention population (analyses E and F)_ 

Within the non-familial secondary prevention SI population (analysis E), the company’s scenario analysis suggests that evolocumab plus ezetimibe is expected to produce an additional 0.42 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £52,811 per QALY gained. Within the ST population (analysis F), evolocumab plus ezetimibe plus statins is expected to produce an additional 0.44 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe plus statins; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £50,880 per QALY gained. 

## _HeFH primary/secondary prevention population (analyses I and J)_ 

For the HeFH primary/secondary prevention SI population (analysis I), the company’s scenario analysis suggests that evolocumab plus ezetimibe is expected to produce an additional 0.96 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe monotherapy; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £25,609 per QALY gained. Within the ST population (analysis J), evolocumab plus ezetimibe plus statins is expected to produce an additional 1.00 QALYs at an additional cost of ******* compared with ezetimibe plus statins; the resulting ICER is estimated to be £24,826 per QALY gained. 

## _3.3 Subgroup analyses_ 

The company’s PAS submission also includes the results of a number of subgroup analyses across individual and combinations of CV risk factors. These are reported on pages 28-32 of the PAS submission[3] and are not reproduced here. In some subgroups, the ICER for evolocumab is estimated to be below £30,000 per QALY gained. As noted in the ERG report,[1] these analyses employ arbitrary manipulations of the individual patient trial data which will ultimately produce biased risk estimates. The ERG considers that it would have been more appropriate to estimate baseline CVD risk from the CPRD/HES dataset and to subsequently adjust these using relative risks from the published literature to reflect these additional risk factors. Consequently, the ERG would advise caution in the interpretation of all of these analyses.

## **4. Discussion and additional ERG exploratory analyses** 

Overall, the ERG is generally satisfied with some of the changes made by the company, although some concern remains regarding the apparently arbitrary logic underlying some of the constraints used in the company’s amended model. The ERG notes that within their new model, the company have addressed only a selected set of issues raised within the ERG’s critique of the company’s original model (see ERG report,[1] Table 46, pages 137-138). Whilst the ERG recognises that some of the concerns identified by the ERG are matters of subjective opinion rather than unequivocal errors, the ERG would advise some caution in the interpretation of the company’s results due to: (a) the circular approach used by the company using a calibrated risk predictions instead of using directly observed CV events; (b) the selected populations used in the model; (c) the likely overestimation of the risk of CV events in the HeFH population (i.e. the calibration factor of 7.1 based on Benn _et al_ (d) uncertainty regarding the relationship between LDL-C reduction and reductions in CV events, and; (e) the use of a model structure which includes multiple composite event states which are populated using many assumptions and little evidence. 

The ERG notes that the most favourable ICERs for evolocumab reported within the company’s PAS submission are those for the HeFH population (HeFH ST ICER=£22,902 per QALY gained; HeFH SI ICER=£23,927 per QALY gained, see Table 1). The calibration rate of 7.1 is a key driver of the costeffectiveness of evolocumab in this population. It is noteworthy that within the company’s model, the calibration factor of 7.1 is applied to the modified ITT population recruited into the RUTHERFORD2 trial; these patients are already, by definition, at an increased risk due to their prior diagnosis of HeFH. The ERG considers that this calibration factor is likely to be an overestimate and notes that the use of a lower calibration factor would produce less favourable ICERs for evolocumab. 

In order to explore the extent of this potential bias, the ERG identified a long-term cohort study and Cox regression analysis assessing the efficacy of statins in patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH, without prevalent CHD) reported by Versmissen _et al._[7] Figure 1 shows the predicted CVD event-free survival curve for the HeFH primary prevention ST population with a starting age of 49 years, based on the amended company’s  model. According to the company’s model predictions, approximately 50% of HeFH patients on statins would experience an event (which may include death from other causes) by the age of 57-58 years (i.e. after 8 to 9 years). For comparison, Figure 2 shows the risk of CHD within the Versmissen _et al_ cohort study _._[7] The Kaplan-Meier curve indicates that the proportion of patients experiencing a CHD event within the same time interval is approximately 10%. Versmissen _et al_ report that the risk of MI in statin-treated patients with FH was not significantly greater than that in an age-matched sample from the general population (hazard ratio=1.44, 95% confidence interval 0.80 to 2.60, _p_ =0.23). Although the Versmissen _et al_ study has potential limitations, in particular its use of an observational design and associated potential for 



<!-- page 874 -->

confounding and the use of CHD rather than CVD as an outcome, this indicates that the company’s calibration factor of 7.1 may inflate the risk of CV events and death within the HeFH population within the model.

<!-- page 875 -->

As previously highlighted within the ERG report, the UK study by Neil _et al_[8] reported a lower standardised mortality ratio (SMR) for CHD in patients with HeFH treated with statins. The SMR for CHD deaths was 1.03 for primary prevention, and 3.88 for secondary prevention in people between 20 and 79 years of age. Within the Neil study, the SMR for all-cause mortality for the period 19922006 was not statistically significant (SMR=0.94, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.05, _p_ =0.31). A recent Norwegian study has also been published based on registry data from 4,688 male and female individuals from the Unit for Cardiac and Cardiovascular Genetics (UCCG) Registry with verified molecular genetic diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia linked to the Norwegian Cause of Death Registry.[9] Within this study, Mundal _et al_ reported that compared with the Norwegian population, CVD mortality was significantly higher in the UCCG Registry in all age groups younger than 70 years (SMR=2.29, 95% CI 1.65 to 3.19 in men and women combined; SMR=2.00, 95% CI 1.32 to 3.04 in men; SMR=3.03, 95% CI 1.76 to 5.21 in women). The SMR for CVD mortality across all ages (including people over the age of 70 years) was 1.56 (1.41 in males and 1.75 in females). This study also reported a nonsignificant SMR for all-cause mortality (SMR=0.87, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.05, _p_ -value not reported). In summary, these studies indicate that there may be a difference in the rate of CVD/CHD mortality for patients with HeFH (although the company’s model appears to overestimate this difference). However, no significant difference has been reported for all-cause mortality. 

Figure 3 compares the modelled survival for the HeFH population from the company’s model to the expected survival for the UK general population using life tables for a 51 year old cohort (corresponding to the starting age in the model). The ERG notes that the risk of all-cause mortality for the HeFH population predicted by the company’s model is considerably greater (approximately 3 times) than the risk of mortality expected within the UK general population. As noted above, this is not in line with the estimates reported by Neil _et al_[8] and Mundal _et al_ .[9]

Whilst there is uncertainty surrounding the rate of CV events in the HeFH population relative to that in the non-familial population, it is likely that the ICERs for evolocumab in the HeFH population are higher than those presented within the company’s PAS submission. Figures 4 and 5 present exploratory analyses undertaken by the ERG using the company’s model to demonstrate the impact of using alternative HeFH calibration factors on the ICERs for evolocumab versus ezetimibe in patients who are able to take statins (ST) and those who are unable to take statins (SI). Table 3 presents a threshold analysis to determine the minimum HeFH calibration factor required in order for the ICER for evolocumab versus ezetimibe to be below £30,000 per QALY gained. These analyses each indicate that the ICER for evolocumab versus ezetimibe increases considerably as the assumed HeFH calibration factor decreases. The threshold analysis results suggest that the calibration factor must be greater than 4.5 to 5.6 in order for the ICER for evolocumab versus ezetimibe to be below £30,000 per QALY gained. As noted above, the calibration factor is applied to an already high-risk population (high cholesterol) and therefore the minimum calibration factor required for evolocumab to achieve an ICER which is below £30,000 per QALY gained compared with the risk from the general population would be considerably higher.

## _(i) Estimation of transition probabilities for people prior to receiving evolocumab and/or ezetimibe_ 

The steps used by the company to estimate transition probabilities in the absence of evolocumab and/or ezetimibe (referred to as “population CV event rates” in the CS) are described in Figure 5. 

**Figure 5: Step-wise sequence of estimating event-specific transition probabilities from patientlevel characteristics (reproduced from CS,[13] Figure 5-4 page 182)** 

**==> picture [469 x 166] intentionally omitted <==**

_CV - cardiovascular_ 

Published risk equations[53,54] are applied to individual patient data (IPD) from the subgroup of patients enrolled in the LAPLACE-2 trial[23] who had a baseline LDL-C>2.5mmol/L and from the modified ITT population of the RUTHERFORD-2 trial[21] to estimate the average aggregate risk of the next CVD event for males and females separately. The Framingham equations for males and females[53] are used to estimate the risk of a first CVD event in people who do not have a history of CVD. The REduction of Atherothrombosis for Continued Health (REACH) Registry equations[54] are used to predict the risk of experiencing a fatal or any CVD event (assumed incorrectly to be non-fatal by the company) in people who have a history of CVD. The company assumes (incorrectly) that the risk predicted for “cardiovascular death” and “next cardiovascular event” from the REACH equations are independent of each other and can be added (effectively producing a total CVD risk ~~). It should also be noted that the predicted risks from both the Framingham and REACH equations are actually probabilities which~~ 

~~are bounded between 0 to 1, but are not treated as such within the company’s model; these are instead~~ 

68 



<!-- page 881 -->

~~assumed to be “event rates” (see Figure 5, box 2 “patient-level CV event rate”). This error in logic is discussed in more detail in Section 5.3.~~ 

The calculated average aggregate risks of CVD events (10-year risk from Framingham[53] and 20month risk from REACH[54] ) are then transformed into annualised rates; these are calculated separately for males and females (using a sex-specific equation from Framingham and a covariate for sex within the REACH equation). Limited details are provided within the CS[13] regarding this step in the process. 

From the company’s model, the age coefficients (for males and females separately) from the risk equations are used to obtain annual age- and sex-specific rates under the assumption that the event rate follows an exponential distribution such that the sum of the CVD event risks is equal to the average aggregate 10-year risk of CVD using the following formula: 

**==> picture [411 x 20] intentionally omitted <==**

## _Where:_ 

_risk_ ( _t_ ) _=annual risk at a given age ∂=risk prediction by risk equation φ=age coefficient in the risk equation age_ ( _t_ ) _=current age_ 

_ρ=mean age_ 

The annual age-specific risks obtained for males and females are then averaged to obtain an average annual age-specific risk; these are capped at a maximum age of 86 years (i.e. the risk is assumed to remain constant after age 85 years) and are subsequently multiplied by either: (a) state-specific calibration factors to reflect the performance of the risk equations in the UK for the non-familial primary hypercholesterolaemia populations (based on the LAPLACE-2 trial[23] ), or (b) an overall calibration factor to reflect the differences in the risk of CVD events between HeFH and non-HeFH patients (HeFH analyses only). Following this process, the company transform the resulting risks onto the probability scale using the following formula: 

_probability =  1-exp (- rate) [ii]_ 

The average aggregate annual age-specific probabilities of CVD events are then apportioned according to specific CVD events based on multinomial logistic regression models (see Section 5.2.2). The average aggregate risks for first CVD events derived from the Framingham equations[53] after calibration are apportioned into ECVD, ACS, IS, HF, CHD death and stroke death events. The risks for subsequent CVD events derived from the REACH Registry equations[54] after calibration are 

69 



<!-- page 882 -->

Section 5.2.2). The ERG notes that based on information provided within the CS[13] and during the clarification process,[35] the baseline risk of experiencing CV events could have been estimated directly from the company’s CPRD and HES analysis, and that the use of the Framingham and REACH equations is not necessary as it does not appear to provide additional information compared with using the CPRD and HES data. In effect, the company’s approach involves estimating CV risk using equations then adjusting these to reflect real-world CPRD/HES data rather than using the CPRD/HES data directly. The ERG sought clarification from the company regarding this matter (see clarification response,[35] question B33). The company’s response stated that: 

“…t _he economic model could indeed have directly used the CPRD study event rates to model an overall high-risk population as per the study cohort definitions. However, this approach would not have permitted us to assess specific high-risk populations such as those with existing CVD with 1 or 2 additional risk factors who remain at the highest residual risk_ .” 

The ERG considers the company’s response to be unsatisfactory because: (a) the analyses in individuals with additional risk factors (AF and 2/3 vascular beds) are presented only within the company’s subgroup analyses and do not reflect the main population specified in the NICE scope,[4] and; (b) the company’s analysis in patients with existing CVD with one or two additional risk factors employs arbitrary manipulations of the IPD which will ultimately produce biased risk estimates. The ERG considers that it would have been more appropriate to estimate baseline CVD risk from the CPRD/HES data and to subsequently adjust these using relative risks from the published literature to reflect these additional risk factors. It is also noteworthy that the company’s process for estimating CVD risk in all populations requires several other assumptions (e.g. removing the effect of age and sex), the validity of which are unclear.

## **Documentation required:** 

Please find information with regards to the request for additional documentation received on 16[th] October 2015 for the proposed Patient Access Scheme (PAS) and potential GP prescribing. 

- A sensitivity analysis which varies 1) the proportion of patients who would transition from secondary care to primary care and 2) time spent in secondary care before patients move to primary care. These sensitivity analyses should take into account that the PAS price will only apply to patients who are prescribed evolocumab through secondary care. The sensitivity analyses should be undertaken for each of the 3 populations in the model (i.e. patients with primary non-familial hypercholesterolaemia without existing CVD, patients with primary non-familial hypercholesterolaemia with existing CVD and patients with HeFH (with or without existing CVD). Please also provide the rationale for the value of the inputs used. 

- Amgen’s commitment to providing the acquisition price to the GP prescribing setting for evolocumab in future, including the example of what Amgen have done for denosumab. 

## **1. Sensitivity analysis for prescribing of evolocumab in primary care** 

We have conducted additional sensitivity analyses whereby we have varied the proportion and time of patients who would transition from secondary care to primary care.  We have used the PAS price for secondary care and NHS list price in primary care as per the request for additional documentation. 

Notably, we believe prescribing through FP10 prescriptions will only occur with a primary care rebate in operation (Section 2). In the absence of this, we agree patients routine lipid management could transition to primary care; however, prescribing and fulfilment of evolocumab would still remain in secondary care since the technology will only be deemed cost-effective by local NHS commissioners alongside a PAS (if recommended).  This was our experience for denosumab; hence the establishment of a primary care rebate model to facilitate transition of care between secondary and primary care. 

The incremental cost-effectiveness results of the sensitivity analyses are presented in Table 1 to Table 3 for evolocumab versus ezetimibe (statin tolerant population).  The results for patients with statin intolerance have not been presented given the general consistency.

   - Evolocumab prescribing setting (secondary or secondary/primary) 

   - Years to transition to primary care

## **2. Patient Access Scheme and confidential commercial discount** 

We wish to confirm our intention to provide evolocumab to the NHS at the same acquisition cost regardless of the care setting (secondary or primary care). As noted, savings associated with lower acquisition costs for medicines with simple PAS compared to list price cannot be realised by the NHS when prescribed through FP10 prescriptions due to the current financial flows. 

We have experience with regards implementation of parallel simple PAS (secondary care) and an equivalent confidential commercial discount (primary care) for an existing medicine that has been recommended through a NICE Technology Appraisal (NICE TA265: Denosumab for the prevention of skeletal-related events in adults with bone metastases from solid tumours). Denosumab was recommended in October 2012 in conjunction with a simple PAS. Whilst the majority of patients with bone metastases are managed in secondary care, primary care prescribing through FP10 prescriptions has occurred in some areas based on localised patient pathways and service re-design opportunities with this medicine. Similarly to evolocumab, we are committed to providing denosumab to the NHS at the same acquisition cost regardless of the care setting (secondary or primary care).   As such, this has been referred to as a confidential commercial discount (financially considered as a primary care rebate) since the PAS was only approved in the context of secondary care. 

To enable Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) to realise the lower acquisition cost, we have developed a primary care rebate process which has been reviewed and approved by PrescQIPP Governance Review Board (further information available at: http://www.prescqipp.info/projects/pharmaceutical-industry-scheme-governance-reviewboard).  CCGs and Amgen follow the process outlined below.  This has been in operation with approximately 10 CCGs over the last two years. 

- CCG representative signs a single contract agreement with Amgen for primary care rebate for all supplies of denosumab. 

- Denosumab is prescribed on a FP10 prescription and dispensed by a community pharmacy at list price. 

- List price acquisition cost is paid by relevant CCG based on patient’s registered GP. 

- CCG pharmacist emails ePACT (NHS Business Services Authority) prescribing data for denosumab to Amgen every three months. 

- Amgen issue a single quarterly rebate to each CCG to ensure that the same net acquisition cost for denosumab as per the approved simple PAS. 

We acknowledge the feedback that since routine lipid management is an area of standard GP practice, there may be a potential transition of patients from secondary to primary care after 2 to 3 years. We would plan to follow the same process if evolocumab prescribing was to transition to primary care in the future for some patients. The primary care rebate model was designed in collaboration with the NHS to ensure minimal administrative burden for NHS staff.  Therefore, CCG representatives (e.g. pharmacist) are only required to complete a single contract agreement at the outset and then provide routinely available ePACT data via email to ensure realisation of the equivalent simple PAS price in primary care. The primary care rebate model has been noted for its ease of administration. 

Evolocumab for primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidaemia [ID765]
